docs.title: pinnrl
docs.text:
pinnrl is a Python package for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) on forward and inverse problems, with a training step compiled per equation. It measures how far an estimate can be trusted and ships the classical method for each problem, so every result has a baseline.

\[ u_\theta(x, t) \approx u(x, t), \qquad \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{residual}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{boundary}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{initial}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}} \]
  • PINN: a network \(u_\theta\) trained to satisfy a differential equation. Unknown parameters of the equation can be trained with its weights \(\theta\).
  • Residual: what is left when \(u_\theta\) is put into the equation. It is zero for an exact solution.
  • Collocation point: a sampled point where the residual is evaluated. No mesh is needed.
  • \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}\): the misfit to measurements. It is optional.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• Researchers studying PINN training, sampling or identifiability, who need a fast trainer, reference solutions and multi-seed protocols.
  • Process and control engineers who want to know what their records can determine before buying a sensor or running a campaign.
  • Teachers and students: the test suite checks every exact solution against its equation and conditions.

docs.title: When to use a PINN
docs.text:
The package's own experiments give a narrow answer. Every number and its source is on When to use a PINN, and when not to.

Do not use a PINN when

  • The forward problem is well posed and a classical solver exists. On the 1-D heat equation, finite differences reach a relative L2 error of about \(7 \times 10^{-4}\) in about 30 ms (classical baselines). A PINN with L-BFGS reaches \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) in 120 s (D01).
  • The model has a cheap, trusted forward solve. On the evaporator, a Kalman filter tracks the fouling to 3.5 % in 0.2 s. The PINN twin reaches 9–16 % in five minutes and fails to train on 22 of 36 runs (J03, J05, J06).
  • You need an interval you can trust and have not checked it. The twin's own 90 % interval covers the truth 25 % of the time (J06).

Consider a PINN when

  • There is no trusted forward solver, or it is too expensive to iterate.
  • An unknown coefficient or function sits inside the equation. It is learned with the solution from sparse, noisy measurements, with no adjoint code to write.
  • One network should replace many solves, or the problem has awkward geometry or many dimensions. A parametric surrogate covers a parameter range to 0.2–2 % (K45).

In every case, run the baseline. The package ships it.

The long-term goal is digital twins: models of one piece of process equipment, kept in step with its sensor records, that estimate its unmeasured states. Read Applications and the Research program.

docs.title: Install and first run
docs.text:
pip install pinnrl
pinnrl-train --pde burgers --arch fourier --epochs 2000
pinnrl-dashboard

The three lines install the package (Python 3.10–3.13), train a PINN on the Burgers equation into ./runs/, and open a browser app to inspect the run. See Getting started.

docs.title: Applications: digital twins
docs.text:
This page is for engineers and researchers deciding whether a PINN fits their plant or asset. It lists where a physics-informed twin helps, by industry, and where it does not.

A PINN-based twin solves an inverse problem on the asset's own sensor data:

\[ (\hat u, \hat\lambda) = \arg\min_{u,\,\lambda} \; \lVert H[u] - y \rVert^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathcal{N}[u; \lambda] = 0 \]
  • Digital twin: a model of one specific physical asset, kept in sync with it through its sensor data. It estimates what cannot be measured, forecasts, and tests decisions before they are applied.
  • \(y\), \(H[u]\): the sensor records the plant already logs, and what those sensors would read on the modelled state \(u\).
  • \(\mathcal{N}[u; \lambda] = 0\): the conservation laws you already know.
  • \(\lambda\): what is unknown: parameters, closures and hidden states. A PINN learns \(u\) and \(\lambda\) together in one training run.
  • Closure: a relation the equations need and the physics does not supply, such as a drying-kinetics curve.

The gap this project targets: detailed simulators are too slow or too rigid to calibrate continuously, and data-driven models do not respect physics and extrapolate poorly. A PINN combines known physics with existing sensor streams.

docs.title: Where a PINN fits
docs.text:
The pitch is the same in every row: your plant already logs X. A physics-informed model can turn X into an estimate of Y, which you can't measure continuously, and keep that estimate calibrated as the equipment ages.

Industry Typical twin Physics (PDEs) Where a PINN helps Food and dairy Spray dryers, evaporators, pasteurizers and UHT lines, fermenters Heat and mass transfer, drying kinetics, fouling growth Soft sensors for residual moisture and fouling resistance from routine temperatures and flows; predicting when cleaning-in-place is due Chemicals and petrochemicals Reactors, distillation columns, heat exchangers Reaction–diffusion–convection, heat transfer Identifying kinetic parameters; estimating hot spots and catalyst deactivation from sparse thermocouples Pharma and biopharma Freeze dryers, bioreactors, continuous lines Heat and mass transfer, moving sublimation fronts Product temperature and drying front in freeze-drying from shelf temperature and chamber pressure (process analytical technology) Pulp, paper and textiles Drying sections, coating lines Coupled heat and moisture transport Moisture profiles across the web from a few scanner readings Metals, mining and materials Furnaces, casting, heat treatment, additive manufacturing Heat conduction with phase change (Stefan problems), thermal stress Solidification front and refractory wear from shell temperatures; melt-pool calibration Power and energy Boilers, turbines, nuclear thermal hydraulics, wind farms Heat transfer, fluid flow, structural dynamics Heat-flux and remaining-life estimation; fast wake surrogates for layout and control Batteries and storage EV packs, grid batteries Electrochemistry (single-particle, Doyle–Fuller–Newman models), heat State of health and parameter identification from voltage and temperature curves District heating and HVAC Pipe networks, building energy Transport (advection) in pipes, heat in walls Hidden temperatures and leaks from supply and return sensors Oil, gas and subsurface Reservoirs, pipelines, geothermal Porous-media (Darcy) flow, multiphase pipe flow History matching (permeability inversion); leak localization Aerospace and defense Engines, airframes, thermal protection Fluid flow, structural mechanics, heat Reconstructing full fields from sparse sensors; identifying loads and damage for structural health monitoring Automotive Thermal management, battery packs, aerodynamics Heat, fluid flow Calibrated thermal models; aerodynamic surrogates for design Semiconductors CVD and epitaxy reactors, rapid thermal processing Reaction–diffusion, heat Wafer temperature maps from a few pyrometers; recipe calibration Built environment and infrastructure Buildings, bridges, tunnels, concrete curing Heat and moisture in porous media, structural dynamics Concrete maturity and strength estimation; structural health monitoring Water and environment Treatment plants, rivers, sewers, groundwater Advection–dispersion–reaction, shallow water Identifying contaminant sources; calibrated flood and dispersion models Healthcare Cardiac, vascular and tumor-growth models Reaction–diffusion, blood flow Patient-specific tissue parameters (conductivity, stiffness) from imaging Agriculture Soil, grain storage, greenhouses Richards equation (soil water), heat and moisture Soil hydraulic parameters from probes; hot spots in grain silos
  • Soft sensor: an estimate of an unmeasured quantity computed from the measured ones.
  • Fouling: a deposit on a heat-transfer surface that grows during a run and lowers heat transfer.
  • Cleaning-in-place: washing the equipment without dismantling it.
  • History matching: adjusting a reservoir model until it reproduces the recorded production.

Out of scope: twins without field physics, such as supply-chain, logistics, IT-network and discrete-event production-scheduling twins. Graph, queueing or discrete-event models serve those better than PDEs.

docs.title: What a PINN-based twin is, and isn't
docs.text:
• It is an estimation layer. It sits above the control system (PLC/DCS), reads the historian (the database of the plant's sensor records) or OPC UA (a standard protocol for reading plant data), and returns estimates with uncertainty and advisory setpoints. It does not replace real-time control loops.
  • It is not a faster CFD. When the physics is fully known and all you need is a forward simulation, use a classical solver.
  • It earns its keep where something important is unmeasured or unknown: a fouling layer, a drying-kinetics curve, a permeability field, a tissue property.
  • Credible deployment also needs a classical baseline for comparison (Kalman filters, moving-horizon estimation) and calibrated uncertainty: a 95 % interval that contains the truth about 95 % of the time.
  • Moving-horizon estimation: a classical estimator that fits the model to a sliding window of recent data.

docs.title: First target: food-powder lines
docs.text:
The first concrete application is the dairy and food-powder line: evaporators feeding spray dryers, as in cheese- and milk-powder plants. The plan:

  1. Falling-film evaporator fouling, estimated from effect-level temperatures and flows.
  2. A spray-dryer soft sensor for residual moisture, with a stickiness-margin advisory.
  3. A coupled line-level twin with measurement design (deciding when to pull a lab sample).

This is the research program. Its experiments live in experiments/ (track J of the backlog), and Process twins documents what is built.
