docs.title: Custom equations
docs.text:
This page shows how to write your own PDE, ODE or system as text and train it with CustomPDE. Read it when the equation you need is not one of the shipped ones.

  • Residual: the equation with every term on the left-hand side. You write it as text; SymPy parses it.
  • PDEBase: the class of every problem. A CustomPDE is one, so the training loop, samplers, optimizers, inverse-problem machinery, pinnrl-train and the dashboard treat it like a shipped equation.
  • Derivatives: taken by the compiled kernel where it applies, by autograd elsewhere.

docs.title: A first equation
docs.text:
\[ u_t - \alpha\, u_{xx} = 0, \qquad u(x, 0) = \sin \pi x, \qquad u(0, t) = u(1, t) = 0, \qquad u_{\text{exact}} = e^{-\alpha \pi^2 t} \sin \pi x \] 
from pinnrl import CustomPDE

pde = CustomPDE(
    "u_t - alpha*u_xx",
    domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
    parameters={"alpha": 0.1},
    initial_condition="sin(pi*x)",
    boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
    exact_solution="exp(-alpha*pi^2*t)*sin(pi*x)",   # optional, enables validate()
)
trainer = pde.build_trainer("fourier", num_epochs=150, num_collocation_points=1024,
                            batch_size=1024, learning_rate=2e-3,
                            early_stopping={"enabled": False})
trainer.train(progress=False)
print(f"relative L2 error: {pde.validate(trainer.model)['l2_error']:.2e}")

CustomPDE:

  • First argument: the residual, the left-hand side of expression = 0.
  • parameters: a value for every parameter in the text.

build_trainer returns a PDETrainer:

  • First argument: an architecture of the packaged defaults (config.yaml).
  • Keyword arguments: override keys of the training block (num_epochs, batch_size, num_collocation_points, num_boundary_points, num_initial_points, learning_rate, weight_decay, optimizer, loss_weights, mode, ...).
  • model: overrides the architecture block, e.g. model={"hidden_dims": [64, 64, 64, 64], "layer_norm": False}.
  • Collocation point: a point where the residual is evaluated.

You can equally build a PINNModel and PDETrainer yourself, as in Getting started.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Written as Meaning u, v, theta a field (network output), as listed in fields (default ["u"]) x, y, z, r, t a coordinate (network input), as listed in domain; t is time u_t, u_xx, u_xy, theta_tt partial derivatives: field, underscore, one coordinate name per differentiation, any order nu, alpha, D, k a parameter: any other name, supplied in parameters sin cos tan exp log sqrt tanh sinh cosh abs sign erf min max atan2 sigmoid relu, pi functions and the constant π; ^ or ** is a power; 2*x, not 2 x
  • Coordinates with several letters work (u_theta), as long as the subscript splits into coordinate names in one way only.
  • A derivative with an unknown coordinate is an error (u_zz when z is not in the domain).
  • A parameter the equations use but parameters does not define is an error.

docs.title: Domains and kinds of problem
docs.text:
domain maps each coordinate to (lo, hi). Spatial coordinates come first, in the order given; t is the time axis.

  • Time-dependent PDE: {"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)}, with an initial_condition.
  • Second order in time (wave, oscillators): detected from _tt in the equations; initial_velocity gives u_t(x, t0) (default 0).
  • ODE: a domain with only t, e.g. {"t": (0, 10)}. The network receives a dummy spatial input that the solution does not depend on.
  • Steady problem (Poisson, Helmholtz): a domain without t. There is no initial term and t is fixed at 0.
  • Higher dimension: {"x": (0, 1), "y": (0, 1), "t": (0, 2)}; u_xx + u_yy is the Laplacian.

docs.title: Initial, boundary and exact solutions
docs.text:
initial_condition, initial_velocity and exact_solution take:

  • A string, for a scalar problem: an expression in the coordinates and parameters. Only the exact solution may use t.
  • A list or {field: expression}, for a system. Fields left out are 0.
  • A callable, u0(x) or u(x, t) returning an (N, k) tensor, when there is no closed form (a numerical reference, interpolated data).

boundary_conditions are the generic ones of PDEBase, applied to every field on every face:

Kind Written as Dirichlet, \(u = g\) {"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}} or {"dirichlet": {"left": 1.0, "right": 0.0}} Neumann, \(u_x = g\) along the face's axis {"neumann": {"value": 0.0}} Periodic {"periodic": {}} Values from the exact solution {"dirichlet": {"type": "exact"}}
  • Face: one end of a spatial axis; left is the lower end, right the upper.
  • Conditions per field are keyed by field name; see Systems.

docs.title: Systems
docs.text:
Give one equation per field, in the order of fields. A Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion system in 2-D:

\[ \begin{aligned} u_t &= D_u \nabla^2 u - u v^2 + F (1 - u) \\ v_t &= D_v \nabla^2 v + u v^2 - (F + k)\, v \end{aligned} \] 
pde = CustomPDE(
    ["u_t - Du*(u_xx + u_yy) + u*v^2 - F*(1 - u)",
     "v_t - Dv*(v_xx + v_yy) - u*v^2 + (F + k)*v"],
    domain={"x": (0, 1), "y": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
    fields=["u", "v"],
    parameters={"Du": 0.16, "Dv": 0.08, "F": 0.035, "k": 0.065},
    initial_condition={"u": "1 - 0.5*exp(-((x-0.5)^2 + (y-0.5)^2)/0.01)",
                       "v": "0.25*exp(-((x-0.5)^2 + (y-0.5)^2)/0.01)"},
    boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}},
)
  • Residual: shape (N, 2). The loss averages over both equations; residual-based sampling uses their norm at each point.
  • Conditions per field: boundary_conditions={"u": {"dirichlet": {"value": 1.0}}, "v": {"neumann": {"value": 0.0}}}. A field left out has none. {kind: options} applies to every field.
  • field_weights: field_weights={"v": 10.0} multiplies that field's residual, initial and boundary errors in the loss. Use it when one component is small or slow and the optimizer would ignore it.
  • Test case for both: the catalogue entry reaction_diffusion_pair, two heat equations exchanging mass at rate k, with a closed form.

docs.title: A residual in Python
docs.text:
When the expression language is not enough (a lookup table, a learned closure, a conditional), pass a callable residual(f, p).

\[ u_t - \alpha\, u_{xx} - s(x) = 0, \qquad s(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x < 0.5 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]
  • f: a Fields accessor with the notation above as attributes (f.u, f.u_xx, f.x, f.t, f.d("u", "x", "t"), f.laplacian("u")). Each derivative is computed once and cached.
  • p: the parameter dict, with nn.Parameter values for the ones being identified.
  • Return: an (N, k) tensor or a list of (N, 1) tensors.
  • time_order=2: pass it with a callable that is second order in time; for text it is detected.
import torch

def residual(f, p):
    source = torch.where(f.x < 0.5, 1.0, 0.0)          # a piecewise forcing
    return f.u_t - p["alpha"] * f.u_xx - source

pde = CustomPDE(residual, domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)}, parameters={"alpha": 0.1},
                initial_condition="0", boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}})

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text:
Any parameter can be identified from data.

\[ \min_{w,\, \alpha} \; \mathcal{L}_{\text{physics}}(w, \alpha) + \lambda_{\text{data}} \, \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big( u_w(x_i, t_i) - y_i \big)^2 \]
  • \(w\): the network weights. \(\alpha\): the parameter to identify.
  • \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{physics}}\): the residual, initial and boundary terms.
  • \(y_i\): an observation at \((x_i, t_i)\). \(\lambda_{\text{data}}\): its weight, loss_weights={"data": 50} below.

Steps:

  1. List the parameter in trainable_parameters, with a starting value in parameter_initial_guesses.
  2. Attach observations: observation_data={"x": ..., "t": ..., "u": ...} or {"path": "obs.npz"}. Without observations and with an exact solution, generate_synthetic_observations creates noisy ones.
  3. Train in mode="inverse"; build_trainer selects it when there are trainable parameters.

See Inverse problems.

pde = CustomPDE(
    "u_t - alpha*u_xx",
    domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
    parameters={"alpha": 0.05},                 # the true value, used for synthetic data
    trainable_parameters=["alpha"],
    parameter_initial_guesses={"alpha": 0.5},
    initial_condition="sin(pi*x)",
    boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
    exact_solution="exp(-alpha*pi^2*t)*sin(pi*x)",
)
pde.generate_synthetic_observations(n_points=200, noise_std=0.01, seed=0)
trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward", num_epochs=500, loss_weights={"data": 50})
trainer.train(progress=False)
print(pde.get_trainable_parameter_values())
  • Log parameterization: the optimizer takes the same absolute step for a PDE parameter as for a weight. For a small positive parameter such as a viscosity of \(10^{-3}\), write exp(log_nu) in the residual and list log_nu as trainable. The step becomes relative and the viscosity stays positive.
  • Cramér–Rao bound: the floor any unbiased estimate can reach. With a closed-form solution, pinnrl.analysis.closed_form_bound(pde, ["alpha"], x, t, sigma) gives it for observations at (x, t) with noise sigma.

docs.title: Unknown functions
docs.text:
Use one when the unknown physics is a function: a coefficient that drifts in time, a heterogeneous field, a closure of the solution.

\[ u_t - \alpha(t)\, u_{xx} = 0, \qquad \alpha(t) = 0.05 + 0.1\, t \ \text{ to be recovered} \]
  • UnknownFunction: a small network of the inputs you name (coordinates or fields), trained with the data in inverse mode.
  • Closure: a term that depends on the solution itself, such as a reaction rate \(f(u)\).
  • Use: give it as an unknown_functions entry and write its name in the equation like a parameter.
  • Subscripts: alpha_x is the derivative of the learned function. The conservative form of a heterogeneous diffusion is u_t - alpha_x*u_x - alpha*u_xx.

Keys of an entry. The constraints are built into the output, so training never leaves the admissible set.

Key Effect positive: true a softplus bounds: [lo, hi] a sigmoid into the interval monotone: {u: increasing} non-negative weights on every path from that input, for a closure such as a reaction rate that grows with concentration anchor: {at: {X: 0.05}, value: 0.0} a value the function is known to take at one point, held exactly by subtracting the network's own value there (a drying rate that vanishes at the equilibrium moisture, a fouling that starts at zero) initial the constant the function starts at; an anchored function starts at its anchor value truth an expression in the inputs: the function the synthetic data came from
  • Anchor with monotone: fixes the sign everywhere. A closure anchored at zero and increasing is non-negative above its anchor, without a softplus that would keep it from reaching zero.
  • truth: used by generate_synthetic_observations and by an exact_solution that mentions the unknown. pde.unknown_function_error("alpha") grades the recovery as a relative \(L^2\) error over the input range.
pde = CustomPDE(
    "u_t - alpha*u_xx",
    domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
    initial_condition="sin(pi*x)",
    boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
    exact_solution="exp(-pi^2*(0.05*t + 0.05*t^2))*sin(pi*x)",   # for alpha = 0.05 + 0.1 t
    unknown_functions={
        "alpha": {"inputs": ["t"], "positive": True, "initial": 0.2, "truth": "0.05 + 0.1*t"},
    },
)
pde.generate_synthetic_observations(n_points=200, noise_std=0.01, seed=0)
trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward", num_epochs=2000)
trainer.train(progress=False)
print(pde.unknown_function_error("alpha"))          # relative L2 of the recovered alpha(t)
alpha_hat = pde.evaluate_unknown("alpha", x, t)     # the function itself, at any points
  • Fixed basis: {"alpha": {"inputs": ["x"], "basis": {"type": "cosine", "modes": 6}}} (or legendre) replaces the network. The unknown is then the coefficient vector fn.coefficients, so each mode's identifiability can be analysed like a parameter and the coefficients can be sampled by the swarm (K48).
  • Closure of the field: takes the field as input and a range to normalise it, {"f": {"inputs": ["u"], "input_ranges": {"u": [-1, 1]}, "monotone": "increasing"}}, used as u_t - D*u_xx - f.
  • No closed form: pass a numerical reference as exact_solution. pinnrl.benchmarks.heat_variable_reference(alpha) solves u_t = (alpha(x, t) u_x)_x by the method of lines and .as_exact_solution() interpolates it.
  • Experiment F09: recovers a drifting alpha(t) and a two-layer alpha(x) this way, and shows which fields the data cannot determine.
  • Storage: the weights are saved next to the model (unknown_functions.pt) and restored by load_run.
  • No weight decay: on unknown functions or on scalar unknowns. Decay is a prior toward zero: a regularizer for network weights, a bias for physics.

docs.title: Measured inputs
docs.text:
A plant model is driven by what was recorded: an inlet temperature, a feed rate, the ambient conditions.

\[ u_t - \alpha\, u_{xx} - q(t) = 0, \qquad u(0, t) = T_{\text{in}}(t), \qquad u(1, t) = 0 \]
  • \(q(t)\), \(T_{\text{in}}(t)\): records, given as inputs entries and used by name in the equations or in boundary values.
  • TimeSeries: a record, built from a CSV or NPZ file ({"path": "left.csv", "time_column": "t", "value_column": "T_left"}) or from arrays.
  • Reading: by linear interpolation at the time of every collocation or boundary point; held constant outside the record.
  • Boundary values: accept expressions in the coordinates, parameters and inputs, so dirichlet: {left: "q", right: "0.2*t"} and neumann: {value: "sin(2*pi*t)"} work alongside plain numbers.
pde = CustomPDE(
    "u_t - alpha*u_xx - q",                                   # a measured source
    domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
    parameters={"alpha": 0.1},
    inputs={"q": {"path": "source.csv", "time_column": "t", "value_column": "q"},
            "T_in": TimeSeries(t_samples, values)},
    boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"left": "T_in", "right": 0.0}},   # a measured boundary
    initial_condition="0",
)
  • YAML: relative path entries are taken from the file's own folder.
  • Snapshot: the run records the inputs by path (or inline when they came from arrays), so load_run rebuilds the driven problem.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
A plant does not deliver the field at random points of space-time. A sensor reports

\[ y_k = h(u)\big|_{t_k - \tau} + \varepsilon_k \]
  • Observation operator \(h\): the map from the field to the reading, written as an expression.
  • \(t_k\): the timestamps. \(\varepsilon_k\): noise, with the sensor's own noise level as standard deviation.
  • delay \(\tau\): the record stamped t reflects the state at t - delay.
  • weight: the sensor's weight in the loss.
Sensor Reports Example PointSensor a sequence of readings at one place a probe BoundarySensor an expression on a wall a flux meter, -alpha*u_x IntegralSensor an integral over the domain a level, a tank temperature
  • Data term: one mean-squared misfit per sensor, next to any scattered observation_data.
  • Scale: in a normalized problem, the misfit of a sensor that reports a field is divided by that field's scale. Set scale= for any other expression.
import numpy as np
from pinnrl.pdes import PointSensor, BoundarySensor, IntegralSensor, sensor_jacobian
from pinnrl.pdes.catalog import from_catalog
from pinnrl.analysis import fisher_information
from pinnrl.pdes.sensors import sensor_noise_vector

times = np.linspace(0.05, 1.0, 40)
pde = from_catalog(
    "heat",
    trainable_parameters=["alpha"], parameter_initial_guesses={"alpha": 0.5},
    sensors=[
        PointSensor(0.3, times, noise=0.01, name="probe"),                         # u(0.3, t)
        BoundarySensor("left", times, "-alpha*u_x", noise=0.02, delay=0.05),       # wall flux, delayed
        IntegralSensor(times, "u", normalize=True, noise=0.01),                    # the mean over x
    ],
)
pde.observe(seed=0)                     # records from the true solution, through the operators
trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward", num_epochs=2000)

# Which layout determines alpha best? The Fisher information of the records, from the closed form.
J = sensor_jacobian(pde, ["alpha"])
print(fisher_information(J, sensor_noise_vector(pde.sensors), ["alpha"]).std)
  • Fisher information: how much the records say about a parameter. The last two lines print the standard deviation of alpha this layout allows.
  • pde.evaluate_expression("-alpha*u_x", model, x, t) is the same machinery for your own derived quantities.
  • sensor.set_values(records) attaches real measurements.
  • pinnrl-train --pde-file records synthetic ones when a spec's sensors carry none.
  • Experiment K02 uses sensor_jacobian to rank layouts.

After training, pde.sensor_misfit(trainer.model) is the one test the run can make on itself:

\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{k} \left( \frac{y_k - \hat{y}_k}{\sigma_k} \right)^2 \le \chi^2_{0.999} \]
  • Chi-square \(\chi^2\): the misfit of the records \(y_k\) under the network's readings \(\hat{y}_k\), in units of each sensor's noise, against its 99.9 % limit (SensorMisfit).
  • A twin whose fields miss the records has also missed the unknown: every failed run of J06 and J07b fails this test.

train_with_restarts trains and tests; while the test fails it starts again from the next seed, and it keeps the best of the attempts.

from pinnrl.training.restarts import train_with_restarts

result = train_with_restarts(
    pde,
    lambda seed: pde.build_trainer("feedforward", num_epochs=2000),
    lambda trainer: trainer.train(progress=False),
    attempts=3,
)
print(result.misfit, result.accepted, result.n_attempts)

docs.title: Parametric surrogates
docs.text:
• Parametric surrogate: a network with the parameter as an extra input. One training covers a range of it, and any value in the range costs one forward pass.

  • List the parameter under parametric with its range: from_catalog("heat", parameters={}, parametric={"alpha": (0.02, 0.5)}).

  • Train. alpha is sampled uniformly with the collocation points and used in the expressions like a coordinate.

  • Call pde.surrogate_misfit(model, x, t, y, thetas) for the data misfit of a batch of parameter values.

  • Boundary and initial conditions apply to the physical axes only.

  • surrogate_misfit is the vectorized forward model a swarm (pinnrl.uq.sample_equivalence_region) or any sampler needs.
  • Experiment K45 measures what such a surrogate loses against per-value training, and uses it as the swarm's forward model.

docs.title: Non-dimensionalization
docs.text:
A network expects inputs and outputs of order one. A problem in metres, seconds and kelvin does not supply them.

\[ \hat{x} = 2\, \frac{x - x_{\text{lo}}}{x_{\text{hi}} - x_{\text{lo}}} - 1, \qquad u = u_0 + s \cdot \text{net}(\hat{x}, \hat{t}) \]
  • \(\hat{x}, \hat{t}\): the domain mapped to \([-1, 1]\).

  • \(u_0\), \(s\): the offset and scale of a field, from scales (a scale, or an (offset, scale) pair).

  • Give each field its magnitude with scales.

  • Pass normalize=True to build_trainer (--normalize on the command line).

The loss terms are taken in those units too:

  • Initial, boundary, data and sensor errors are divided by \(s\).
  • The residual is multiplied by the time span over \(s\) (the magnitude of \(u_t\)).
  • The equations stay as written, in physical units, and the trained model answers in them.

A heat problem on a 1,000 mm slab over an hour, with temperatures around 300 K:

pde = CustomPDE(
    "u_t - alpha*u_xx",                                      # mm^2/s, mm, s, K
    domain={"x": (0, 1000.0), "t": (0, 3600.0)},
    parameters={"alpha": 50.0},
    initial_condition="300 + 50*sin(pi*x/1000)",
    boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 300.0}},
    scales={"u": (300.0, 50.0)},                             # around 300 K, varying by 50 K
)
trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward", normalize=True, num_epochs=1000)
  • Result (test_normalization.py): after 1,000 Adam steps the maximum error is 248 K for the raw model and 2 K for the normalized one. The same problem on the unit square trains to a few percent.
  • The run snapshot keeps the bounds and scales in its model block, so load_run rebuilds the scaled model.

docs.title: A faster step: the compiled kernel
docs.text:
pinnrl.native is a small C++ kernel, compiled on first use, that takes the residual's derivatives and the weight gradient without autograd. The mechanism is in The native engine.

What it is

  • General kernel: carries the derivatives forward through the layers next to the value, then takes the weight gradient by one reverse pass.
  • Compiled step: C++ written for your equations, compiled once (about 1.5 s per equation and machine) and cached. It takes over at evaluation 32, so a short run never waits for the compiler.
  • Default: build_trainer and pinnrl-train use it wherever it applies and autograd everywhere else, without notice. Loss and gradients are the same to rounding.

When it applies

  • General kernel: equations given as text (or a registry class such as HeatEquation), derivatives of any order, no unknown functions; a feed-forward network of Linear and tanh, with or without LayerNorm, float32 on the CPU; macOS (Accelerate) or Linux (OpenBLAS, apt install libopenblas-dev) with a C++ compiler.
  • Compiled step: also needs a time-dependent problem and the squared loss. It covers trainable parameters, measured inputs, unknown functions of the coordinates, normalize=True and layer normalization.
  • Stays on autograd: an unknown function of a field, or a derivative of one.

The full list is in engine.md.

How to switch it off, and how to check

trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward")
print(pde.native_active(trainer.model))      # True where the kernel runs; autograd otherwise

trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward", derivatives="autograd")   # never the kernel
  • derivatives="autograd": never the kernel. From the command line: pinnrl-train --pde-file spec.yaml --derivatives autograd.
  • derivatives="native": the earlier name of the default, still accepted.
  • PINNRL_NATIVE_SPECIALIZE=off: keeps the general kernel. An integer sets the number of evaluations before the switch.
  • engine.md shows how to tell the compiled step apart.

Measured step times

  • I11: heat with the packaged network (layer normalization on), 32 ms by autograd, 10.4 ms by the kernel.
  • I17: heat with a 4 × 64 network, 4.8 ms by the general kernel, 3.7 ms by the compiled step. On an Apple M4 the compiled step is ahead of JAX on every equation measured; on Linux x86 JAX's forward mode is a few percent ahead on plain networks at low order.

What the rest of the package sees

Nothing downstream has to know which engine ran. A gradient that is itself differentiated (create_graph=True, as in the Hessian spectrum and the sensitivity analyses of pinnrl.analysis) is taken by autograd on the same function.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
1. Write the same specification as YAML.
  2. Pass it with --pde-file in place of --pde.
  3. Use every other flag as usual, including --mode inverse --identify r.

The Fisher–KPP equation:

# fisher_kpp.yaml
name: Fisher-KPP
equations: "u_t - D*u_xx - r*u*(1 - u)"
domain:
  x: [-10, 10]
  t: [0, 4]
parameters: {D: 1.0, r: 1.0}
initial_condition: "1/(1 + exp(x))"
boundary_conditions:
  dirichlet: {left: 1.0, right: 0.0}

pinnrl-train --pde-file fisher_kpp.yaml --arch fourier --epochs 2000
  • The run folder's config.yaml keeps the specification, so load_run and the dashboard rebuild the problem.
  • CustomPDE.from_yaml(path) and pde.to_dict() convert in both directions.

docs.title: Examples of every kind
docs.text:
Each is a complete, trainable problem and an entry of the shipped catalogue (next section), so from_catalog(key) gives the same object.

A nonlinear scalar PDE (Burgers; shock formation for small ν):

\[ u_t + u\, u_x - \nu\, u_{xx} = 0 \] 
pde = CustomPDE("u_t + u*u_x - nu*u_xx", domain={"x": (-1, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
                parameters={"nu": 0.01 / 3.14159}, initial_condition="-sin(pi*x)",
                boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}})

Second order in time, with an initial velocity (telegraph equation, exact solution known):

\[ u_{tt} + 2 \gamma\, u_t - c^2 u_{xx} = 0 \] 
pde = CustomPDE("u_tt + 2*gamma*u_t - c^2*u_xx", domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)},
                parameters={"c": 1.0, "gamma": 0.5},
                initial_condition="sin(pi*x)", initial_velocity="-gamma*sin(pi*x)",
                boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
                exact_solution="exp(-gamma*t)*cos(sqrt(c^2*pi^2 - gamma^2)*t)*sin(pi*x)")

A third-order dispersive equation (KdV soliton):

\[ u_t + 6\, u\, u_x + u_{xxx} = 0 \] 
pde = CustomPDE("u_t + 6*u*u_x + u_xxx", domain={"x": (-15, 15), "t": (0, 2)},
                parameters={"c": 1.0}, initial_condition="c/2/cosh(sqrt(c)/2*x)^2",
                boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
                exact_solution="c/2/cosh(sqrt(c)/2*(x - c*t))^2")

A steady boundary-value problem (Helmholtz in 2-D; no t, no initial condition):

\[ u_{xx} + u_{yy} + k^2 u = (k^2 - 2 \pi^2) \sin \pi x \, \sin \pi y \] 
pde = CustomPDE("u_xx + u_yy + k^2*u - (k^2 - 2*pi^2)*sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)",
                domain={"x": (0, 1), "y": (0, 1)}, parameters={"k": 4.0},
                boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
                exact_solution="sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)")

An ODE (logistic growth; the field is N, the only coordinate is t):

\[ \dot{N} = r\, N \left( 1 - N / K \right) \] 
pde = CustomPDE("N_t - r*N*(1 - N/K)", domain={"t": (0, 10)}, fields=["N"],
                parameters={"r": 1.0, "K": 10.0, "N0": 1.0}, initial_condition="N0",
                exact_solution="K/(1 + (K/N0 - 1)*exp(-r*t))")

A system of ODEs (SIR epidemic; one equation per field, initial values per field):

\[ \dot{S} = -\beta S I, \qquad \dot{I} = \beta S I - \gamma I, \qquad \dot{R} = \gamma I \] 
pde = CustomPDE(["S_t + beta*S*I", "I_t - beta*S*I + gamma*I", "R_t - gamma*I"],
                domain={"t": (0, 50)}, fields=["S", "I", "R"],
                parameters={"beta": 0.3, "gamma": 0.1},
                initial_condition={"S": "0.99", "I": "0.01", "R": "0"})

A process model (a continuous stirred-tank reactor with an Arrhenius rate \(k\), which grows with temperature):

\[ \dot{C} = \frac{C_{\text{in}} - C}{\tau} - k\, C, \qquad \dot{T} = \frac{T_{\text{in}} - T}{\tau} + \Delta H\, k\, C - UA\, (T - T_c), \qquad k = k_0\, e^{-E_a / (R T)} \] 
pde = CustomPDE(["C_t - (Cin - C)/tau + k0*exp(-Ea/(R*max(T, 0.1)))*C",
                 "T_t - (Tin - T)/tau - dH*k0*exp(-Ea/(R*max(T, 0.1)))*C + UA*(T - Tc)"],
                domain={"t": (0, 5)}, fields=["C", "T"],
                parameters={"Cin": 1.0, "Tin": 1.0, "tau": 1.0, "k0": 5.0, "Ea": 2.0, "R": 1.0,
                            "dH": 0.5, "UA": 0.5, "Tc": 1.0},
                initial_condition={"C": "1", "T": "1"})

A coupled PDE system with a constraint (unsteady Stokes flow; the third equation has no time derivative):

\[ u_t + p_x = \nu \nabla^2 u, \qquad v_t + p_y = \nu \nabla^2 v, \qquad u_x + v_y = 0 \] 
pde = CustomPDE(["u_t + p_x - nu*(u_xx + u_yy)", "v_t + p_y - nu*(v_xx + v_yy)", "u_x + v_y"],
                domain={"x": (0, 1), "y": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)}, fields=["u", "v", "p"],
                parameters={"nu": 0.1},
                initial_condition={"u": "sin(2*pi*x)*cos(2*pi*y)", "v": "-cos(2*pi*x)*sin(2*pi*y)"},
                boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}})

Many dimensions (heat in five space dimensions, six network inputs; name the coordinates and the subscripts follow):

\[ u_t - \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{5} u_{x_i x_i} = 0 \] 
pde = CustomPDE("u_t - alpha*(u_x1x1 + u_x2x2 + u_x3x3 + u_x4x4 + u_x5x5)",
                domain={f"x{i}": (0, 1) for i in range(1, 6)} | {"t": (0, 1)},
                parameters={"alpha": 0.02},
                initial_condition="sin(pi*x1)*sin(pi*x2)*sin(pi*x3)*sin(pi*x4)*sin(pi*x5)",
                boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"value": 0.0}},
                exact_solution="exp(-5*alpha*pi^2*t)*sin(pi*x1)*sin(pi*x2)*sin(pi*x3)*sin(pi*x4)*sin(pi*x5)")

Finance (Black–Scholes in time to maturity; the coordinate is the asset price S, the field the option value V):

\[ V_t - \tfrac{1}{2} \sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} - r\, S\, V_S + r\, V = 0 \] 
pde = CustomPDE("V_t - 0.5*sigma^2*S^2*V_SS - r*S*V_S + r*V", domain={"S": (1, 200), "t": (0, 1)},
                fields=["V"], parameters={"sigma": 0.2, "r": 0.05, "K": 100.0},
                initial_condition="max(S - K, 0)",
                boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"left": 0.0, "right": 100.0}})

docs.title: The catalogue
docs.text:
pinnrl.pdes.catalog.CATALOG holds forty-three such specifications:

Family Entries Parabolic heat in 1-D to 5-D, with a source, advection–diffusion, Fisher–KPP, Allen–Cahn, Cahn–Hilliard, Burgers, porous medium, Black–Scholes Hyperbolic wave in 1-D and 2-D, telegraph, convection, Klein–Gordon, sine–Gordon Dispersive KdV with one or two coefficients, the Euler–Bernoulli beam, Schrödinger as a real system Steady Poisson in 2-D and 4-D, Helmholtz, a convection–diffusion boundary layer, Bratu ODEs logistic, damped oscillator, pendulum, Lotka–Volterra, Van der Pol, Lorenz, SIR, a CSTR Systems a coupled reaction–diffusion pair with a closed form, Gray–Scott, Brusselator, linear shallow water, Stokes Other a three-state Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation 
from pinnrl.pdes.catalog import CATALOG, from_catalog

pde = from_catalog("kdv_soliton")
pde = from_catalog("burgers", parameters={"nu": 0.1})   # override any entry
print(len(CATALOG), sorted(CATALOG)[:5])

Every entry with a closed-form solution is checked by the test suite: the exact solution, used as the network, must zero the residual and match the initial condition. The catalogue is thus also the regression test of the expression framework.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The derivative notation applies to fields, not to expressions: write (u^2)_xx as 2*u_x^2 + 2*u*u_xx, or use a callable residual.
  • Where the compiled kernel does not apply, derivatives are taken by nested autograd. Order four and above is then slow and numerically noisy, as for the shipped Cahn–Hilliard equation. Cost grows with the number of coordinates and with the order, so a 5-D Laplacian is five second-derivative passes.
  • A boundary condition applies to both faces of an axis alike (Dirichlet takes left/right values); conditions that differ by face in kind, or Robin conditions, need a callable residual or a subclass.
  • An unknown function is a smooth network: a jump in the true coefficient is recovered as a steep ramp, and a field the data barely feel (see F09) collapses to the constant that fits best. Check identifiability before trusting the recovered shape.
  • Without normalize=True the network sees raw coordinates and raw field values; a problem in physical units needs the non-dimensionalization step, or hand scaling.
  • Integral terms, delays and non-local operators are outside the expression language.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
This page describes the browser app that launches runs, follows them as they train and compares their results. It also runs the fouling monitor on plant data.

pinnrl-dashboard                       # http://127.0.0.1:8050/, opens a browser tab
pinnrl-dashboard --port 8051 --no-browser
  • Runs folder: ./runs/, relative to the directory you start the dashboard from. It is the folder pinnrl-train uses.
  • Launched runs: ordinary pinnrl-train processes. They keep going if you close the browser.
  • Port: if the port is taken, the next two are tried.

docs.title: Live Training
docs.text:
New Training is a form over every pinnrl-train option: the PDE, architecture, budget, sampling strategy, optimizer, LR schedule, adaptive weights, loss function and mode. Defaults come from config.yaml for the selected PDE.

  • Sampling strategy: the rule that places the collocation points, where the equation's residual is evaluated. The RL bandit is an experimental one.
  • Inverse mode: training that also identifies parameters of the equation. The form asks for the parameters, their initial guesses, and the observation source: synthetic noisy samples of the exact solution, or an .npz file.
  • Well dataset: a simulation dataset of The Well. Choosing one fills in its recommended mode and architecture.

Monitor follows a run as it trains. It shows:

  • the loss components and the learning rate;
  • the parameter trajectory in inverse mode, against the true value when known;
  • interactive 3-D surfaces of the predicted u(x, t) and the PDE residual.

The surfaces are read from the run's live_snapshot.npz, written every validation_frequency epochs plus at the start and the end. 2-D PDEs are shown as a time slice.

docs.title: Collocation & Solution
docs.text:
For a finished run, this tab shows:

  • the predicted and exact solution surfaces, with a time slider (the exact panel is empty for PDEs without a closed form);
  • the point-wise error;
  • where the collocation points were placed over training, which is how you check what an adaptive sampler did.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
This tab is the soft sensor of the evaporator twin on plant data. It runs the fouling monitor. No network is trained, so the result is there in a few seconds.

  • Soft sensor: an estimate of a quantity the plant does not measure, computed from the sensors it has.
  • Fouling resistance: the extra resistance to heat transfer of the deposit on the tube.
  • Fouling monitor: a Kalman filter on the evaporator model, with the fouling resistance as a level and a rate.
  • Historian export: the plant's recorded sensor data, as CSV or Parquet.
  • Tag map: a YAML file that says which column of the export is which signal (format). A model: block in it overrides the tube's parameters (length, U, velocity, ...).

Give the historian export and the tag map. The view shows:

Output Content Fouling resistance The estimate at each record with its 90 % band (what was known at the time), the hindsight estimate from the whole record, the cleaning threshold, and the projected time of reaching it with its interval Outlet records The records against the filter's one-step predictions Prediction misfit (in the summary) In units of the sensor noise. Near 1 when the model explains the records; a larger value says the band should not be trusted
  • Open interval: a time to clean whose upper end is open means the fouling rate is not yet clearly positive.
  • Steam record uncertainty: a steam-temperature offset mimics fouling (0.5 K for 30 %, experiment J04). Enter how well the steam record is trusted and the offset is estimated alongside. This widens the band to what the data support (J06).
  • Rate walk \(q\): how fast the fouling rate \(r\) may change, with \(\tau\) the time over which it may change by its own size:
\[ q = \frac{r}{\sqrt{\tau}} \]
  • The default suits a steady drift. On a curve that bends it gives a narrow band around a biased estimate.
  • A larger value is the safe choice, at the price of a wider time to clean.
  • Write demo data puts a synthetic 20-minute export and its tag map in runs/process_demo/ and fills the form. The two files are a template for a real export.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Select several finished runs to overlay their loss curves and compare final metrics side by side.

  • Delete: runs can be deleted from the selector, with a confirmation step. Only folders inside the runs directory can be removed.
  • Load in Python: use pinnrl.training.train.load_run (see Training).

docs.title: Datasets (The Well)
docs.text:
This page shows how to train on the simulation datasets of The Well and use their snapshots as observations.

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl\lVert u_\theta(x_i, t_i) - u_i \bigr\rVert^2 \]
  • The Well: a collection of large, high-fidelity PDE simulation datasets (Polymathic AI, BSD-3). pinnrl registers 11 of them.
  • \((x_i, t_i, u_i)\): a sampled point of a simulation snapshot and the field values stored there.
  • \(u_\theta\): the network. Fitted to the snapshots alone, it is a neural surrogate of the simulation.
  • Channel: one stored field component. The network has one output per channel.
pip install 'pinnrl[well]'
pinnrl-train --pde heat --dataset active_matter --arch fno --epochs 200 --dataset-steps 9
  • --dataset: sets the mode to the dataset's recommendation (data_only for every registered dataset) unless you pass --mode.
  • --pde (or --pde-file): still required. In data_only mode it is a placeholder: the dataset's domain, dimension and channel count replace the PDE's, and the physics terms are dropped.

How a run reads the data:

  1. Data streams from the Hugging Face mirror (hf://datasets/polymathic-ai/).
  2. The run reads the first --dataset-steps time steps of each of --dataset-traj trajectories (simulation runs) from --dataset-split (train, valid or test).
  3. It samples --dataset-points (x, t, u) tuples. --dataset-seed fixes the sample.
  4. The slice is cached in ~/.cache/pinnrl/well. Set PINNRL_WELL_CACHE to change that.
Setting Value Default steps, 2-D datasets up to 101 (the_well's rollout cap) Default steps, 3-D datasets 11, which keeps memory and download size in check Dashboard the launch form has a matching "Time steps" field Fewer steps a much smaller download: notebook 04 reads 9 steps, about 26 MB per trajectory instead of about 230 MB

docs.title: Registered datasets
docs.text:
Domains, time steps and channel counts are taken from each dataset's own files. The spatial domain is the same in every file. dt × steps is the time step and the number of stored steps of the first training file. Five datasets have files that differ:

Dataset How its files differ rayleigh_taylor_instability one file per Atwood number, spanning 29.5 to 118 time units helmholtz_staircase one file per frequency, spanning 2.5 to 100 viscoelastic_instability files store 20 or 60 steps rayleigh_benard, planetswe the step size varies by up to 1.6 %

A PDE fed by a Well dataset therefore takes its time window from the observations it loads, not from the registry. The run's config.yaml records the window, so load_run rebuilds it without the data.

Name Physics Spatial domain dt × steps active_matter 2-D active nematic fluid [0, 10]² 0.25 × 81 rayleigh_benard 2-D thermal convection [0, 4] × [0, 1] 0.25 × 200 shear_flow 2-D shear flow, Kelvin–Helmholtz roll-up [0, 1]² 0.1 × 200 rayleigh_taylor_instability 3-D buoyancy-driven mixing [0, 1]³ 1.0 × 119 (varies by file) turbulent_radiative_layer_2D 2-D radiatively cooling shear layer [−0.5, 0.5] × [−1, 2] 1.6 × 101 MHD_64 3-D magnetohydrodynamic turbulence [0, 1]³ 0.01 × 100 gray_scott_reaction_diffusion 2-D reaction–diffusion patterns [−1, 1]² 10 × 1001 viscoelastic_instability 2-D elastic turbulence [0, 2π] × [−1, 1] 1.0 × 20 (or 60, by file) acoustic_scattering_maze 2-D acoustic scattering, spatially varying density and sound speed [0, 1]² 0.02 × 202 helmholtz_staircase 2-D Helmholtz (frequency-domain) scattering [−8, 8] × [−0.5, 3.5] 2.0 × 50 (varies by file) planetswe Shallow water on a sphere (colatitude θ, longitude φ in radians; cell centres) θ ∈ [0.009, 3.132], φ ∈ [0, 6.271] 1.0 × 1008

Limits of the registry:

  • None of these datasets is governed by one of pinnrl's PDE classes, so every entry defaults to data_only.
  • The acoustic and Helmholtz sets involve variable coefficients and a frequency-domain formulation. The constant-speed wave equation does not represent them.
  • euler_multi_quadrants is not registered. Its open-boundary files record negative trajectory counts, which the_well 1.2 cannot open, and the periodic variant is not on the mirror.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• data_only: plain regression on the snapshots; the residual, boundary and initial terms are dropped.
  • data_augmented: the snapshots plus the residual of a PDE.
  • inverse: as data_augmented, with trainable parameters in the PDE.

Use data_augmented and inverse with your own observations of a system that one of the shipped equations governs. --mode overrides the dataset's recommendation, so a Well dataset can still be combined with a PDE as an explicit modelling choice, as notebook 04 shows.

From Python, pinnrl.datasets.load_well_slice(name, split, n_traj, n_points, seed, n_steps=...) returns the same {"x", "t", "u"} tensors, usable as PDEConfig.observation_data. Notebook 04 trains an FNO-style network on active_matter end to end.

docs.title: The native engine
docs.text:
How pinnrl computes a training step. You do not need this page to use the engine: it is the default.

  • To use it: Custom equations.
  • Its measurements: Benchmarks, experiment I17.
  • Its functions: API reference.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A PINN minimises the squared residual of an equation. For heat,

\[ L(w) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} r(x_n, t_n)^2, \qquad r = u_t - \alpha\, u_{xx}, \]

where \(u\) is the network with weights \(w\). A step needs \(u_t\), \(u_{xx}\) and \(\partial L / \partial w\).

  • Residual \(r\): what is left when the network is put into the equation. Zero for an exact solution.
  • Collocation points \((x_n, t_n)\): the points where the residual is evaluated.
  • Reverse-mode differentiation (autograd): the chain rule applied backwards from the output. One pass per derivative order, each over the graph of the one before.

The textbook step applies reverse mode twice for \(u_{xx}\) and a third time for \(w\). Its cost grows with the order: 8.7 ms for heat, 43.6 ms for Cahn–Hilliard in eager PyTorch (I17).

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Carry the derivatives forward with the value, in one pass, then take one reverse pass written by hand.

Layer File What it does General kernel jets.cpp, native.mlp_jets Derivatives of any order, for any equation; residual and loss stay in PyTorch Step compiled per equation specialize.py, step.h C++ generated for one set of equations; one call returns the loss term and every gradient Rational tanh fast_tanh.h The activation both use

docs.title: Taylor-mode streams
docs.text:
The network is a stack of layers

\[ a = W h + b, \qquad h = \tanh(a). \]

The kernel carries a set of streams through it.

  • Stream: one array per derivative, for all points at once.
  • Multi-index \(\alpha\): how many times each input is differentiated. \(u_{xxt}\) is \(\alpha = (2, 1)\) over \((x, t)\).
  • Taylor coefficient: the derivative divided by a factorial, \(u_\alpha = D^\alpha u / \alpha!\). Stream 0 is the value.
  • Downward closed: if \(\alpha\) is carried, so is every \(\beta \le \alpha\). \(u_{xxt}\) brings \(u, u_x, u_t, u_{xx}, u_{xt}\).

native.taylor_streams builds the set and sorts it by degree. Heat needs 4 streams, KdV 5, Cahn–Hilliard 6.

Through a linear layer each stream passes linearly, and the bias enters the value only:

\[ a_\alpha = W h_\alpha \quad (\alpha \ne 0), \qquad a_0 = W h_0 + b. \]

All streams of all \(N\) points are stacked in one \((S N \times \text{width})\) matrix, so a layer is one matrix product.

Through tanh, with \(s = \tanh(a)\) and \(q = 1 - s^2\) (so \(s' = q\, a'\)), for \(\alpha_i > 0\):

\[ \alpha_i\, s_\alpha = \sum_{\beta \le \alpha,\ \beta_i \ge 1} \beta_i\, a_\beta\, q_{\alpha - \beta}, \qquad q_\gamma = \delta_{\gamma 0} - \sum_{\beta \le \gamma} s_\beta\, s_{\gamma - \beta}. \]

The reverse pass is the same recurrence read backwards.

Through layer normalization, per row of a layer:

\[ c = a - \operatorname{mean}(a), \qquad v = \operatorname{mean}(c^2) + \varepsilon, \qquad r = v^{-1/2}, \qquad y = \gamma\, c\, r + \beta. \]

The streams follow by the same arithmetic for the mean, the product and the inverse square root.

docs.title: The general kernel
docs.text:
jets.cpp implements the recurrences for any stream set.

  1. Tables builds the index tables of the recurrences from the multi-indices.
  2. pinn_jets_forward carries the streams through the layers and keeps them in a work buffer.
  3. PyTorch computes the residual and the loss from the output streams.
  4. pinn_jets_backward returns the weight gradient when PyTorch asks for it.

mlp_jets wraps steps 2 and 4 as a torch.autograd.Function, so the outputs are ordinary tensors.

It applies to:

  • a feed-forward stack of Linear and tanh, with or without LayerNorm before each tanh (native.supported_stack is the test);
  • float32 on the CPU;
  • macOS (Accelerate) or Linux (OpenBLAS).

Its generality has a cost: each term of each recurrence is one loop over arrays of megabytes, and the two passes are separate calls with PyTorch between them.

docs.title: The step compiled per equation
docs.text:
For equations given as text, pinnrl.native.specialize writes C++ for those equations and compiles it. One call returns \(L\) and every gradient.

The generated file includes jets.cpp and step.h and defines five functions:

Function Generator Body gen_tanh_fwd, gen_tanh_bwd tanh_program One loop over a layer each way, straight-line code for exactly the streams used gen_norm_fwd, gen_norm_bwd norm_program Per row, three loops over the features each way gen_residual residual_code Per point: \(r\) for every equation, \(r^2\), and the adjoint of every stream
  • Adjoint: the derivative of the loss with respect to an intermediate quantity. The reverse pass starts from the adjoints of the output streams, \(\partial L / \partial u_\alpha = 2\, r\, \partial r / \partial u_\alpha \cdot \alpha! / N\).
  • Fused loop: one loop that does the work of several, so each array is read once.

How residual_code gets the adjoints:

  1. It takes the SymPy expressions CustomPDE parsed.
  2. It differentiates each residual with respect to every symbol (sympy.diff).
  3. It shares subexpressions (sympy.cse) and prints single-precision C.
  4. If a function has no C form, it returns None and the general kernel carries on.

step.h's blocked_residual runs the batch in blocks of points: forward, residual, reverse, with the gradients summed over the blocks.

What the compiled code reads at run time, so one build serves a problem while its numbers change:

  • Parameters of the equations. Trainable ones get \(\partial L / \partial \theta\) from the same loop.
  • Per-point values: measured inputs and unknown functions of the coordinates, evaluated by PyTorch. Their adjoints are returned, and PyTorch backpropagates into the unknown function's own weights.
  • Scaling of a network built with normalize=True: mapped inputs for the kernel, physical coordinates for the residual, and one factor per stream.

CustomPDE._step_spec builds a problem's description (ResidualSpec); CustomPDE._compiled_residual_loss calls the step.

docs.title: When it takes over
docs.text:
Compiling takes about 1.5 s, once per set of equations and machine.

  1. Evaluations 1 to 31 use the general kernel.
  2. At evaluation 16 the build starts in a background thread.
  3. At evaluation 32 the compiled step takes over, waiting for the compiler if it must.

The switch is at exactly evaluation 32 whether the library was cached or not, so a run does not depend on build time. PINNRL_NATIVE_SPECIALIZE changes the number.

docs.title: The cache
docs.text:
• Where: ~/.cache/pinnrl/native (PINNRL_NATIVE_CACHE moves it).
  • Files: jets-<hash>.so, evaporator-<hash>.so, and one step-<hash>.so per set of equations.
  • Key: a hash of the generated source, jets.cpp, step.h, fast_tanh.h and a version tag. An upgrade rebuilds what changed.
  • Clearing it: deleting the directory is always safe.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text: PINNRL_NATIVE_BLOCK sets the points per block (default 1,024). On an Apple M4, blocks of 1,024 are as fast as the whole batch and smaller ones are slower (I17). The blocks are independent, which a threaded version would use (roadmap).

docs.title: The rational tanh
docs.text:
\[ \tanh(x) \approx \frac{x\, P(x^2)}{Q(x^2)}, \qquad |x| \le 7.905, \]

with \(P\) of degree 6 and \(Q\) of degree 3 in \(x^2\), the form Eigen uses (fast_math::tanhf_rational).

Time per element Error Rational form 0.4 ns within \(2.4 \times 10^{-7}\) Accelerate's vvtanhf 1.1 ns

It has no exponential and no branch, so the compiler vectorises it. A step evaluates about 1.3 million of them (I17, Apple M4).

docs.title: What the rest of the package can rely on
docs.text:
• The same numbers. Residual, loss and gradients agree with autograd to float32 rounding (\(10^{-7}\)–\(10^{-5}\) relative). test_native.py and test_native_specialize.py check each case.
  • A gradient can be differentiated again. With create_graph=True, the gradient is taken by autograd on the same function. Hessian-vector products and pinnrl.analysis work, at autograd speed.
  • torch.func sees the ordinary module. Inside jvp, vmap or grad, PyTorch evaluates the network.

  • A silent fallback. Where one layer of the engine does not apply, the next one down runs.

  • Hessian-vector product: the second derivative of the loss applied to a vector, \(H v\), without forming \(H\).

docs.title: Where it does not apply
docs.text: Situation What runs Another architecture or activation (Fourier features, SIREN, ResNet), dropout autograd A GPU (mps, cuda) or float64 autograd No C++ compiler, or no OpenBLAS on Linux autograd A residual given as a Python function autograd An unknown function of a field, or a derivative of an unknown function autograd A loss other than the squared one; a steady problem general kernel A function in the equation with no C form general kernel A parameter made differentiable outside trainable_parameters general kernel derivatives="autograd" autograd, by request

docs.title: Which engine ran
docs.text:
from pinnrl import native
from pinnrl.pdes.catalog import from_catalog

pde = from_catalog("heat")
trainer = pde.build_trainer("feedforward", num_collocation_points=256, batch_size=256)

print(native.available(), native.unavailable_reason())   # True None where the kernel builds
print(pde.native_active(trainer.model))                  # True: the kernel serves this problem

x, t = pde.generate_collocation_points(256)
loss = pde.compute_loss(trainer.model, x, t)["residual"]
print(type(loss.grad_fn).__name__)   # _ResidualStepBackward once the compiled step has taken over

The last line prints an ordinary PyTorch node for the first 31 evaluations and _ResidualStepBackward from the 32nd.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Default Effect PINNRL_NATIVE_SPECIALIZE 32 Evaluations before the compiled step takes over; off or 0 disables it PINNRL_NATIVE_BLOCK 1024 Points per block of the compiled step PINNRL_NATIVE_CACHE ~/.cache/pinnrl/native Where compiled libraries are kept CXX first of clang++, g++, c++ The compiler PINNRL_NATIVE_CXXFLAGS empty Extra compiler flags PINNRL_NATIVE_LDFLAGS empty Extra linker flags PINNRL_REQUIRE_NATIVE unset In the tests: fail instead of skipping when the kernel cannot be built

docs.title: When a build fails
docs.text:
Nothing breaks: the run goes on by autograd and a warning is logged once.

  1. Print the reason: python -c "from pinnrl import native; print(native.unavailable_reason())".
  2. no C++ compiler found: run xcode-select --install on macOS, or install g++ on Linux.
  3. compiling jets.cpp failed on Linux: apt install libopenblas-dev, or point PINNRL_NATIVE_CXXFLAGS and PINNRL_NATIVE_LDFLAGS at OpenBLAS.
  4. the specialised step could not be built (a warning): the general kernel stays in charge. PINNRL_NATIVE_SPECIALIZE=1 reproduces it at the first evaluation.

The kernels build on macOS and Linux only.

docs.title: Extending it
docs.text:
1. A new activation: add its Taylor recurrence, forward and reverse, to jets.cpp and to tanh_program, and an entry in supported_stack.
  2. A new term in the compiled step (boundary points, the optimizer): add it to the driver in step.h, with the per-equation part generated in specialize.py.
  3. Check it: every case of test_native_specialize.py compares loss and gradient with autograd; experiments/I17_step_head_to_head/run.py times the step.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
This page lists the ten equations that ship with pinnrl (the keys of pinnrl-train --pde): each equation, its symbols, its default problem and its exact solution.

Key PDE Where it arises What makes it hard for a PINN heat, heat_2d \(u_t = \alpha abla^2 u\) Heat conduction, diffusion of species, the pricing kernel behind Black–Scholes Little; the baseline. High-frequency initial data decays fast and is easy to under-resolve. wave \(u_{tt} = c^2 abla^2 u\) Acoustics, vibrating strings and membranes, electromagnetics Second order in time, so it needs the initial velocity. Energy is conserved, so errors don't damp out. burgers \(u_t + u\,u_x = u\,u_{xx}\) A 1-D model of fluid flow and shock formation; traffic flow For small \( u\) a near-discontinuous shock forms. The canonical test for adaptive sampling. convection \(u_t + \mathbf{v}\cdot abla u = 0\) Transport of heat, mass or pollutants by a flow It looks trivial, but PINNs fail for large \(v\) (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021). Information only travels along characteristics. kdv \(u_t + \alpha\,u\,u_x + eta\,u_{xxx} = 0\) Shallow-water waves, plasma waves; solitons A third derivative, and a localized pulse that must move at exactly the right speed. allen_cahn \(u_t = \varepsilon^2 abla^2 u + r\,(u - u^3)\) Phase separation in alloys, image segmentation Thin interfaces of width \(\sim\varepsilon\), with fast dynamics and metastable states. cahn_hilliard \(u_t = M\, abla^2 ig(u^3 - u - \kappa\, abla^2 u ig)\) Spinodal decomposition, polymer blends, battery electrodes Fourth order, mass-conserving and stiff, with fine-scale structure. black_scholes \(V_ au = frac12 \sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} + r S V_S - r V\), with \( au\) the time to maturity European option pricing A kink in the payoff at the strike; spatial and temporal scales that differ by orders of magnitude. pendulum \( heta'' + b\, heta' + (g/L)\sin heta = 0\) A nonlinear oscillator: mechanics, control, robotics An ODE posed as a PINN. Long time horizons accumulate phase error.

Subscripts are derivatives: \(u_t = \partial u/\partial t\), \(u_{xx} = \partial^2 u/\partial x^2\).

Training is scored against the exact solution. tests/unit_tests/test_physics_consistency.py verifies that each one satisfies, up to float32 round-off:

  • the PDE: relative residual below 1e-4;
  • the initial condition: error below 1e-6;
  • the boundary conditions.

Two are evaluated numerically: Burgers (the Cole–Hopf solution) and the pendulum (a high-accuracy ODE integration). The Allen–Cahn x2_cos benchmark has no closed form and is scored against a numerical reference.

docs.title: The equations one by one
docs.text: The domains, parameters, conditions and architectures below are the defaults of config.yaml.

docs.title: Heat (heat)
docs.text:
\[ u_t = \alpha\, u_{xx}, \qquad u(x, t) = \sin(2\pi x)\, e^{-4\pi^2 \alpha t} \]
  • \(u\): temperature. \(\alpha\): thermal diffusivity, 0.01.
  • Domain: \(x \in [0, 2]\), \(t \in [0, 10]\).
  • Conditions: periodic in \(x\); \(u(x, 0) = \sin(2\pi x)\) (frequency: 2 periods on [0, 2]).
  • Exact solution (sin_exp_decay): in general \(A \prod_d \sin(2\pi k x_d / L_d)\, e^{-\alpha \sum_d (2\pi k / L_d)^2 t}\), with \(k\) = frequency periods over the axis length \(L_d\).
  • Architecture: fourier.

docs.title: Heat in 2-D (heat_2d)
docs.text:
\[ u_t = \alpha\,(u_{xx} + u_{yy}), \qquad u(x, y, t) = \sin(2\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)\, e^{-8\pi^2 \alpha t} \]
  • \(\alpha\): 0.01.
  • Domain: \((x, y) \in [0, 1]^2\), \(t \in [0, 5]\).
  • Conditions: \(u = 0\) on the four faces; \(u(x, y, 0) = \sin(2\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)\).
  • Exact solution (sine_2d): in general \(A \sin(k_x \pi x)\sin(k_y \pi y)\, e^{-\alpha \pi^2 (k_x^2 + k_y^2) t}\).
  • Architecture: fourier.

docs.title: Wave (wave)
docs.text:
\[ u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}, \qquad u(x, t) = \sin(\pi x)\cos(c \pi t) \]
  • \(u\): displacement. \(c\): wave speed, 1.
  • Domain: \(x \in [0, 1]\), \(t \in [0, 1]\).
  • Conditions: \(u = 0\) at both ends; \(u(x, 0) = \sin(\pi x)\), released from rest (\(u_t(x, 0) = 0\)).
  • Exact solution (sine): a standing wave; in \(d\) dimensions \(A \prod_d \sin(k\pi x_d)\cos(\omega t)\) with \(\omega = c k \pi \sqrt{d}\).
  • Architecture: siren.

docs.title: Burgers (burgers)
docs.text:
\[ u_t + u\,u_x = u\,u_{xx}, \qquad u(x, t) = rac{\int u_0(y)\,\varphi_0(y)\, e^{-z^2}\,dz}{\int \varphi_0(y)\, e^{-z^2}\,dz}, \quad y = x - \sqrt{4 u t}\,z \]
  • \(u\): velocity. \( u\): viscosity, 0.01.
  • Shock: a near-discontinuous front; it forms at \(x = 0\) for small \( u\).
  • Domain: \(x \in [-1, 1]\), \(t \in [0, 1]\).
  • Conditions: \(u(\pm 1, t) = 0\); \(u_0(x) = -\sin(\pi x)\).
  • Exact solution (cole_hopf, 1-D): the Cole–Hopf quotient above with \(\varphi_0(y) = \exp ig(-\cos(\pi y)/(2\pi u) ig)\), integrated by the trapezoid rule (pinnrl.benchmarks.reference.burgers_cole_hopf).
  • Architecture: resnet.

docs.title: Convection (convection)
docs.text:
\[ u_t + v\,u_x = 0, \qquad u(x, t) = \sin\big(\pi (x - v t)\big) \]
  • \(u\): a transported quantity. \(v\): flow velocity (velocity), 1.
  • Characteristic: a line \(x - vt = \text{const}\) along which \(u\) is carried unchanged.
  • Domain: \(x \in [0, 2]\), \(t \in [0, 1]\).
  • Conditions: periodic in \(x\); \(u(x, 0) = \sin(\pi x)\).
  • Exact solution (sin): the initial profile moved with the flow, \(u_0(x - vt)\).
  • Architecture: fourier.

docs.title: Korteweg–de Vries (kdv)
docs.text:
\[ u_t + \alpha\,u\,u_x + \beta\,u_{xxx} = 0, \qquad u(x, t) = \frac{3c}{\alpha}\operatorname{sech}^2\!\Big(\tfrac12\sqrt{c/\beta}\,(x - x_0 - c t)\Big) \]
  • \(u\): wave height. \(\alpha\): nonlinearity, 6. \(\beta\): dispersion, 1.
  • Soliton: a single pulse that keeps its shape and moves at speed \(c\) (speed, 1) from \(x_0\) (position, 0).
  • Domain: \(x \in [-15, 15]\), \(t \in [0, 5]\). 1-D only.
  • Conditions: \(u = 0\) at both ends; the soliton at \(t = 0\).
  • Exact solution: soliton.
  • Architecture: siren.

docs.title: Allen–Cahn (allen_cahn)
docs.text:
\[ u_t = \varepsilon^2 u_{xx} + r\,(u - u^3), \qquad u(x, t) = \tanh\!\Big(\frac{\sqrt{r}\,x}{\sqrt{2}\,\varepsilon}\Big) \]
  • \(u\): phase, \(\pm 1\) in the two phases. \(\varepsilon\): interface width (epsilon), 0.1. \(r\): reaction rate (reaction_rate), 1.
  • Kink: a stationary front between the two phases.
  • Domain: \(x \in [-1, 1]\), \(t \in [0, 1]\).
  • Conditions: boundary values taken from the exact solution; the kink at \(t = 0\).
  • Exact solution (tanh): the kink. It does not move.
  • No exact solution: the x2_cos initial condition, \(u_0 = x^2 \cos(\pi x)\) (see below).
  • Architecture: fourier.

docs.title: Cahn–Hilliard (cahn_hilliard)
docs.text:
\[ u_t = M\,\partial_{xx}\big(u^3 - u - \kappa\,u_{xx}\big), \qquad u(x, t) = \tanh\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2\kappa}}\Big) \]
  • \(u\): concentration. \(M\): mobility (mobility), 1. \(\kappa\): gradient energy (kappa), 0.01.
  • Domain: \(x \in [-1, 1]\), \(t \in [0, 1]\).
  • Conditions: boundary values from the exact solution and \(u_x = 0\) on each face (fourth order needs two); the kink at \(t = 0\).
  • Exact solution (tanh): the stationary kink.
  • No exact solution: the random initial condition for spinodal-decomposition runs.
  • Architecture: resnet.

docs.title: Black–Scholes (black_scholes)
docs.text:
\[ V_\tau = \tfrac12 \sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} + r S V_S - r V, \qquad V(S, \tau) = S\,\Phi(d_1) - K e^{-r\tau}\,\Phi(d_2) \] \[ d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)\,\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{\tau} \]
  • \(V\): option price. \(S\): asset price. \(\tau\): time to maturity (the t input).
  • \(\sigma\): volatility, 0.2. \(r\): risk-free rate, 0.05. \(K\): strike, 100. \(\Phi\): the standard normal distribution function.
  • Domain: \(S \in [0, 200]\), \(\tau \in [0, 1]\).
  • Conditions: boundary values from the exact solution; the call payoff \(V(S, 0) = \max(S - K, 0)\).
  • Exact solution (black_scholes, 1-D): the European call price. For option_type: put, \(V = K e^{-r\tau}\,\Phi(-d_2) - S\,\Phi(-d_1)\).
  • Architecture: feedforward.

docs.title: Pendulum (pendulum)
docs.text:
\[ \theta'' + b\,\theta' + \frac{g}{L}\sin\theta = 0 \]
  • \(\theta\): angle. \(b\): damping (damping), 0.1. \(g\): gravity, 9.81. \(L\): length, 1.
  • Domain: \(t \in [0, 10]\), with a dummy \(x\) the solution does not depend on.
  • Conditions: \(\theta(0) = 0.5\) rad, \(\theta'(0) = 0\); periodic in the dummy \(x\).
  • Exact solution (ode): none in closed form. The trajectory is integrated with scipy to a relative tolerance of 1e-11.
  • Architecture: resnet.

docs.title: Shipped defaults
docs.text:
Override any default with flags or your own config.

Key Domain × time Details heat [0, 2] × [0, 10] Heat heat_2d [0, 1]² × [0, 5] Heat in 2-D wave [0, 1] × [0, 1] Wave burgers [−1, 1] × [0, 1] Burgers convection [0, 2] × [0, 1] Convection kdv [−15, 15] × [0, 5] Korteweg–de Vries allen_cahn [−1, 1] × [0, 1] Allen–Cahn cahn_hilliard [−1, 1] × [0, 1] Cahn–Hilliard black_scholes S ∈ [0, 200] × τ ∈ [0, 1] Black–Scholes pendulum t ∈ [0, 10] Pendulum

The Allen–Cahn and Cahn–Hilliard defaults start from their stationary kinks. That makes them consistency checks, not hard dynamics problems.

The dynamic Allen–Cahn benchmark (as in Wu et al., 2023) is

\[ u_t = 0.001\,u_{xx} + 5\,(u - u^3), \qquad u_0 = x^2\cos(\pi x), \qquad u(\pm 1, t) = -1, \qquad t \in [0, 1] \]

pinnrl-benchmark sampling runs it in rescaled time \(\tau = 5t\), that is \(\varepsilon^2 = 0.0002\), \(r = 1\) and \(\tau \in [0, 5]\).

To set it up yourself:

  1. Set initial_condition: {type: x2_cos}.
  2. Set boundary_conditions: {dirichlet: {value: -1}}.
  3. Set exact_solution: {} (the default exact BCs come from the kink).
  4. Score against pinnrl.benchmarks.reference.allen_cahn_reference.

docs.title: Adding a PDE
docs.text:
Write it: CustomPDE("u_t + u*u_x - nu*u_xx", domain={"x": (-1, 1), "t": (0, 1)}, parameters={"nu": 0.01}) builds a trainable problem from the residual.

  • It covers scalar PDEs, ODEs, steady problems and systems, in Python or as a YAML file for pinnrl-train --pde-file. See Custom equations.
  • The catalogue holds 43 ready problems. An entry that shares a key with this page, such as heat, has its own domain and parameters.

To ship one with the package:

  1. Subclass PDEBase and implement compute_residual (and _exact_solution if one exists).
  2. Add one PDESpec line to pinnrl/pdes/registry.py and a block to config.yaml. The new PDE then appears in the CLI and the dashboard.
  3. Add its exact-solution check to test_physics_consistency.py.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes a new user from installation to a first trained PINN, on the command line and in Python.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install pinnrl            # or: uv add pinnrl
  • Python: 3.10–3.13.
  • PyTorch: installed as a dependency. It runs on CPU, Apple GPU (mps) or CUDA.
  • Compiled engine: the default training step is compiled C++ and needs a C++ compiler at first use. Without one, everything runs on PyTorch autograd. See The native engine.
Extra (pip install 'pinnrl[name]') Adds pinnrl[well] Loaders for The Well benchmark datasets pinnrl[notebooks] Jupyter, for the tutorial notebooks in the repository pinnrl[docs], pinnrl[dev] Building these docs; tests and linters

docs.title: First run from the command line
docs.text:
pinnrl-train --pde burgers --arch fourier --epochs 2000 --device cpu
  • --pde: a key (heat, heat_2d, wave, burgers, convection, kdv, allen_cahn, cahn_hilliard, black_scholes, pendulum) or the display name ("Burgers Equation").
  • --arch: the network architecture, here Fourier features.
  • --device: a device that is not available falls back to CPU.
  • Other settings: they come from the packaged config.yaml. Override them with flags (see Training), or pass --config my.yaml.
  • Engine: --derivatives auto (the default) uses the compiled engine where it applies. --derivatives autograd switches it off.

Each run writes a folder under ./runs/ in the current directory:

File Contents config.yaml The exact configuration used metadata.json Run info and status, final and best validation loss, true and identified parameters (inverse mode) history.json (and an identical metrics.json) Per-epoch losses, learning rate and, in inverse mode, parameter values final_model.pt Model weights (reload with pinnrl.training.train.load_run) experiment.log, live_snapshot.npz The training log; the prediction and residual grid the dashboard plots visualizations/final_training_history.png, final_solution_comparison.png, collocation_evolution.png Plots
  • Inverse mode: training that also identifies parameters of the equation from measurements.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
pinnrl-dashboard                 # opens http://127.0.0.1:8050/
pinnrl-dashboard --port 8051 --no-browser

The dashboard configures and launches runs, shows the solution and residual surfaces as training proceeds, and compares finished runs.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The shortest route is your equation as text. Here it is the heat equation with diffusivity \(\alpha = 0.1\) and a known exact solution \(u^*\):

\[ u_t - \alpha\, u_{xx} = 0, \qquad u(x, 0) = \sin(2\pi x), \qquad u^*(x, t) = e^{-4\alpha\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x) \]
  • CustomPDE: builds the problem from the text.
  • build_trainer: builds a trainer with the packaged defaults.
from pinnrl import CustomPDE

pde = CustomPDE("u_t - alpha*u_xx", domain={"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)}, parameters={"alpha": 0.1},
                initial_condition="sin(2*pi*x)", boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}},
                exact_solution="exp(-4*alpha*pi^2*t)*sin(2*pi*x)")
trainer = pde.build_trainer("fourier", num_epochs=150, num_collocation_points=1024, batch_size=1024,
                            learning_rate=2e-3, early_stopping={"enabled": False})
trainer.train(progress=False)
print(f"relative L2 error: {pde.validate(trainer.model)['l2_error']:.2e}")

See Custom equations for systems, ODEs, callables and the YAML form.

The same pieces, spelled out: a shipped PDE class (HeatEquation) with its PDEConfig, a PINNModel and a PDETrainer.

import torch

from pinnrl.config import Config, ModelConfig, TrainingConfig
from pinnrl.neural_networks import PINNModel
from pinnrl.pdes import HeatEquation, PDEConfig
from pinnrl.training import PDETrainer

device = torch.device("cpu")
training = TrainingConfig.from_dict({
    "num_epochs": 200,
    "batch_size": 500,
    "num_collocation_points": 500,
    "num_boundary_points": 100,
    "num_initial_points": 100,
    "optimizer_config": {"learning_rate": 5e-3, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    "scheduler_type": "constant",
    "early_stopping": {"enabled": False},
})

# u_t = alpha * u_xx on [0, 1] x [0, 1], periodic in x, u(x, 0) = sin(2 pi x)
pde = HeatEquation(PDEConfig(
    name="Heat Equation",
    domain=[[0.0, 1.0]],
    time_domain=[0.0, 1.0],
    parameters={"alpha": 0.1},
    boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}},
    initial_condition={"type": "sine", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    exact_solution={"type": "sin_exp_decay", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    dimension=1,
    device=device,
    training=training,
))

config = Config()
config.device, config.training = device, training
config.model = ModelConfig.from_architecture(
    "fourier",
    {"hidden_dims": [64, 64, 64], "mapping_size": 32, "scale": 4.0, "activation": "tanh"},
    input_dim=2,
    output_dim=1,
)
model = PINNModel(config, device=device)

PDETrainer(model, pde, config=config, device=device).train(progress=False)
metrics = pde.validate(model)
print(f"relative L2 error: {metrics['l2_error']:.2e}")

validate returns four metrics:

  • l2_error: the relative L2 error \(\lVert u - u^* \rVert / \lVert u^* \rVert\) of the network \(u\) against the exact solution \(u^*\).
  • mse, max_error, mean_error: the mean squared, maximum and mean errors.
