• Concepts explains the loss, sampling and architecture choices behind these settings.
  • When to use a PINN says which problems suit the method.
  • The tutorial notebooks cover a first PINN, an architecture comparison, the RL sampler, The Well, inverse problems, and (06–08) the identification-baseline, conditioning, and stability-and-uncertainty experiments, reviewed from their raw results.

docs.title: What has been built
docs.text: The record of every release: what each one set out to do, what was built, and what the experiments it served found. Newest first. The terse per-release list of changes is the changelog; what comes next is the roadmap. Experiment codes (B01, J06, ...) name folders under experiments/, each with a README stating the question, the protocol and the result.

docs.title: Unreleased: v0.9 so far
docs.text:
The engine release. The compiled kernel became the default, a benchmark against every alternative showed where it was behind, and the two mechanisms that benchmark named were built into the package. The terse list is in the changelog; what is still open is on the roadmap.

  • A head-to-head with the alternatives (I17). Done: the same step in eager PyTorch, torch.compile, torch.func, JAX (reverse, forward and Taylor mode) and DeepXDE on nine equations (Benchmarks). The first run had JAX's forward mode 1.2–1.3× ahead of the kernel and named why (fused per-equation loops, a rational tanh); with both built in, pinnrl is first on all nine on an Apple M4 (1.1–1.8× JAX, 2.4–7.7× eager PyTorch, 2.7–9.9× DeepXDE, about 3× PhysicsNeMo where that runs). On a Linux x86 runner JAX's forward mode is 1–11 % ahead on seven plain-network problems; pinnrl leads at fourth order and with layer normalization.
  • derivatives="auto" as the default. Done: the kernel wherever it applies, autograd elsewhere, silently. A gradient of the kernel that is differentiated again (analysis.spectrum, analysis.surrogate, any Hessian-vector product) is taken by autograd on the same function, and torch.func transforms see the ordinary module, so no tool has to know which engine ran.
  • A step compiled per equation. Done: pinnrl.native.specialize writes C++ for the equations given as text (the Taylor recurrences through tanh as one fused loop for exactly the streams they use, the residual and its adjoint inlined by SymPy), compiles it once and caches it; the general kernel serves the first 32 evaluations, so a short run never waits. 1.3–1.7× over the general kernel on an Apple M4, 1.1× on Linux x86, where the matrix products dominate.
  • The compiled step for the inverse problems, scaled networks and layer normalization. Done: the step returns the gradients of trainable parameters, takes measured inputs and unknown functions of the coordinates as per-point values with their adjoints returned, handles a network's input and output scaling (normalize=True), and runs layer normalization through generated row loops of its own, 1.3–1.4× the general kernel with normalization on. Each case is checked against autograd in tests/unit_tests/test_native_specialize.py.
  • A faster tanh in the kernels. Done: a rational approximation (the form Eigen uses) in place of Accelerate's vvtanhf and the Cephes form on Linux, 0.4 against 1.1 ns an element at float32 accuracy (2.4e-7).
  • A manual benchmark workflow. Done: .github/workflows/benchmark.yml runs experiment I17 on a Linux x86 runner, started by hand.

docs.title: v0.8: performance and the PINN's case (released 2026-11-18)
docs.text:
• Time breakdown of a step, and the same step in C++ and Rust (I01, I11). Done: the step is arithmetic (sampling, optimizer and bookkeeping under a tenth); tanh and the double-backward passes dominate; a framework-free step on Accelerate takes 3.6 ms in either language against 8.8 ms in PyTorch and 10.6 ms in the trainer.
  • The kernel in the trainer. Done: pinnrl.native and build_trainer(derivatives="native"), 10.6 → 5.4 ms a step on the benchmark problem with the same gradients to rounding; opt-in; macOS, plain tanh networks, first and pure second derivatives.
  • Layer normalization in the kernel, so the packaged default network benefits (I12). Done: 32 → 10.4 ms a step on the default network. The check against autograd exposed a PyTorch defect, a wrong third-order derivative of nn.LayerNorm (weight gradients of second-order residuals 2–3 % off); the package's networks now use ExactLayerNorm.
  • Mixed and third- and fourth-order derivatives (KdV, Cahn–Hilliard) (I13). Done: the kernel carries general Taylor coefficients through tanh and layer normalization; residual, loss and weight gradient agree with autograd to rounding on heat, KdV, a mixed \(u_{xxt}\), the beam and Cahn–Hilliard, and the step gains 1.9–4× on the plain network and 3–7× with layer normalization, the more the higher the order; the special cases of I11/I12 lose under 5 %.
  • A Linux build on OpenBLAS, tested in CI (I14). Done: the same source builds with g++ -lopenblas on first use, with a vectorised tanh of its own; CI installs OpenBLAS and fails rather than skips the kernel tests. On the same machine the Linux step gains 1.4–3.0× against 1.9–4.7× under Accelerate: Taylor mode saves the elementwise work, not the matrix products, and without Apple's AMX those are two thirds of the step.
  • One value pass for boundary and initial points; the registry's PDE classes through the kernel (I15). Done: every face and the initial points share one kernel call (worth 2 % of the heat step), and PDEBase.compute_derivatives goes through the kernel for the registry's classes, which gain 1.7–2.7× on a plain network and 2.3–4.7× with layer normalization; pinnrl-train --derivatives native now applies to every problem.
  • Compiled right-hand sides for the method-of-lines reference solvers, which the classical estimators spend their time in (I16). Done: the evaporator's model under a compiled SDIRK4 integrator with exact per-cell stage solves (reference(method="native"), native_propagator, monitor_fouling(integrator="auto")); 3–8× per solve on smooth inputs, 50–100× on a plant record whose kinks collapse BDF, a batch fit from 106 s to 0.7 s with the same estimate; the monitor 1.6×, its time now in the filter's Jacobian and matrix exponential.
  • A process unit whose forward solve is not a cheap initial-value problem (a transient or counter-current dryer, a droplet size distribution, wall deposition): the first place the PINN twin's case can be tested, after three units on which the classical estimator through the reference solver won. Done: pinnrl.process.CounterCurrentDryer (J13), the air against the falling droplets: the steady state is a boundary-value problem solved by shooting (100 ms, twenty times the co-current tower) and the transient a hyperbolic system with characteristics both ways, which the method of lines with a sparse Jacobian integrates in 0.04–0.6 s. The PINN's case is not made: a fit of the curve's two parameters and the wall loss from one transient record takes 10 s and lands within the linear prediction, while the PINN twin fails the misfit test on every run (its forward solve, with the equations scaled and the residual weight tuned, stays at 12–15 % on the moisture). What it would take is a model with no method-of-lines form at all.
  • The line-level twin: a multi-pass evaporator feeding the dryer, with errors propagated across the units (J10). Done: pinnrl.process.ProcessLine chains evaporator passes into the dryer (the concentrate sets the droplets' solids and the solids flow) with steady, reference, records and propagate (the variance budget of the powder by source, linear and Monte Carlo). On a four-hour shift with three fouling passes, the powder inherits the feed flow and the droplet size once the fouling is monitored, but propagation is the wrong estimator for it: the dryer's own records determine the powder to ±0.005 against ±0.09 by propagation (±0.001 with every record), information flows downstream only (the dryer's records leave the fouling at its prior), and the first pass's fouling is one unknown with the feed's calibration; ten simulated shifts confirm the linear predictions.

docs.title: v0.7: process twins (released 2026-11-12)
docs.text:
• pinnrl.process: the falling-film evaporator with its method-of-lines reference simulator and custom_pde() form (J01, J02 done); fouling estimation from outlet sensors (J03: the drift to 9–16 %, at the surrogate's limit) and its identifiability (J04: the data allow 5 % on the end value; U and the constant fouling are one unknown; the steam temperature is the nuisance that matters). The drying droplet (pinnrl.process.DryingDroplet, J07) is the second unit: its forward PINN solve reaches 8–14 %; the free-function closure collapses to a constant from a cold start and reaches 1.7–2.1 % from a pointwise estimate of the record (J07b), with a 1-in-3 risk of leaving the basin. The intervals are measured (J06, 100 data sets): a batch fit through the reference solver and a trend filter on 51 cells are calibrated (0.91–0.99) where the model is right and the fouling's assumed form contains the truth; an 11-cell model, a ramp assumed for a curve that bends, or a steam record trusted beyond its accuracy each break it, and the PINN twin fails to train on 22 of 36 runs and has no calibrated interval. A learned closure is checked by DryingDroplet.record_misfit through the reference solver (J07c catches every failure of J07b), and a monotone closure fitted by shooting reaches 1.5 % from a cold start on every seed (J07d): on the two units built so far the classical estimators win, and the PINN's case is a model without a cheap trusted forward solve. UnknownFunction(anchor=...) holds a value at a point (J07e: the closure zero at equilibrium by construction removes the pointwise start's 60–90-fold misfit, and the PINN refinement then adds nothing), and pde.sensor_misfit with train_with_restarts is the acceptance test and restart rule a twin applies to itself. The dryer-scale model is pinnrl.process.SprayDryer, the droplet coupled to its air in a co-current tower (J11): one solve takes 5 ms, so the estimator is again a fit through the reference; a tower's instruments determine the two parameters of a known curve form (±0.03 from five operating points) and 4–6 of a free-form closure's 11 directions, yet predict the powder moisture outside the campaign to 1–2 %. Open: a tower whose forward solve is not a cheap initial-value problem (transient, counter-current, a size distribution, wall deposition), where the PINN's case can first be tested. The stickiness margin is SprayDryer.stickiness_margin (J08): the twin gives it at the outlet to 1.0–1.5 K where a lab assay gives 1.6–3.2 K and the air's water balance 23–59 K. K09 (linearized stability) is done: the physics is convectively stabilised and not stiff; the discretised operator's spectrum is a pseudospectrum.
  • Classical estimators on the same models: pinnrl.process.ExtendedKalmanFilter with an RTS smoother and FallingFilmEvaporator.fouling_state_space (J05: on a known model the filter beats the PINN twin by a wide margin at a thousandth of the cost; the PINN's case is the partly unknown model). pinnrl.process.MovingHorizonEstimator adds bounds on states and disturbances (J05b: the filter's accuracy on the evaporator at 10–35 times the cost; the growth constraint smooths without correcting). augment_local_linear_trend, time_to_threshold and monitor_fouling are the drift model, the time to the next cleaning and the packaged fouling monitor J06 arrives at.
  • Historian adapter: CSV or Parquet plus a tag map to sensor definitions. Done: pinnrl.process.Historian (wide and long exports, quality flags, dated timestamps, unit conversion, windows and resampling) and Historian.apply(tag_map), which gives the inputs as TimeSeries, the sensors with their records, and records() for the filters; see Process twins.
  • A dashboard "Process" view: soft-sensor trends with uncertainty bands, and time to the next cleaning. Done: the Process tab runs monitor_fouling on an export and a tag map and plots the fouling with its band, the projected cleaning time with its interval and the outlet records against the model; see Dashboard.
  • Bayesian measurement design for sensors and lab sampling (J09; P24). Done: pinnrl.analysis.posterior_covariance, target_std, information_gain and greedy_design; on the evaporator with every instrument error admitted, the steam offset and the four mass-balance instruments jointly limit the fouling estimate (10.6 %), no single calibration pays, a condensate meter halves it and with a 4 K steam swing reaches 2.8 %; lab samples buy little and are best at the end, a quarter and past the middle of the window. See Benchmarks.
  • Type checking (mypy) across the package. Done: uv run mypy passes on the 66 modules of pinnrl (default strictness, configured in pyproject.toml) and runs in CI next to ruff.

docs.title: v0.6: richer unknowns and inputs (released 2026-11-04)
docs.text:
• Field-valued unknowns: a learnable coefficient field \(\alpha(x, t)\) or closure \(f(u)\), with positivity and monotonicity constraints. Done: CustomPDE(unknown_functions=...) with UnknownFunction; F09 recovers \(\alpha(t)\) to 4 % and a two-layer \(\alpha(x)\) in shape on heat, and shows which fields the data cannot determine.
  • Coupled multi-field systems (output_dim > 1) with per-field BCs and loss weights. Done: CustomPDE(boundary_conditions={field: ...}, field_weights=...); the catalogue's reaction_diffusion_pair trains to its closed form in test_coupled_systems.py.
  • Measured inputs: BCs and forcing from interpolated time series. Done: CustomPDE(inputs={"q": {"path": "left.csv"}}, boundary_conditions={"dirichlet": {"left": "q"}}); test_measured_inputs.py trains heat with its boundary following a CSV.
  • Sensor operators: point, boundary and integral observations with per-sensor noise and delay. Done: CustomPDE(sensors=[PointSensor, BoundarySensor, IntegralSensor]), pde.observe, sensor_jacobian; K02 ranks layouts by their Fisher information and trains on sensor records (F05's fixed probes are one PointSensor each; its results predate the module).
  • Non-dimensionalization helpers (a reference scale per variable). Done: CustomPDE(scales=...) + build_trainer(normalize=True) / --normalize; a heat problem in millimetres, seconds and kelvin trains like the unit problem (test_normalization.py). J01 will be the first process model to use it.
  • High-dimensional stability: dimension sweeps of stability constants and quadrature error. Done: K08, heat and convection in \(d = 1 \ldots 5\); the quadrature gap is dimension-independent, the stability constant grows with the condition errors, and high-dimensional convection collapses to zero.

docs.title: v0.5: the inverse-modelling core (released 2026-10-26)
docs.text:
The goal is to estimate unknown physics with known validity conditions and calibrated uncertainty. Diagnostics come before UQ methods, because an unidentifiable or ill-conditioned problem has no meaningful error bar.

  1. User-defined equations. CustomPDE: any PDE, ODE, steady problem or system from its residual as text (SymPy-parsed, autograd derivatives) or a Python callable, with expression-valued initial and exact solutions, identifiable parameters, and pinnrl-train --pde-file. Every later module (diagnostics, UQ, the process models of v0.7) is written against it rather than against one class per equation. Done: test_custom_pde.py checks parity with the shipped Heat, Burgers and pendulum residuals; see Custom equations.
  2. Theory pages. Well-posedness and conditional stability; structural vs practical identifiability; the Bayesian view (loss = negative log-posterior, data weight = 1/σ²); sources of uncertainty; calibration; the numerical-analysis bridge (Lax equivalence, stability constants, PINN error estimates). Done: Theory, four pages cited by DOI; the maintainer's reference papers are still to be added. Every later module cites the condition it relies on.
  3. Identification baseline. Scalar parameters vs noise, sensors, initial guess and data weight. Done: F01–F05 in experiments/ and Benchmarks. The surrogate floor is 2 % (heat), 20 % (KdV soliton) and 150 % (Burgers shock); above it the estimator is near-efficient. The data-weight question is K39.
  4. pinnrl.analysis: conditioning diagnostics. The sensitivity Jacobian by the implicit-function theorem on the trained surrogate; Fisher information, Cramér–Rao bound, correlations and eigen-directions; the loss-Hessian (Lanczos) and tangent-kernel spectra. Done: pinnrl.analysis; K01 (validated on heat and KdV, wrong on the unresolved Burgers shock), K03 and F07 are in experiments/. Profile likelihood is a driver (F07), not yet an API.
  5. Disturbance and stability analysis. Perturbation suites for data and for the problem; the linear prediction of the estimate's shift; empirical stability constants. Done: pinnrl.analysis.disturbance; K05 (bias and delay shifts match \(F^{-1}J^\top\Sigma^{-1}\delta y\) to 20 %), K06 (the surrogate respects the equation's stability above its own field error) and K07 (\(C \approx 1\) for linear evolution equations; the beam's error is set by its boundary terms) are in experiments/.
  6. pinnrl.uq: calibrated uncertainty. A likelihood-based data term (σ sets the weight and the misfit tolerance); deep ensembles with a dispersion diagnostic; a Laplace approximation that reuses the Hessian machinery of pinnrl.analysis; the region of equivalence as the primary output, sampled by a cloud particle swarm over the parameters on a parametric surrogate \(u_w(x, t; \theta)\), with intervals, percentiles and CDFs by counting (theory); coverage, width and CRPS metrics. Done: pinnrl.uq; F06/K10 (the Laplace width is exact for the random error, the 2 % bias costs coverage, ensembles over seeds cover 13 %, the physics region 90 %), K39 (the noise-model weight is worse than the tuned one because the surrogate's error is systematic) and K46 (the swarm confirms the ellipse at these noise levels and under-samples its edges) are in experiments/. K47 (the weighted swarm is centred but 0.5–0.7 as wide as the posterior) and K45 (one parametric surrogate covers the prior range to 0.2–2 % and the swarm on its misfit reproduces the closed-form region) complete the item.
  7. Sampling follow-ups for P02. B02 (more PDEs), B03 (the RAD k, c grid), B04 (resampling frequency), B08 (point-count scaling). Done: no sampler beats uniform significantly on smooth problems; the resampling cadence changes the Burgers error threefold and the study default moves to 10 steps; good RAD settings lie on c ≈ k/2 and a zero floor with a sharp exponent fails; the error scales as N^−1/3 on Burgers and not at all on Allen–Cahn. P02 can be drafted.

docs.title: v0.4: clean, verified, documented (released 2026-10-24)
docs.text:
• Physics audit: every exact solution satisfies its PDE, IC and BC; real Dirichlet, Neumann and periodic BCs; correct 2-D derivatives. Done: test_physics_consistency.py is green.
  • One training loop (PDETrainer.train / train_steps), one PDE registry, one entry point per action.
  • A working, experimental RL bandit sampler; RAD with k/c.
  • Numerical reference solutions. Done: Burgers reproduces Basdevant et al. (1986), \(u_x(0, 1.6037/\pi) = -152.00516\) for \(\nu = 0.01/\pi\); the Allen–Cahn solution is grid-converged.
  • B01/B06 sampling benchmark, 10 seeds at equal steps and equal evaluations. Done: Benchmarks, experiments/B01_sampling_equal_compute/.
  • Docs rewritten and audited against the code; ruff with docstring linting; strict docs build.
  • Bug batch from the documentation audit (Well loader coordinates, LRW zero-gradient weighting, network defaults, dashboard plots). Done: each fix has a test that fails without it (test_audit_regressions.py, test_well_loader.py).
  • Release. Done: CI and scripts/verify_release.sh are green, and v0.4.0 is on PyPI via trusted publishing.

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text:
This page is for anyone who wants to estimate parameters or functions of an equation from measurements. It states the loss, the workflow, the settings an inverse run needs, and the conditions under which the answer can be trusted.

Examples: a thermal diffusivity from temperature traces, a wave speed from surface seismograms, a fouling resistance from evaporator temperatures, a volatility from option prices.

A PINN learns the solution and the parameters in one optimization:

\[ \min_{\theta,\,\lambda}\; \mathcal{L} = w_r\,\mathcal{L}_\text{residual}(\theta, \lambda) + w_b\,\mathcal{L}_\text{boundary} + w_i\,\mathcal{L}_\text{initial} + w_d \operatorname{mean} \lvert u_\theta(x_\text{obs}, t_\text{obs}) - u_\text{obs} \rvert^2 \]
  • \(\lambda\): the unknown parameters of the equation. They are trainable tensors, updated with the network weights \(\theta\).
  • \(\mathcal{L}_\text{residual}\): the mean squared residual \(\mathcal{N}[u_\theta; \lambda]\) of the equation at the collocation points (sampled points inside the domain). It ties \(\lambda\) to physically consistent solutions.
  • Data term: the last term, the misfit at the observations \((x_\text{obs}, t_\text{obs}, u_\text{obs})\). It pulls the solution toward the measurements.
  • \(w_r, w_b, w_i, w_d\): the loss weights residual, boundary, initial and data.

Classical methods run a forward solver many times, plus its adjoint or an ensemble of solves. A PINN needs neither: one optimization returns \(u_\theta\) and \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
pinnrl-train --pde heat --arch fourier --epochs 3000 --device cpu \
  --mode inverse --identify alpha --initial-guess alpha=0.5 \
  --obs-points 200 --obs-noise 0.01

What the run does:

  1. It makes alpha trainable, starting from 0.5.
  2. Without --obs-path, it samples observations from the PDE's exact solution at the configured (true) parameters and adds Gaussian noise. This is a recovery test whose answer is known.
  3. It trains the network and alpha together.
  4. It records the true and recovered values in the run's metadata.json.
Flag Default Meaning --identify NAME none A scalar parameter of the PDE to identify. Any one can be chosen, and the flag can be repeated --initial-guess NAME=VALUE the configured value Starting value of that parameter --obs-points 200 Number of synthetic observations --obs-noise 0.01 Standard deviation of their Gaussian noise --obs-path file.npz none Your own observations (see Your own measurements)

The command above keeps the packaged weight decay and gradient clipping. Add --weight-decay 0 --gradient-clipping 0 for an accurate estimate (see below).

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
1. Build a TrainingConfig with mode="inverse", no weight decay and no gradient clipping.
  2. Build the PDE with trainable_parameters and parameter_initial_guesses.
  3. Attach observations (synthetic here).
  4. Build the model and train.
  5. Read the estimate with pde.get_trainable_parameter_values().
import torch

from pinnrl.config import Config, ModelConfig, TrainingConfig
from pinnrl.neural_networks import PINNModel
from pinnrl.pdes import HeatEquation, PDEConfig
from pinnrl.training import PDETrainer

device = torch.device("cpu")
training = TrainingConfig.from_dict({
    "mode": "inverse",
    "num_epochs": 1500,
    "batch_size": 256,
    "num_collocation_points": 256,
    "optimizer_config": {"learning_rate": 5e-3, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    "scheduler_type": "constant",
    "early_stopping": {"enabled": False},
    "gradient_clipping": 0.0,
    "loss_weights": {"residual": 1.0, "boundary": 10.0, "initial": 10.0, "data": 50.0},
})

pde = HeatEquation(PDEConfig(
    name="Heat Equation",
    domain=[[0.0, 1.0]],
    time_domain=[0.0, 1.0],
    parameters={"alpha": 0.05},                      # the truth, used for synthetic data
    boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}},
    initial_condition={"type": "sine", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    exact_solution={"type": "sin_exp_decay", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    dimension=1,
    device=device,
    training=training,
    trainable_parameters=["alpha"],
    parameter_initial_guesses={"alpha": 0.5},        # start 10x off
))
pde.generate_synthetic_observations(n_points=200, noise_std=0.005, seed=0)

config = Config()
config.device, config.training = device, training
config.model = ModelConfig.from_architecture(
    "fourier",
    {"hidden_dims": [64, 64, 64], "mapping_size": 32, "scale": 4.0, "activation": "tanh"},
    input_dim=2,
    output_dim=1,
)
model = PINNModel(config, device=device)
PDETrainer(model, pde, config=config, device=device).train(progress=False)
print(pde.get_trainable_parameter_values())          # notebook 05 recovers about 0.0499

docs.title: Regularisation defaults for inverse runs
docs.text:
The packaged defaults are forward-fit defaults. An inverse run must start from weight_decay=0 and gradient_clipping=0.

Setting Packaged default Inverse runs Why optimizer_config.weight_decay 0.0005 0 It pulls the network toward zero and the parameter absorbs the bias (F01, D01) gradient_clipping 1.0 (the default of TrainingConfig; not in config.yaml) 0 Clipping at norm 1 slows the network and leaves a field error the parameter absorbs (F01, D01) Weight decay on the unknowns \(\lambda\) always 0 always 0 The trainer puts identified parameters and unknown functions in their own Adam group without decay (found in F09) optimizer adam Adam, then an L-BFGS finish (optimizer="adam_lbfgs", or lbfgs_steps in train_windows; see Training) The finish halves the error and the bias again (D01) loss_weights.data 10 search 10–100 See When the inversion is well posed

The evidence, on the heat diffusivity \(\alpha\) (F01, D01):

  • Packaged defaults: the relative error of \(\hat\alpha\) stays at 1.5–2 % whatever the number of observations (F01).
  • Both off: 0.1–0.2 % on clean data (F01). With noise 0.01 the error falls with the number of observations along the Cramér–Rao bound, the smallest standard deviation any unbiased estimate can have for the given sensors and noise.
  • Both off, with an L-BFGS finish: 0.2 %, against 0.4 % for Adam alone (D01). D01's ablation attributes about half of the old floor to each of the two settings.
  • F11 (change point) saw the same effect: under the defaults a 3.6 % field error was absorbed into a smaller jump placed early, and three times the training did not help.
  • The packaged defaults are unchanged, so set both to 0 yourself. Troubleshooting lists the symptom under "An identified parameter stalls 1–2 % from the truth".

docs.title: Unknown functions
docs.text:
When the unknown is a function, replace the scalar by an unknown_functions entry of a CustomPDE:

\[ u_t = \big(\alpha(x)\,u_x\big)_x, \qquad \alpha(\cdot) \approx \text{a second network} \]
  • Unknown function: a coefficient that depends on the coordinates or on the solution. Examples: a diffusivity that drifts as a surface fouls, a coefficient that varies along the equipment, a closure \(f(u)\).
  • Closure: a relation the equation needs and the physics does not supply.
  • Constraints: declare the function positive, bounded or monotone. Its network trains with the data under them.
  • Grading: pde.unknown_function_error(name) compares it with the truth the synthetic data came from.

What this recovers on the heat equation (F09):

  • a linear drift \(\alpha(t)\), to a few percent;
  • a step in \(\alpha(t)\), as a steep ramp;
  • a two-layer field \(\alpha(x)\), to its shape;
  • not a centred bump in \(\alpha(x)\): the solution hardly depends on it.

docs.title: Your own measurements
docs.text:
Point observations:

  1. Save an .npz file with arrays x of shape (N, d), t of shape (N, 1) and u of shape (N, 1).
  2. Pass it with --obs-path, in the dashboard (Observation source → File), or as PDEConfig(observation_data={"path": ...}).

A Well dataset can also serve as the observation source.

Plant records are better described as sensors. Each sensor \(s\) adds its own misfit term to the data loss:

\[ \mathcal{L}_\text{data} \mathrel{+}= w_s \operatorname{mean} \left\lvert \frac{H_s[u_\theta] - y_s}{c_s} \right\rvert^2 \]
  • Sensor: records \(y_s\) with an operator \(H_s\): a probe at a fixed place read over time, a wall flux, an integral. Each has its noise and delay.
  • \(w_s\), \(c_s\): its weight (default 1) and scale (default 1, or the field's scale when the problem is normalised).
  • Fisher information: how much a sensor layout says about the unknowns, computed from the sensitivities of the readings.

Steps:

  1. Declare the sensors: CustomPDE(sensors=[PointSensor(x0, times), ...]).
  2. Attach the readings: sensor.set_values(records).
  3. Before training, compute sensor_jacobian to get the Fisher information of the layout and choose the sensors.

docs.title: When the inversion is well posed
docs.text:
• The data must excite the parameter. Diffusivity cannot be recovered from a steady state, because it leaves no signature there. Observations must cover the regime where the parameter acts.
  • Balance the data weight. Too small, and the parameter barely moves from its initial guess. Too large, and the network fits the noise and the physics stops constraining it. The example above (256 collocation points, 200 observations, noise 0.005) uses 50; 10–100 is a reasonable range to search.
  • Check identifiability before trusting a number. Several parameters, or a parameter field, may not be uniquely determined by the sensors you have. The theory pages state the conditions, and pinnrl.analysis computes the Fisher bound when a closed form exists.
  • A field is identified only where the solution feels it. For \(u_t = (\alpha(x) u_x)_x\) the sensitivity to a local relative change \(\delta\alpha / \alpha\) is proportional to the flux there:
\[ \frac{\delta u}{\delta \alpha / \alpha}(x) \;\propto\; \alpha\,u_x \]
  • \(\alpha\) is invisible where \(u_x\) vanishes.
  • A localized perturbation is smoothed by diffusion before it reaches the sensors.
  • The check: compare the truth's solution with the one of the best constant (heat_variable_reference makes this one line). If they differ by less than the trained network's own error, the data cannot resolve the field.

docs.title: The software paper
docs.text:
A paper describes the package's goals, its design and its benchmarks in one citable place: the statement of need, the state of the field, the trainer, the inverse-modelling toolbox, the process units, the native engine, and tables from the experiments (the training step against PyTorch, JAX and DeepXDE; forward accuracy against classical solvers; sampling at equal compute; parameter identification and calibration; the process twins against their classical estimators).

  • Source: paper/paper.md, with its references in paper/paper.bib.
  • Status: a draft in the repository; not yet submitted.
  • Reproducing its tables: each one names the folder under experiments/ whose script produces it; the same numbers are on the benchmarks page.

docs.text:
Until the paper is published, cite the software:

  author = {Garcia Ventura, Jose},
  title  = {pinnrl: physics-informed neural networks with adaptive collocation sampling},
  url    = {https://github.com/josegarciav/PINNs-RL-PDE}
}

The package started as the MSc thesis On Solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) (University of the Basque Country UPV/EHU, 2025), which is here.

docs.title: Process twins
docs.text:
This page shows how to build the twin of a process unit with pinnrl.process: the model of each unit, what a plant measures on it, and which estimator recovers what it cannot measure. It is for readers who know machine learning and want the process-engineering side; the full results are in Benchmarks (experiments J01–J13).

  • Twin: a model of a running unit, kept in step with its records, that reports quantities no instrument measures.
  • Reference solver: a classical numerical solver of the unit's model. It plays the plant in the experiments and the forward model in the classical estimators.
  • Classical estimator: one that needs no neural network (a Kalman filter, a least-squares fit through the reference solver). Every PINN result is compared with one.

pinnrl.process holds reference simulators of the units, the same models as CustomPDE problems for the PINN, the classical estimators, and an adapter for plant-historian data.

docs.title: The units
docs.text:
Unit Class Unknown a plant cannot measure Falling-film evaporator tube FallingFilmEvaporator the fouling resistance \(R_f(t)\) Drying droplet DryingDroplet the drying-rate closure \(f(X)\) Spray-dryer tower (co-current, steady) SprayDryer the same closure, seen through the air Counter-current tower (steady and transient) CounterCurrentDryer the curve's parameters and the wall loss, from a transient The line: evaporator passes feeding the dryer ProcessLine every unit's unknowns, and which one the powder inherits

Each class has two faces:

  • reference: the reference solver, an ODE integrator or the method of lines (space derivatives replaced by differences on a grid, which leaves ODEs in time).
  • custom_pde(): the same equations with their inputs, scales and sensors, for the PINN.

docs.title: The falling-film evaporator
docs.text:
• Falling film: a thin liquid film that runs down the inside of a steam-heated tube and boils as it goes, which concentrates the liquid.
  • Fouling: a deposit that grows on the heated wall and adds a resistance \(R_f\) to the heat flow. The tube is cleaned when \(R_f\) reaches a limit.
\[ \begin{aligned} W_t + v\,W_z &= -\frac{v\,P\,q}{\lambda}, \\ X_t + v\,X_z &= \frac{v\,X\,P\,q}{\lambda\,W}, \\ q &= \frac{T_s(t) - T_b(X)}{1/U + R_f(t)}, \qquad T_b(X) = T_{sat} + k_{bpe}\,X . \end{aligned} \]
  • \(W(z, t)\): liquid mass flow, kg/s. \(X(z, t)\): solids mass fraction.
  • \(z\): distance down the tube of length \(L\) (10 m). \(v\): film velocity (0.5 m/s, 20 s of residence).
  • \(q\): wall heat flux, W/m². \(P\): wetted perimeter. \(\lambda\): latent heat of evaporation.
  • \(T_s(t)\): steam temperature. \(T_b\): boiling point of the film. \(T_{sat}\): the solvent's saturation temperature. \(k_{bpe}\): boiling-point elevation, the rise of the boiling point per unit of solids.
  • \(U\): clean heat-transfer coefficient (2,000 W/m²K). \(R_f(t)\): fouling resistance, m²K/W.
  • Inlet: \(W(0, t) = W_{in}(t)\), \(X(0, t) = X_{in}(t)\), the feed.

Measured:

  • the inputs \(T_s(t)\), \(W_{in}(t)\), \(X_{in}(t)\);
  • the outlet \(X(L, t)\) and \(W(L, t)\).

Unknown:

  • \(R_f(t)\). Only the sum \(1/U + R_f\) enters, so a monitor estimates the change of resistance since a reference state (J04).

Headline (J05): an extended Kalman filter on an 11-cell model recovers \(R_f(t)\) to 3.5 % in L2 in 0.2 s; the PINN twin reaches 9–16 % in five minutes and fails to train on 22 of 36 runs (J03, J06). Every estimator is in Benchmarks.

Finding: with the model's structure known, the classical estimators reach the data limit at a thousandth of the PINN twin's cost. The steam temperature is the input that limits every estimator (J04).

The other units have their model where the page uses them: the droplet, the co-current tower, the counter-current tower and the line.

The plant used in the rest of the page: a fouling ramp, a recorded steam signal, noisy outlet records.

import numpy as np
from pinnrl.process import FallingFilmEvaporator

T = 600.0
steam = lambda t: 355.15 + np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 400.0)   # recorded, K
plant = FallingFilmEvaporator(T_s=steam, R_f=lambda t: 1e-4 * t / T)
ref = plant.reference(t_max=T, nz=51, nt=121)               # one output every 5 s
times = ref.t[1:]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
records = np.stack(                                         # outlet solids and flow, with noise
    [ref.X.u[-1, 1:] + 0.002 * rng.standard_normal(times.size),
     ref.W.u[-1, 1:] + 0.001 * rng.standard_normal(times.size)], axis=1)

docs.title: Estimating a drifting parameter
docs.text:
\[ \frac{ds}{dt} = f(t, s, \theta), \qquad y_k = h(t_k, s) + v_k, \qquad v_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R) . \]
  • \(s\): the model's state (here \(W\) and \(X\) on a coarse grid). \(\theta\): the drifting unknown (here \(R_f\)).
  • \(y_k\): the record at time \(t_k\). \(R\): its noise covariance.
  • Extended Kalman filter (EKF): at each record, corrects the model's prediction by the record, each weighted by its uncertainty; the model is linearized at the current estimate.
  • Smoother: a backward pass that estimates each time from the whole record (the hindsight estimate).
  • Process noise \(Q\): how much each state may wander between records.

With the structure known and one slowly drifting unknown, this filter on a coarse method-of-lines model is the estimator to beat (J05). The unknown joins the state in one of two ways:

Drift model Equations Suits Limit Random walk (augment_random_walk) \(\dot\theta = w\) a parameter that wanders on a steady drift it lags, or needs so much process noise that its band is several times wider than its error Local linear trend (augment_local_linear_trend) \(\dot\theta = \rho,\ \dot\rho = w\) a parameter that drifts steadily honest only while the rate changes slowly
  • \(w\): white noise of intensity \(Q\). \(\rho\): the drift's rate.
  • The trend follows a ramp without lag and gives the rate a prognosis needs.
from pinnrl.process import ExtendedKalmanFilter, augment_local_linear_trend

nz = 11                                                     # a coarse model is enough for the filter
model = FallingFilmEvaporator(T_s=steam, R_f=0.0)
f, h, s0 = model.fouling_state_space(nz)                    # f(t, s, [R_f]), h(t, s), steady start
n = s0.size
ekf = ExtendedKalmanFilter(
    augment_local_linear_trend(f, n, 1),                    # state = [s, R_f, dR_f/dt]
    lambda t, x: h(t, x[:n]),
    Q=np.concatenate([np.zeros(n + 1), [(1e-9) ** 2]]),     # only the rate wanders
    R=np.array([0.002**2, 0.001**2]),
)
x0 = np.concatenate([s0, [0.5e-4, 0.0]])
P0 = np.diag(np.concatenate([np.full(n, 1e-6), [(1e-4) ** 2, (1e-6) ** 2]]))
res = ekf.run(times, records, x0, P0, smooth=True)
lo, hi = res.interval(0.9)                                  # (K, n + 2) each
print(f"R_f(T) = {res.filtered[-1, n]:.2e} in [{lo[-1, n]:.2e}, {hi[-1, n]:.2e}]  (truth 1.00e-04)")

The level and the rate give the time until the unknown reaches a limit \(\theta^*\), here the fouling at which the tube is cleaned:

\[ \tau = \frac{\theta^* - \theta}{\rho} . \]
  • time_to_threshold samples \(\tau\) from the level, the rate and their block of the covariance. The interval is asymmetric.
  • When the rate is not clearly positive, part of the draws never arrive: probability < 1 and an infinite upper end.
from pinnrl.process import time_to_threshold

idx = [n, n + 1]
tt = time_to_threshold(res.filtered[-1, n], res.filtered[-1, n + 1],
                       res.filtered_cov[-1][np.ix_(idx, idx)], threshold=2e-4)
print(f"cleaning in {tt.median / 60:.0f} min, 90 % interval "
      f"[{tt.lower / 60:.0f}, {tt.upper / 60:.0f}] min (truth 10 min)")

Such an interval can be trusted under three conditions (J06 measures each):

  1. The drift model fits the drift. A random walk's band is honest only where it is wide; a trend's only while the rate changes slowly.
  2. The model's own error is below the interval's width. A coarse grid biases the estimate by more than a tight interval allows.
  3. Every input the unknown can be traded against is measured to that accuracy or estimated alongside. For the evaporator that is the steam temperature (J04), which enters the state as one more constant with its prior.

monitor_fouling packages this for the evaporator: the trend filter on a 51-cell model, optionally with the steam record's offset as one more state. It returns the fouling with its band, the hindsight estimate, the records against the filter's predictions, and the time to clean.

from pinnrl.process import monitor_fouling

mon = monitor_fouling(FallingFilmEvaporator(T_s=steam), times, records,
                      steam_bias_std=0.3, threshold=2e-4)      # the steam record trusted to 0.3 K
print(mon.summary())

The estimators spend their time in the reference solve. Experiment I16 put the evaporator's method-of-lines model in C++ (pinnrl.native.evaporator), with an L-stable fourth-order SDIRK integrator.

  • reference(..., method="native") uses it, with the inputs sampled every 5 s and interpolated by a spline.
  • FallingFilmEvaporator.native_propagator(nz, steam_bias, trend) gives the filters a propagate(t0, t1, x) (ExtendedKalmanFilter(..., propagate=...)).
  • monitor_fouling(..., integrator="auto") takes it wherever it builds.
  • SciPy's BDF remains the default of reference and the fallback everywhere.

docs.title: Moving-horizon estimation
docs.text:
\[ \min_{x_0,\ w_1..w_N}\ \lVert x_0 - \bar x_0 \rVert^2_{P_0^{-1}} + \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lVert w_k \rVert^2_{Q^{-1}} + \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lVert y_k - h(t_k, x_k) \rVert^2_{R^{-1}} \quad \text{with} \quad x^{lo} \le x_0 \le x^{hi},\quad w^{lo} \le w_k \le w^{hi} . \]
  • Moving-horizon estimation (MHE): at every record, re-solve this least-squares problem over the last \(N\) records (horizon).
  • \(x_0\): the state at the window's start. \(\bar x_0\), \(P_0\): what the earlier records say about it (the arrival cost).
  • \(w_k\): one disturbance per record for each state with process noise. \(x_k\) follows the model from \(x_0\) and the \(w_k\).
  • Bounds: lower and upper on \(x_0\), noise_lower and noise_upper on the \(w_k\).

For a linear model without bounds, MovingHorizonEstimator is the Kalman filter, whatever the horizon. Use it for what the filter cannot express: bounds on the states and on the disturbances, such as a fouling resistance that only grows.

from pinnrl.process import MovingHorizonEstimator, augment_random_walk

Q = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n), [(1e-6) ** 2]])            # R_f a random walk
mhe = MovingHorizonEstimator(augment_random_walk(f, n, 1), lambda t, x: h(t, x[:n]),
                             Q=Q, R=np.array([0.002**2, 0.001**2]), horizon=12)
lower = np.r_[np.full(n, -np.inf), 0.0]                     # R_f >= 0
grow = mhe.run(times, records, np.concatenate([s0, [0.5e-4]]),
               np.diag(np.concatenate([np.full(n, 1e-6), [(1e-4) ** 2]])),
               lower=lower, noise_lower=0.0, stride=12)     # disturbances >= 0, one solve a minute
print(grow.t[-1], grow.filtered[-1, -1])

Results on the evaporator (J05b):

  • Cost: 10 to 35 times the filter, about three linearizations of the window per solve. stride solves every few records.
  • Accuracy: the filter's, because the evaporator's nonlinearity is mild.
  • What it adds: the constraint.

docs.title: Plant data: a historian export and a tag map
docs.text:
• Historian: the plant's database of instrument readings. Its export is a table of readings in plant units, with gaps and bad readings.
  • Tag: the name of one instrument signal, such as TT205.PV.
  • Tag map: which tag is which signal of the model, and how to convert it.

Historian.from_file reads:

  • a column per tag, or a row per reading (with an optional quality flag);
  • CSV or Parquet (Parquet needs pyarrow);
  • numeric or dated timestamps.
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from pinnrl.process import Historian

rows = ["timestamp,TT205.PV,DT310.PV,FT320.PV"]            # degC, % solids, kg/h
for k, t in enumerate(times):
    rows.append(f"{t:.0f},{steam(t) - 273.15:.3f},{100 * records[k, 0]:.4f},{3600 * records[k, 1]:.3f}")
export = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "evaporator.csv"
export.write_text("\n".join(rows) + "\n")

tag_map = {
    "inputs": {"T_s": {"tag": "TT205.PV", "offset": 273.15}},                 # degC -> K
    "sensors": [
        {"tag": "DT310.PV", "name": "outlet X", "location": 10.0, "expression": "X",
         "gain": 0.01, "noise": 0.002},                                        # % -> fraction
        {"tag": "FT320.PV", "name": "outlet W", "location": 10.0, "expression": "W",
         "gain": 1 / 3600, "noise": 0.001},                                    # kg/h -> kg/s
    ],
}
data = Historian.from_file(export).apply(tag_map)
print(data.t_max, data.inputs["T_s"], data.sensors)

The result feeds both kinds of estimator:

  • The PINN twin: the inputs are TimeSeries and the sensors carry their records, as custom_pde takes them.
  • A process model: series.numpy is the same signal as a plain function.
  • A filter: data.records() is the array it runs on.
model = FallingFilmEvaporator(T_s=data.inputs["T_s"].numpy, R_f=0.0)
hist_times, hist_records = data.records(["outlet X", "outlet W"])
pde = model.custom_pde(t_max=data.t_max, sensors=data.sensors,
                       unknown_fouling={"bounds": [0.0, 5e-4], "positive": False})
print(hist_records.shape, len(pde.sensors))

Shortcuts and options:

  • monitor_from_historian(data) runs the fouling monitor on such a window.
  • The dashboard's Process view does the same from the two file paths.
  • write_demo_export(folder) writes a synthetic export and its tag map to start from.
  • window: [t0, t1] in the map cuts an interval and shifts it to \(t = 0\).
  • every and aggregate (interp, mean, last) put a tag on a regular grid, which sensors need to share for records().
  • The map can be a YAML file with the same keys.

docs.title: Checking a learned closure
docs.text:
The unit is the drying droplet: one droplet of a solids solution in hot air, as on a single-droplet rig.

  • Closure: a relation the balance equations need but do not supply, here the drying rate as a function of the moisture.
  • Dry-basis moisture \(X\): kg of water per kg of solids.
  • Characteristic drying curve \(f(X)\): the drying rate divided by that of a fully wet surface. It is 1 above the critical moisture \(X_{cr}\) and 0 at and below the equilibrium moisture \(X_{eq}\).
\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dX}{dt} &= -r, \qquad r = \frac{h_m A\,\big(\rho_{vs}(T) - Y \rho_a\big)}{m_s}\, f(X), \\ \frac{dT}{dt} &= \frac{h A\,(T_a - T) - \lambda\, m_s\, r}{m_s\,(c_s + c_w X)}, \\ f(X) &= \min\!\left(1,\ \left(\frac{X - X_{eq}}{X_{cr} - X_{eq}}\right)^{n}\right) . \end{aligned} \]
  • \(T\), \(T_a\): droplet and air temperature. \(Y\): humidity ratio of the air, kg of water per kg of dry air. \(\rho_a\): air density.
  • \(r\): drying rate per unit of solids. \(m_s\): solids mass of the droplet. \(A\): its surface.
  • \(h\), \(h_m\): heat- and mass-transfer coefficients (Ranz–Marshall correlations of the droplet's diameter).
  • \(\rho_{vs}(T)\): vapour density at saturation. \(c_s\), \(c_w\): heat capacities of solids and water.
  • \(n\): exponent of the falling-rate part of the curve. Defaults: \(X_{eq} = 0.05\), \(X_{cr} = 1.0\), \(n = 1.5\).

Measured:

  • the droplet's mass \(m = m_s (1 + X)\);
  • its temperature \(T\).

Unknown:

  • the closure \(f(X)\).

Headline (J07d): shooting with a monotone piecewise-linear closure on 24 knots recovers \(f(X)\) to 1.5–1.6 % on every seed in 8–10 s; a PINN with \(f\) an unknown function, from a cold start, collapses to a constant on every seed (J07). Every estimator is in Benchmarks.

  • Shooting: adjust the unknowns until the reference solver's output matches the record.

Finding: with an ODE model and a reference solver that takes a closure, an unknown function is a few dozen bounded parameters, and shooting beats the PINN.

The network that produced a closure is not the judge of it: in J07b a closure 20 % off came with fields that fitted the record to 1 %. The check is independent of the network:

  1. Solve the model with the closure by the reference solver.
  2. Compare with the record by the reduced chi-square.
\[ \chi^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( \frac{y_i - \hat y_i}{\sigma_i} \right)^2 . \]
  • \(y_i\): a reading. \(\hat y_i\): the model's value. \(\sigma_i\): the reading's noise.
  • Reduced chi-square: about 1 when the closure explains the record to its noise.
  • DryingDroplet.record_misfit returns it for the mass, the temperature and both.
from pinnrl.process import DryingDroplet

dr = DryingDroplet()
run = dr.reference(200.0, nt=2001)
t_rec = np.arange(1.0, 201.0)
mass = np.interp(t_rec, run.t, run.m) + 0.005 * dr.m0 * rng.standard_normal(t_rec.size)
temp = np.interp(t_rec, run.t, run.T) + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(t_rec.size)
candidate = lambda X: np.clip((X - dr.X_eq) / (1.3 - dr.X_eq), 0.0, 1.0) ** 1.5   # a critical moisture 30 % off
print(dr.record_misfit(t_rec, mass, temp, 0.005 * dr.m0, 0.5)["total"],              # about 1
      dr.record_misfit(t_rec, mass, temp, 0.005 * dr.m0, 0.5, closure=candidate)["total"])

The rule from J07c:

  1. Reject a refined closure whose misfit is above its start's.
  2. Read the level: only a misfit near 1 says the closure reproduces the record.

With the network class, give the closure what is known of it:

  • Anchor: unknown_rate={"bounds": None, "anchor": {"at": dr.X_eq, "value": 0.0}} in custom_pde makes the closure zero at the equilibrium moisture by construction. That alone takes a pointwise estimate's misfit from 60–90 to about 2 (J07e).
  • The network's own fit: pde.sensor_misfit(trainer.model) is the same test without a reference solver.
  • Restarts: train_with_restarts restarts on that misfit.

docs.title: Which measurement to add
docs.text:
\[ \Sigma = \left( P_0^{-1} + J^\top R^{-1} J \right)^{-1} . \]
  • \(\Sigma\): posterior covariance of the unknowns around the operating point.
  • \(P_0\): prior covariance. Each instrument error is an unknown with its accuracy as the prior.
  • \(J\): sensitivities of the records to the unknowns. \(R\): measurement-noise covariance.

\(\Sigma\) does not depend on what the records turn out to be, so a sensor or a calibration is priced from the sensitivities alone, before buying it.

  • A calibration is a tighter prior.
  • A new measurement is more rows of \(J\).
from pinnrl.analysis import greedy_design, information, posterior_covariance, target_std

def outlet(theta):                                  # records for theta = [R_f mean (1e-4), R_f slope, steam offset]
    ev = FallingFilmEvaporator(T_s=lambda t: steam(t) - theta[2],
                               R_f=lambda t: 1e-4 * (theta[0] + theta[1] * (2 * t / T - 1)))
    r = ev.reference(t_max=T, nz=51, nt=121)
    return r.X.u[-1, 1:], r.W.u[-1, 1:]

nominal, steps = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.0]), np.array([0.02, 0.02, 0.02])
cols = []
for j in range(3):                                  # central differences through the reference solver
    up, dn = nominal.copy(), nominal.copy()
    up[j] += steps[j]
    dn[j] -= steps[j]
    cols.append([(a - b) / (2 * steps[j]) for a, b in zip(outlet(up), outlet(dn))])
JX, JW = (np.stack([c[i] for c in cols], axis=1) for i in range(2))
F = information(JX, 0.002) + information(JW, 0.001)
end = np.array([1e-4, 1e-4, 0.0])                   # R_f(T) = 1e-4 (mean + slope)
for label, steam_std in (("steam trusted to 0.3 K", 0.3), ("calibrated to 0.03 K", 0.03)):
    cov = posterior_covariance(F, [np.inf, np.inf, steam_std])
    print(f"{label}: R_f(T) to {target_std(cov, end) / 1e-4:.1%}")
lab = greedy_design(list(JX[11::12]), 0.0005, 2, prior_std=[np.inf, np.inf, 0.3],
                    base_information=F, target=end)  # two lab assays of the outlet solids: when?
print([float(times[11::12][i]) for i in lab.chosen], [f"{c / 1e-4:.1%}" for c in lab.criterion])

Experiment J09 does this for the evaporator with six instrument errors:

  • The estimate is limited by the steam offset and, jointly, by the four mass-balance instruments.
  • A condensate meter and a larger, faster steam swing are worth more than any calibration.
  • Check a design that matters by fitting simulated records, as J09 does.

docs.title: From the rig to the tower
docs.text:
A droplet rig records the droplet itself; a tower records the air. SprayDryer is the droplet coupled to its air: a plug flow of equal droplets that travel down the tower with the air (co-current), at steady state.

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dX}{d\tau} &= -r, \\ \frac{dT_p}{d\tau} &= \frac{h A\,(T_a - T_p) - \lambda\, m_s\, r}{m_s\,(c_s + c_w X)}, \\ \frac{dY}{d\tau} &= \frac{F_s}{G}\, r, \\ \frac{dT_a}{d\tau} &= -\frac{\dfrac{F_s}{m_s}\, h A\,(T_a - T_p) + G\, c_v\,(T_a - T_p)\,\dfrac{dY}{d\tau} + U_w\, \pi D\, v_p\,(T_a - T_{amb})}{G\,(c_a + c_v Y)} . \end{aligned} \]
  • \(\tau = z / v_p\): residence time of the droplets. \(z\): distance below the atomiser. \(v_p\): droplet velocity.
  • \(X\), \(T_p\): moisture and temperature of the droplets. \(Y\), \(T_a\): humidity ratio and temperature of the air.
  • \(r\): the droplet's drying rate, with the same closure \(f(X)\) and the local \(Y\).
  • \(F_s\): solids flow, kg/s. \(G\): dry-air flow, kg/s. \(c_a\), \(c_v\): heat capacities of dry air and vapour.
  • \(U_w\): wall loss coefficient. \(D\): tower diameter. \(T_{amb}\): ambient temperature.
  • Start: the droplets' state at the atomiser and the inlet air (\(T_{in}\), \(Y_{in}\)).

Measured (records(), one operating point):

  • air temperatures at six heights;
  • the outlet air's humidity;
  • the powder's moisture, from the lab.

Unknown:

  • the closure \(f(X)\), or the two parameters \(X_{cr}\) and \(n\) of a known form;
  • the nuisances: the wall loss and the droplet size.
from pinnrl.process import SprayDryer

tower = SprayDryer()                                         # 8 m, air at 180 degC, 250 um droplets
profile = tower.reference()                                  # X, T_p, Y, T_a along the height; 5 ms
print(profile.outlet(), tower.balances(profile)["energy"])
slow = tower.with_closure(lambda X: 0.7 * tower.droplet.drying_curve(X))
print(tower.records()["T_air"] - 273.15, slow.records()["T_air"] - 273.15)
print(tower.operating_point(T_in=438.15, solids_flow=0.012).records()["X_out"])
print(tower.stickiness_margin(profile)[-1])                  # T_p - T_g(X) at the outlet, K

What the twin gives that no instrument does is the stickiness margin:

\[ \Delta T = T_p - T_g(X), \qquad T_g = \frac{w_s\, T_{gs} + k\, w_w\, T_{gw}}{w_s + k\, w_w}, \qquad w_w = \frac{X}{1 + X},\quad w_s = 1 - w_w . \]
  • Glass transition \(T_g\): the temperature above which an amorphous solid softens. Water lowers it (the Gordon–Taylor relation above).
  • Stickiness margin \(\Delta T\): how far a particle is above its glass transition. Particles stick to the wall and cake when it passes a material limit.
  • \(T_{gs}\), \(T_{gw}\): glass transitions of the dry solids and of water. \(k\): the Gordon–Taylor constant of the pair.

Headline (J08): the twin, run forward with the identified closure, gives the outlet margin to 1.0–1.5 K, against 1.6–3.2 K for a lab assay hours later. With the curve's form known, five operating points identify its two parameters and predict the powder moisture at a new operating point to 1–2 % (J11).

Finding: identify the closure on the rig and carry it to the tower; at dryer scale estimate a few numbers and the nuisances.

J12 prices the measurements at dryer scale:

  • Pay: better thermocouples, more operating points, replicate lab assays.
  • Does not pay: a droplet-size measurement.

docs.title: The counter-current tower
docs.text:
The air enters at the bottom against the falling droplets. The droplets' state is known at the top and the air's at the bottom.

\[ \begin{aligned} X_t + v_p\, X_z &= -r, \\ T_t + v_p\, T_z &= \frac{h A\,(T_a - T) - \lambda\, m_s\, r}{m_s\,(c_s + c_w X)}, \\ Y_t - v_a\, Y_z &= \frac{v_a}{G}\, S, \\ T_{a,t} - v_a\, T_{a,z} &= -\frac{v_a}{G}\, \frac{Q + c_v\,(T_a - T)\, S + U_w\, \pi D\,(T_a - T_{amb})}{c_a + c_v Y} . \end{aligned} \]
  • \(z\): distance down from the atomiser. \(T\): droplet temperature. The other fields are those of the co-current tower.
  • \(v_p\): droplet velocity, downward. \(v_a = G / (\rho_a A_{tower})\): air velocity, upward.
  • \(S = (F_s / v_p)\, r\): water the droplets give to the air per metre of height.
  • \(Q = \dfrac{F_s}{m_s v_p}\, h A\,(T_a - T)\): heat they take from it per metre.
  • Boundaries: \(X\), \(T\) at the top (\(z = 0\)); \(Y\), \(T_a\) at the bottom, the inlet air \(T_{in}(t)\), \(Y_{in}(t)\).
  • Time scales: the droplets cross the tower in 5.3 s, the air in 106 s.

Measured (records, over a transient):

  • air temperatures at five heights;
  • the humidity of the air leaving at the top;
  • the moisture of the powder leaving at the bottom.

Unknown:

  • the curve's parameters \(X_{cr}\) and \(n\);
  • the wall loss \(U_w\).

Solvers:

  • CounterCurrentDryer.steady solves the steady state, a boundary-value problem, by shooting on the air's state at the top: about 100 ms, against 5 ms for the co-current tower.
  • transient integrates the transport equations by the method of lines with a sparse Jacobian. Ten minutes take 0.04–0.13 s for a smooth step and 0.34–1.3 s for an inlet record with 10 s knots, on 51 to 401 cells (J13).
  • custom_pde writes the same four fields in \((z, t)\) for the PINN: the inlet air as time-series inputs, the steady profiles as the initial condition, each equation divided by its own scale. identify= names the parameters to estimate.
import numpy as np
from pinnrl.process import CounterCurrentDryer

tower = CounterCurrentDryer(T_in=lambda t: 433.15 + (15.0 if t > 10.0 else 0.0))   # a step of the inlet air
profile = tower.steady()                                   # X, T_p, Y, T_a down the tower; the BVP by shooting
print(profile.outlet(), tower.balances(profile)["energy"], tower.stickiness_margin(profile)[-1])
response = tower.transient(600.0, nz=201)                  # the step response by the method of lines
records = tower.records(response, probe_heights=(0.5, 2.0, 3.5, 5.0, 6.5))
print(records["T_air"][:, -1] - 273.15, records["X_out"][[0, -1]])
pde = tower.custom_pde(600.0, identify=["Xcr", "ncdc"], initial_guesses={"Xcr": 0.7, "ncdc": 1.0})

Headline (J13): bounded least squares through one transient record takes 10 s and recovers \(X_{cr}\), \(n\), \(U_w\) within the linear prediction (±0.011, ±0.015, ±0.003) on all three data sets; the PINN twin on the same record takes 110–140 s and all six runs are rejected by the misfit test (reduced chi-square 5–9).

Finding: the steady state has no cheap initial-value solve, the case the roadmap set for the PINN twin, but the transient does, and the classical fit through it wins.

docs.title: The line
docs.text:
ProcessLine chains evaporator passes and hands the concentrate to the dryer.

\[ \begin{aligned} W^{(k+1)}_{in}(t) &= W^{(k)}(L, t), \qquad X^{(k+1)}_{in}(t) = X^{(k)}(L, t), \\ F_s(t) &= W_c(t)\, X_c(t), \qquad \text{droplet solids fraction} = X_c(t), \\ \sigma_y^2 &= \sum_j \left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta_j}\, \sigma_j \right)^2, \qquad \text{share}_j = \frac{1}{\sigma_y^2} \left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta_j}\, \sigma_j \right)^2 . \end{aligned} \]
  • \(W^{(k)}\), \(X^{(k)}\): flow and solids of pass \(k\), each pass an evaporator tube as above.
  • \(W_c\), \(X_c\): the concentrate, the outlet of the last pass. \(F_s\): the dryer's solids flow.
  • \(y\): a target (the concentrate's solids, the powder's moisture, its stickiness margin).
  • \(\theta_j\), \(\sigma_j\): an uncertain quantity of a unit and its standard deviation.
  • The dryer is quasi-steady: its residence time is seconds against the evaporator's hours of fouling.

Methods:

  • steady: the line at an instant.
  • reference: the shift. The passes by the method of lines, the dryer at every output time.
  • records: what the line's instruments report.
  • propagate: linear and Monte-Carlo propagation of each unit's uncertainty to the three targets, with each source's share of the variance.

Measured:

  • each pass's outlet solids and flow;
  • the dryer's air temperatures and outlet humidity;
  • lab assays of the powder.

Unknown:

  • every unit's unknowns (twelve in J10), and which one the powder inherits.
from pinnrl.process import ProcessLine

line = ProcessLine.default(fouling=[lambda t: 2e-5 * t / 14400, lambda t: 4e-5 * t / 14400, 0.0])
print(line.steady()["X"], line.steady(t=14400.0)["powder"])      # 10 % -> 41 % solids; the powder after four hours
shift = line.reference(4 * 3600.0, nz=51, dryer_every=4)          # three passes, then the dryer every 2 min
budget = line.propagate({"R_f_0": 6e-6, "R_f_1": 5e-6, "X_cr": 0.1, "d0": 25e-6, "W_feed": 0.002}, t=14400.0)
print(budget["linear"]["powder"])                                  # std of the powder moisture and the shares

Headline (J10): at the end of a shift, the standard deviation of the powder moisture is 0.094 from the fouling monitor on each pass followed by propagation, 0.0054 from the dryer's own online records, and 0.0011 from every record of the line.

Findings:

  • The information flows downstream only. The dryer's instruments determine its powder but not the fouling behind it.
  • The first pass's fouling is one unknown with the feed's calibration.

docs.title: Research program
docs.text:
This page states what the project is trying to establish and in what order: the objective, the rules every result follows, and the papers planned.

Objective: estimate unknown physics (parameters, coefficient fields, closures and hidden states of a real system) from its routine sensors, with uncertainty you can trust. The first application is digital twins of food-powder lines, meaning evaporators and spray dryers (see Applications).

Inverse modelling is the method. An estimate \(\hat\lambda\) of the unknowns \(\lambda\) from data \(y\) is only useful if three things hold:

\[ \underbrace{F = J^\top \Sigma^{-1} J \ \text{invertible}}_{\text{identifiable}} \qquad \underbrace{\lVert \delta\hat\lambda \rVert \le C\,\lVert \delta y \rVert}_{\text{stable}} \qquad \underbrace{P\big(\lambda \in I_{95}\big) \approx 0.95}_{\text{calibrated}} \]
  • Identifiable: the sensors determine the unknowns. \(F\) is the Fisher information, built from the sensitivity \(J = \partial y / \partial \lambda\) of the readings and the noise covariance \(\Sigma\).
  • Stable: small disturbances \(\delta y\) in the data give small changes \(\delta\hat\lambda\) in the estimate. \(C\) is the stability constant.
  • Calibrated: a 95 % interval \(I_{95}\) contains the truth about 95 % of the time.
  • Closure: a relation the equations need and the physics does not supply.

The program establishes those conditions on problems with known answers before applying them to plant equipment.

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
• Theory: the theory pages state the conditions (well-posedness, identifiability, calibration, stability) that the inverse-modelling modules rely on.
  • Papers: experiments/PAPERS.md is the paper backlog: 27 papers in four tiers, each with its question, contribution, prerequisite papers, target venues and status.
  • Experiments: experiments/BACKLOG.md lists the 166 experiments behind them, tracks A–K. Track K holds the 50 conditioning, stability and uncertainty-quantification (UQ) baselines for Tier 1.
  • Folders: each experiment runs in its own experiments/<ID>_<slug>/ folder with its question, setup, result and conclusion.

Rules for every result:

  1. Equal budgets, with the method's own overhead counted.
  2. Paired seeds (five for main claims), reported as median and IQR with a paired Wilcoxon test.
  3. A classical baseline wherever one exists (finite differences, Kalman filters, moving-horizon estimation, adjoint methods).
  4. Stated validity conditions.

docs.text:
