docs.text: What is planned, in the order the research program needs it. Each item states what a user gains and, where it can be said in advance, when it counts as done. Within a release, items are worked top to bottom. What is already built is on the history page.

docs.title: Where this goes
docs.text:
Eight releases built three things: a PINN trainer whose derivatives run in a compiled kernel, an inverse-modelling toolbox that says when an estimate can be trusted (identifiability, stability, calibrated intervals, a misfit test), and four process simulators with their classical estimators. Two findings shape what comes next:

  • On every unit with a cheap reference solve, the classical estimator beat the PINN twin (J05, J07d, J11, J13). The PINN's case is narrower than the literature claims: models with no trusted forward solve, unknown functions inside the equations, and amortised or parametric use, where one network replaces thousands of solves.
  • The "RL" in pinnrl is one contextual bandit that chooses collocation cells and does not beat uniform sampling at equal cost (B01/B06). Meanwhile the package owns what reinforcement learning is usually short of: fast, validated, physically meaningful simulators (a line shift in 1.6 s, an evaporator solve in milliseconds) with realistic sensors, hidden states and economic stakes.

The direction follows from both: pinnrl becomes the place where physics-informed models and sequential decisions meet. PINNs estimate what the plant does not measure; reinforcement learning and optimal control decide what to do about it (how to run, when to clean, what to measure next), in environments built from the same equations, graded against the classical controller as the estimators were graded against the Kalman filter.

Theme Release What a user gains Accuracy per second (research bets, below) v0.9–v0.10 A lower error in the same time, by an optimizer, an architecture and a training controller built for physics-informed losses The engine, everywhere v0.9 The fastest PINN step on a CPU on every problem the package solves and on every machine; custom networks at the same speed; twins that run outside Python Tests that protect the architecture every release Nothing existing breaks when a component is added; dead code removed The dashboard as an experiment tracker v0.9–v0.10 Runs searched, compared and traced from data to result pinnrl.gym: process environments and control v0.10 Standard RL environments of real unit operations, with baselines (PID, MPC) and a twin in the loop Decisions that serve the inverse problem v0.11 What to measure, where to sample and how to train, learned as policies and compared with the greedy designs Discovering unknown physics v0.12 From a learned closure to an equation with an error bar; model-form error named instead of absorbed Simulation at scale v0.13 One network across operating points; new units and geometries; inference in microseconds A stable platform v1.0 An API that does not move under a user; the software paper The platform matured (see below) v2.0–v6.0 Control, discovery, scale and an autonomous twin, each proven on simulated plants The plant v7.0 Live data in, advice with intervals out, validated on a real line

docs.title: Research bets: accuracy per second
docs.text:
On an Apple M4 the engine leads on the time of a step (I17). A user feels something else: the error reached in a given time. The bets below aim at that number, and they come before any publication. Each is a claim that can fail.

The measure

\[ \varepsilon(T) = \frac{\lVert u_\theta - u \rVert_2}{\lVert u \rVert_2} \quad \text{after wall-clock time } T \text{ on one CPU core} \]
  • \(u_\theta\): the trained network.
  • \(u\): the exact or reference solution.
  • Protocol: ten seeds, median and interquartile range, the nine equations of I17 plus published suites (PINNacle, PDEBench), the same machine for every method.

The structure the bets use

\[ L(\theta) = \tfrac12 \lVert r(\theta) \rVert^2, \qquad r = \big(w_r\, r_{\text{pde}},\; w_b\, r_{\text{bc}},\; w_0\, r_{\text{ic}}\big) \]
  • \(r(\theta)\): every residual of the problem stacked in one vector (equation, boundary, initial).
  • Least-squares problem: a loss that is a sum of squares. Adam and L-BFGS treat it as a generic function; the methods below use the squares.
  • Jacobian \(J = \partial r / \partial \theta\): how each residual moves with each weight. The engine can apply \(J\) and \(J^\top\) to a vector at the cost of a step, without forming \(J\).
Bet The idea Baseline to beat It fails if R1. A least-squares optimizer Levenberg–Marquardt steps \(\delta = -(J^\top J + \lambda I)^{-1} J^\top r\), solved matrix-free with the engine's \(J v\) and \(J^\top w\) Adam then L-BFGS at equal time It does not reach the published Gauss–Newton errors (about \(10^{-6}\) on heat) on one CPU core in minutes, or is not at least 100 times below Adam then L-BFGS at equal time on six of the nine equations R2. The last layer solved, not trained With \(u_\theta = \sum_j c_j \phi_j(x; \vartheta)\) and a linear equation, \(r\) is linear in \(c\): solve \(c\) by least squares at every step and optimize only \(\vartheta\) (variable projection) R1 without it No gain in \(\varepsilon(T)\) on the linear problems (heat, 2-D heat) R3. Conditions built into the network \(u_\theta = g + d \cdot N_\theta\) with \(g\) matching the initial and boundary data and \(d\) vanishing there, compiled like the rest Penalty terms with tuned weights The error is not lower without any loss weight to tune R4. A learned training controller A policy sets the damping \(\lambda\), the resampling and the restarts of R1 from the loss history, trained across equations Marquardt's and Nielsen's damping rules It does not beat the rules on equations it was not trained on R5. A benchmark others accept \(\varepsilon(T)\) curves against DeepXDE and JAX baselines on public suites, scripts in the repository The best published number per task The lead of R1–R3 does not survive on problems the package was not tuned on R6. A network designed for the loop (below) A trunk cached once and a small head per step, so a model queried millions of times in a reinforcement-learning loop costs microseconds and adapts by a least-squares update A general network retrained by Adam; the reference solver as environment The loop is not 10 times faster, or the policy is worse than one trained on the solver
  • Levenberg–Marquardt: Gauss–Newton with a damping term \(\lambda I\) that keeps the step inside the region where the linearization holds.
  • Matrix-free: the linear system is solved by conjugate gradients, which needs only products with \(J\) and \(J^\top\).
  • Variable projection: eliminating the parameters a model is linear in, and optimizing over the rest.

What is new and what is not (from a literature review of November 2026; absence means "not found", not "proven absent"):

Bet Already published Not found, and what the bet has to show R1 Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt, natural-gradient and self-scaled quasi-Newton methods for PINNs, matrix-free and with Taylor mode, three to five orders below Adam on GPUs in double precision The same accuracy on one CPU core in comparable time; the measured cost of \(Jv\) and \(J^\top w\) against one gradient; where a dense solve beats the matrix-free one; single precision; inverse problems R2 Random-feature and extreme-learning-machine solvers; variable projection on hidden weights The solve timed in compiled code, and combined with R1 and R3 R3 Distance-function and functional-connection ansatz, also paired with an exact last-layer solve The three together with trained hidden weights; time-dependent nonlinear problems; inverse problems R4 Learned damping on classical least squares, with thin evidence; adaptive sampling and loss weights, which rarely beat simple baselines at equal compute Control of damping, switching and restarts for R1, trained across equations and tested on unseen ones, against Marquardt's and Nielsen's rules. A null result is worth reporting R5 Suites that report final error (PINNacle, the jaxpi leaderboard) Error against wall-clock time, CPU timings, a small-network track, inverse problems scored on identifiability and calibration R6 The trunk-and-head form (DeepONet); online last-layer adaptation in flight control and Koopman control Recursive least squares on a physics-trained cached basis; closed-form action gradients; latency on one CPU core; a policy trained on the model against one trained on the solver
  • The bar for R1 is higher than first written. Published Gauss–Newton results reach errors near \(10^{-6}\) on heat and \(10^{-7}\) on Poisson in minutes on a GPU. Ten times better than Adam is not enough: R1 has to reach those errors on a CPU core.
  • A warning for R6. In one benchmark of predictive control on reactors, PINN surrogates were slower than the mechanistic model in every case, because of the cost of derivatives. R6 exists to remove that cost and must be judged against that result.
  • For industry. No PINN validated on plant data for an evaporator or a spray dryer was found; plants run grey-box models with predictive control. Readiness there is a lifecycle matter (historian validation, shadow mode, drift monitoring, change control), which is what v6.0 and v7.0 are for.

R1 has a research plan and a first prototype in experiments/D10_least_squares_optimizer/ (PLAN.md, run.py). The plan goes beyond Levenberg–Marquardt: nine moves that use what a physics-informed loss is (the residual's flow integrated like a stiff ODE, a coarse classical solve as the preconditioner, training as filtering over a stream of fresh points, small blocks solved exactly with the sampler choosing them, the linear layer solved and the basis grown, continuation in a physical parameter, the equation's own time as the training loop, multipliers in place of loss weights) and an agent that chooses among them, which is R4 widened from damping to moves. Each has a test and a condition under which it is dropped.

First measurements (one core, three seeds, heat, Burgers and KdV): at 60 s Levenberg–Marquardt reaches \(6 \times 10^{-7}\) on heat and \(6 \times 10^{-6}\) on KdV, 120 and 220 times below Adam then L-BFGS, and only 3 times below on Burgers. An extended Kalman filter over a stream of fresh points is slower for the first minute and then ahead on all three: at 180 s, \(2 \times 10^{-5}\) on Burgers (65 times below Levenberg–Marquardt), \(1.5 \times 10^{-9}\) on heat, \(10^{-7}\) on KdV. Solving the last layer reaches \(5 \times 10^{-9}\) on heat in 60 s. Four of the seven moves tried were dropped. At 180 s the filter is 350 (Burgers) to 35,000 (heat) times below Adam then L-BFGS. Twenty seconds of Levenberg–Marquardt before the filter remove its slow start at no loss. Open: the filter's covariance costs the square of the number of weights; kept only within each layer it holds on heat and KdV and loses a factor of 20 on Burgers. At 12,737 weights a low-rank form keeps level with Levenberg–Marquardt, not ahead: the filter's lead does not yet survive the size. A memory that grows with the stream (short early, long late) puts the filter ahead of Levenberg–Marquardt from the first seconds on heat and KdV, and 150, 17 and 12 times below it at 180 s on heat, Burgers and KdV. Adam then L-BFGS was too weak a baseline. Self-scaled Broyden (Urbán, Stefanou and Pons, 2024) with little or no Adam first reaches \(2 \times 10^{-10}\) to \(4 \times 10^{-10}\) on heat and KdV in 180 s. R1's bar is now the best published method at every moment of the run. Against it the filter leads until 68 s on heat and 37 s on KdV, and on Burgers throughout, 14 times at the end, on the same loss. The filter then self-scaled Broyden meets the bar on heat. On KdV nothing here does after 37 s. On Allen–Cahn the filter meets it alone: 250 times below the best self-scaled Broyden at 20 s, 2.3 times at 180 s (\(3.3 \times 10^{-6}\)), and it never lands on a wrong solution, where Broyden does on up to two seeds of three. Burgers at \(\nu = 0.003/\pi\) defeats every method on uniform points: the front is 8 times narrower than their spacing. The filter breaks down there from covariance windup; a step limit on the change in \(u\) makes it stable at no cost by steps on the smooth equations, and it then stops near 0.3. Levenberg–Marquardt on points redrawn from the residual every 5 steps fits the front to 1.1e-03, 50 times below the same method on uniform points. On a sharp front the points decide, and so a fair baseline places its points too: self-scaled Broyden on residual points is 30 times better on Burgers and takes the filter's lead there. With the step limit and rows drawn from the residual the filter leads Burgers again from 30 s, by 1.5 to 3 times, and keeps its Allen–Cahn lead.

Order of work: R1 as a prototype in plain PyTorch first (to measure what it buys), then in the engine; R2 and R3 on top; R5 throughout; R4 and R6 last, because R4 needs R1 and R6 needs R2. The review is in the repository's reports/ folder when it is kept there.

docs.title: R6. A network designed for the loop
docs.text:
A reinforcement-learning loop calls the physics model at every step of every episode: millions of evaluations, each for a new state and action, often with a small update in between. A general network recomputes everything at each call. This bet is an architecture, built together with the engine, in which almost nothing has to be recomputed.

\[ u_\theta(x, t;\, z) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j(z)\, \phi_j(x, t), \qquad c(z) = A\, h(z) + b \]
  • \(z\): what changes at every step of the loop (the state, the action, the operating point, the estimated parameters).
  • Trunk \(\phi_j(x,t)\): features of space and time and their derivative streams. They do not depend on \(z\), so they are computed once and cached.
  • Head \(c(z)\): a small map from the loop's variables to the coefficients. It is all that runs per step.
  • Linear in \(c\): for a fixed trunk the residual is linear or low-order in the coefficients, so an update is a least-squares solve (R2), not a gradient-descent run.
Property How the design gets it Done when A query costs microseconds Cached trunk streams; the head is one small matrix product; batched over parallel environments in one call One core serves a stated number of queries per second, with \(\partial u / \partial z\) included The model adapts inside the loop Recursive least squares on \(c\) as new sensor data arrive, one rank update per measurement The twin tracks a drifting parameter at every environment step The policy can differentiate through it \(\partial u / \partial z\) in closed form from the head, exact, no graph A policy gradient through the model matches finite differences Rollouts stay stable The network advances the state over one control interval, with the physics residual and a bound on its growth built in A long rollout does not drift from the reference solver It runs outside Python Fixed widths and block sizes chosen for the cache; exported as C with the engine's export The exported model reproduces the Python one to rounding
  • Recursive least squares: updating a least-squares solution when one more data point arrives, without solving again from the start.
  • Rollout: applying the model to its own output step after step, as a simulator does.
  • Control interval: the time between two actions of the controller.

Baseline to beat: the same task with a general 4 × 64 network retrained by Adam, and with the reference solver as the environment. It fails if a policy trained on this model does not match one trained on the solver, or if the loop is not at least ten times faster than with the general network. It builds on R2 (the linear last layer) and feeds pinnrl.gym, where the PINN world model is planned.

docs.title: v0.9: the engine, everywhere
docs.text:
In progress. Already built in this release (history): the compiled kernel is the default engine; a benchmark against PyTorch, JAX and DeepXDE on nine equations (I17); a step compiled per equation, which covers forward and inverse problems, scaled networks and layer normalization (1.3–1.4× the general kernel with normalization on). The aim of what remains is that the engine's lead holds on every problem the package solves and on the machines most users have, and that everything later (control, design, discovery) is built on it.

  • The rest of the step in the compiled call. The boundary and initial points, the loss reduction and Adam inside the same call (0.5 ms of heat's 3.5); L-BFGS on the compiled gradients in float64, since L-BFGS is what does the learning on the stiff process problems (J13); steady problems; unknown functions of a field (a closure \(f(u)\)), which still run on autograd. Gain: one call per step on every problem, and second-order training at engine speed.
  • Beyond one core, beyond one machine. The step's matrix products are single-threaded on Apple's matrix unit, where threads do not add. On Linux and x86 the blocks of the compiled step are independent and can run on a core each. Gain: the lead held on the machines most users have; timed there first, since I17's table is one Apple M4.
  • Custom architectures. A declarative network description (blocks, widths, activations, normalization, input embeddings, skip connections) that both the autograd path and the kernel run; activations beyond tanh (sin for SIREN, gelu, silu) by their Taylor recurrences; Fourier features. Gain: a user's architecture is not a reason to fall back.
  • Many networks in one call. Ensembles, the swarm of pinnrl.uq, restarts and hyperparameter sweeps trained as a batch of networks through one threaded kernel call. Gain: a calibrated ensemble for the price of a few single runs; train_with_restarts in parallel.
  • Inference outside Python. Export a trained twin to a dependency-free C source or shared library (values and derivatives), and to ONNX; a throughput benchmark (evaluations per second per core). Gain: a soft sensor that runs in a PLC gateway, a historian calculation or a spreadsheet plug-in at plant rate.
  • Prebuilt wheels. Platform wheels with the kernels compiled (macOS arm64/x86, Linux x86/aarch64), so no compiler is needed. Gain: pip install pinnrl is enough.
  • Stretch: a Metal/CUDA backend for large batches; the kernel is a CPU design and small networks are where it wins.

docs.title: Every release from v0.9: tests that protect the architecture
docs.text:
A release must not break what exists. The suite today has about 900 tests and covers 96 % of the lines it measures, but it measures neither the dashboard, the launcher nor the training command line, and line coverage says little about whether a new component is caught when it breaks a contract.

  • Contract test: one test, written once, that every implementation of an extension point must pass (every equation, every network, every sampler, every process unit).
  • Integration test: a test that runs several parts together, as a user does (train, save, reload, analyse, display).
  • Dead code: code that no test, no entry point and no documented use reaches.
Step What is built Done when T1. Contracts for the extension points A registry-driven suite: a new equation, architecture, sampler, optimizer or process unit is picked up automatically and must satisfy the same contract (shapes; the exact solution has zero residual; the compiled step equals autograd; save and reload give the same output) Adding a component without touching the tests still tests it T2. Engine equivalence by generation Random equations (orders, mixed terms, fields, parameters, unknown functions) checked compiled step against autograd A defect planted in the generator's output is caught T3. Pipelines end to end Train, checkpoint, reload, analyse, and read the run in the dashboard, for the forward, inverse and process paths, through the command line and the Python API Each documented workflow is one test T4. Compatibility Run folders and checkpoints written by earlier releases still load A fixture per released version T5. Coverage that counts everything The dashboard, the launcher and the training command line come back into the measurement Coverage of the whole package stays above 75 % (the present gate of 90 % on the measured part stays) T6. Tests judged by what they catch Mutation testing on the core modules: a test that never fails when the code is altered is rewritten or removed A mutation score is reported per module T7. Dead code removed Unreached code found by coverage and a static scan, then deleted or given a test The scan is clean and runs in CI

Rule for new tests: no assertion that restates the implementation. A test states a property a user relies on, or a contract a new component must meet.

docs.title: The dashboard as an experiment-tracking tool
docs.text:
Today the dashboard launches, monitors and compares runs. The aim is a tool a team can use to track experiments and follow their data from the record to the result.

  • Run: one training or estimation, with its configuration, metrics, checkpoints and figures.
  • Lineage: which data, which code version and which settings produced a result.
  • Artifact: a file a run produced (a model, a figure, a table).
Step What a user gains Done when D1. A run store with a schema Every run indexed: configuration, metrics, tags, code version, data fingerprint; search and filter over thousands of runs A query over 5,000 runs returns in under a second D2. Compare and diff Curves overlaid, configurations diffed, error against wall-clock time, seeds grouped with median and spread Two runs can be explained apart from one screen D3. Lineage and artifacts From a figure back to the run, the data and the commit; an artifact browser; export of a run as a report Every number in a report links to its run D4. Live operation Launch, queue, stop and resume runs; live loss, residual maps and engine status; alerts when the misfit test fails A study of 100 runs is managed without a terminal D5. The process view, grown Sensors, estimated states with intervals, fouling monitors and the line's variance budget, on recorded or replayed data An engineer reads a shift from one page D6. Design and reliability A design system (layout, colour, type), keyboard access, tested callbacks, a separate data layer under the pages The pages are covered by T3 and usable on a laptop screen D7. Working with other tools Import and export to MLflow and Weights & Biases formats A run moves in and out without loss of its metrics

docs.title: v0.10: pinnrl.gym, process environments and control
docs.text:
The simulators become environments with the Gymnasium interface, so any RL library can train on them, and the package ships the baselines that an RL result must beat.

  • The environments. Evaporator-v0 (actions: steam temperature, feed flow; hidden: fouling), SprayDryer-v0 and CounterCurrentDryer-v0 (actions: inlet air temperature, feed rate; constraint: the stickiness margin), Line-v0 (the passes and the dryer together). Observations are the plant's sensors with their noise, delays and lab assays that arrive hourly, so the problems are partially observed as a plant is. Disturbances come from a model or from a historian export replayed. Done when each environment passes Gymnasium's checker and a random policy runs at a stated number of steps per second.
  • Tasks with money in them. Setpoint tracking of the powder moisture; energy per kilogram of powder under a moisture specification and a stickiness limit (a constrained problem); when to clean (the fouling monitor's time-to-threshold turned into an optimal-stopping decision against production lost); start-up and product changeover. Each task has a reward in physical units and a documented constraint.
  • Throughput. Vectorised environments on the compiled integrators; the dryer's steady and transient solves in C++ as the evaporator's are (I16). Gain: millions of environment steps an hour on a laptop, which is what RL needs and what a CFD-based environment cannot give.
  • Baselines first. PID loops, linear MPC on the linearised model and nonlinear MPC through the reference solver, each with the EKF or MHE as its state estimator. Rule, as for the estimators: an RL policy is reported against MPC with the same information, and where MPC wins the documentation says so.
  • Agents. Adapters for Stable-Baselines3 and CleanRL, and one reference PPO and SAC in the package for reproducibility; the existing DQN becomes one agent behind the same interface.
  • The twin in the loop. Policies that act on the estimator's state and its interval (the EKF's fouling and band, the powder soft sensor), and training under the uncertainty the inverse tools quantify: domain randomisation over the equivalence region of pinnrl.uq instead of over arbitrary ranges. Gain: a policy robust to exactly the model errors the data cannot rule out, the sim-to-real gap stated in the units of the identifiability analysis.
  • Safe and offline RL. Constrained policies for the stickiness margin (a shield from the twin's interval); offline RL from historian data with the simulator as the evaluation ground truth. Gain: a path to a plant, where exploration on the equipment is not allowed.
  • PINN world models. Where an environment has no cheap solve, a parametric PINN as the differentiable model inside model-based RL, with policy gradients through the surrogate. This is the PINN's case restated for control, and it is tested where it belongs: against the solver-based environment on a unit that has one.

docs.title: v0.11: decisions that serve the inverse problem
docs.text:
The inverse problem contains decisions that are made greedily or by hand today. They become policies, each with its greedy baseline already in the package.

  • Sequential experiment design. Which operating point to run next and when to pull a lab sample, to identify a closure or a fouling law fastest. Baseline: analysis.greedy_design (J09, J12), which is myopic and linear-Gaussian; candidates: Bayesian optimal design and an RL policy on the design environment. Gain: a campaign plan for a pilot tower in fewer runs, with the expected interval before the first run is made.
  • Sensor placement and maintenance. Where to put a thermocouple, which instrument to recalibrate, as a budgeted decision under the same information currency.
  • A training gym (PINNTraining-v0). The PINN's own training as an environment: actions are the sampling distribution, the loss weights, the learning rate and when to restart; the reward is the error gained per residual evaluation. The bandit, RAD, the adaptive weights and the schedules become policies in one interface, and classical bandits (UCB, Thompson, EXP3; C07) and a policy-gradient sampler (C09) join them. Gain: the sampling study (B01–B08) becomes a leaderboard anyone can add to, and a learned training controller is tested for transfer across equations (C10).
  • Acceptance and restarts as a policy. train_with_restarts chooses the next seed blindly; a policy that reads the misfit and the loss curve chooses whether to continue, restart or switch optimizer.

docs.title: v0.12: discovering unknown physics
docs.text:
The package identifies parameters and free-form functions. The step beyond is to say what the function is, whether the model's form is wrong, and how the plant is being run.

  • From a learned closure to an equation. Sparse regression of a fitted UnknownFunction on a library of candidate terms (the SINDy idea applied to the closure, not the whole equation), with the candidates' identifiability checked first and the selected form refitted through the reference solver and judged by the misfit test. Gain: a drying-rate law an engineer can read and publish, with an interval on every coefficient.
  • Model-form error, named. A structured discrepancy term next to the known physics, constrained so it cannot absorb what the parameters explain (F08); a report that separates "the parameters are uncertain" from "the equations are wrong". Model selection between candidate closures by Laplace evidence and held-out misfit.
  • Hybrid models. Known balances with learned terms where the physics is missing (wall deposition, agglomeration), using the anchor and monotonicity constraints so the learned part stays physical.
  • Units without a method-of-lines form. A droplet size distribution (population balance) and wall deposition in the dryer, the first models where the PINN twin has no cheap classical rival. This is the open item of J13: the place the PINN's case can still be made.
  • Ways of working. From historian data: operating regimes and transitions (changepoints and clustering on the twin's states, not on raw tags), the differences between shifts or recipes expressed as differences in estimated parameters, and drift that precedes a quality excursion. Gain: the twin explains how the line is actually run, which is the question a plant asks first.
  • Amortised identification. A network trained on simulated records that maps a new record to parameters and intervals in one pass (simulation-based inference), checked for calibration as J06 checked the filters. Gain: identification in milliseconds for a fleet of units.

docs.title: v0.13: simulation at scale
docs.text:
• Parametric surrogates. One network across operating points, geometries and parameters (inputs beyond x, t), trained against the reference solver where one exists and by the residual where none does. Gain: what-if studies and design sweeps without a solve per point, and the world model v0.10 needs.
  • Hard constraints and decomposition. Exact initial and boundary conditions by output transform (D09); domain decomposition and time marching for long horizons and sharp fronts; separable networks for 2-D and 3-D (E09).
  • A unit library with a plugin interface. Wiped-film evaporators (P22), plate heat exchangers, membrane filtration, fluidised-bed drying, the cleaning cycle itself; a documented base class so a user's unit gets the reference solver, the PINN form, the estimators and a gym environment from one definition. Gain: the method leaves food powders for pharmaceuticals, batteries and chemicals without a rewrite.
  • Pretraining on The Well. The dataset loader is in place; operator backbones pretrained on simulation data and fine-tuned with a residual, tested on whether pretraining buys accuracy at equal compute.

docs.title: v1.0: a stable platform
docs.text:
The 0.x releases may still move the API. 1.0 is the promise that they stop.

  • A stable API. A deprecation policy, semantic versioning that means it, and one documented public surface for the trainer, the inverse tools, the process units and the gym.
  • The software paper (P06). The package described and benchmarked in one citable place, with the head-to-head of v0.9 and the control baselines of v0.10.
  • Reproducibility. Every figure in the documentation regenerated by one command from a pinned environment.

docs.title: v2.0 to v6.0: the platform before the plant
docs.text:
The plant is not next. A twin that advises a real line has to be right when nobody can check it, so the platform first has to be far more capable, and proven on simulated plants where the truth is known. The major versions are the stages of that; their content will be set as the 0.x work shows what holds up.

Release Stage Done when v2.0 Control that earns its place. pinnrl.gym as a benchmark suite: tasks, baselines and a leaderboard for constrained, partially observed process control A learned policy beats nonlinear MPC on at least one task at equal information, or the suite documents why none does v3.0 Discovery as a workflow. Records in; parameters, closures as equations, model-form error and operating regimes out, with intervals The workflow recovers planted physics on every unit of the library, blind v4.0 Scale. Parametric and operator surrogates, 2-D and 3-D units, flowsheets of many units, a GPU backend where the batch justifies it A whole line's what-if study runs interactively v5.0 The autonomous twin. A twin that identifies itself, tests its own misfit, redesigns its measurements, retrains and says when it should not be trusted, unattended It runs for simulated months through drift, faults and recipe changes without a silent failure v6.0 The plant rehearsal. The whole stack against a simulated plant behind real interfaces (OPC UA, MQTT, a historian), with public pilot-scale data wherever it exists Advice in shadow mode is scored against the simulated truth, and the failures are reported

docs.title: v7.0: the plant
docs.text:
Deliberately far out: nothing here starts until v6.0's rehearsal has passed.

  • Live data. OPC UA and MQTT connectors next to the historian adapter; the monitor as a service that runs for weeks, with alarms on the misfit test.
  • Advice with intervals (P25). Setpoint recommendations and cleaning schedules from the controllers, shown in the dashboard with what they are expected to gain and how sure the twin is.
  • Validation on a real line (P26). The simulated-plant results repeated on plant data, with the failures reported.

docs.title: Not planned
docs.text: A hosted service and monetization (until the research results justify it); a custom PDE-builder UI; a general-purpose RL library (the agents come from the libraries that exist; pinnrl supplies the environments, the baselines and the twin); CFD-scale solvers.

docs.title: Training
docs.text:
This page is for anyone who trains a network with pinnrl, from the command line or from Python. It states the loss, lists every option with its packaged default, and gives the workflows as steps.

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = w_r\,\mathcal{L}_r + w_b\,\mathcal{L}_b + w_i\,\mathcal{L}_i + w_d\,\mathcal{L}_d, \qquad \mathcal{L}_r = \frac{1}{N_r}\sum_{j=1}^{N_r} \ell\big(\mathcal{N}[u_\theta](x_j, t_j)\big) \]
  • \(\mathcal{N}[u_\theta]\): the residual of the equation \(\mathcal{N}[u] = 0\) on the network \(u_\theta\).
  • Collocation point: a point \((x_j, t_j)\) inside the domain where the residual is evaluated. A batch holds \(N_r\) of them.
  • \(\mathcal{L}_b\), \(\mathcal{L}_i\), \(\mathcal{L}_d\): the same mean for the boundary-condition error, the initial-condition error and the misfit \(u_\theta - u_\text{obs}\) to the observations. \(\mathcal{L}_d\) is zero when none are attached.
  • \(\ell\): the error's square (mse, the default), its absolute value (mae) or the Huber function (huber).
  • \(w_r, w_b, w_i, w_d\): the loss weights residual, boundary, initial and data.

The mode selects which terms count. The physics terms are \(\mathcal{L}_r\), \(\mathcal{L}_b\) and \(\mathcal{L}_i\).

mode Terms in the loss Trained forward (default) physics terms, plus data if observations are attached \(\theta\) inverse physics terms and data \(\theta\) and the selected parameters of the equation (see Inverse problems) data_augmented physics terms and data \(\theta\) data_only data only \(\theta\)

Outside forward, a data weight of zero or less is replaced by 1.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
pinnrl-train --pde <key> --arch <architecture> [options]

Unset options come from the packaged config.yaml: its training block, the chosen architectures entry, and the PDE's block in pde_configs. Pass --config my.yaml to use your own.

Group Flags Problem --pde (key or display name) or --pde-file (your own equation as YAML, see Custom equations), --arch (feedforward, resnet, fourier, siren, fno, attention, autoencoder), --config, --device (cpu, mps, cuda; falls back to CPU) Budget --epochs, --batch-size, --collocation-points, --boundary-points, --initial-points, --lr Sampling --collocation-distribution (uniform, stratified, residual_based); --rl for the experimental bandit sampler (1-D) Optimizer --optimizer (adam, lbfgs, adam_lbfgs), --lr-scheduler (cosine, reduce_lr), --weight-decay, --gradient-clipping, --early-stopping (on, off) Loss --adaptive-weights (off, lrw, rbw), --loss-function (mse, mae, huber), --huber-delta Mode --mode (forward, inverse, data_only, data_augmented) Engine --derivatives (auto, autograd; native is an old alias of auto), --normalize Inverse --identify NAME (repeatable), --initial-guess NAME=VALUE, --obs-path file.npz, --obs-points, --obs-noise Datasets --dataset NAME, --dataset-split, --dataset-traj, --dataset-points, --dataset-steps, --dataset-seed, --dataset-base

Examples:

# Burgers with residual-based adaptive sampling and Adam followed by L-BFGS
pinnrl-train --pde burgers --arch fourier --epochs 3000 \
  --collocation-distribution residual_based --optimizer adam_lbfgs

# 2-D heat with gradient-balanced loss weights
pinnrl-train --pde heat_2d --arch fourier --adaptive-weights lrw
  • Each run is saved in ./runs/<timestamp>_<PDE display name>_<arch>_<rl|no_rl>/.
  • A Well run has the dataset name in place of the PDE (see Getting started).
  • Early-stopping patience is counted in epochs. Validation runs every validation_frequency epochs.

docs.title: Options and defaults
docs.text:
Defaults are the values of the training block of the packaged config.yaml. The full key list is in the configuration reference.

Budget

Key Flag Default Meaning num_epochs --epochs 3000 Epochs batch_size --batch-size 2048 Collocation points per optimizer step num_collocation_points --collocation-points 5000 Collocation points per epoch num_boundary_points --boundary-points 5000 Points per boundary face num_initial_points --initial-points 5000 Points on the initial condition
  • Epoch: max(1, num_collocation_points // batch_size) optimizer steps on freshly sampled batches. With lbfgs it is one full batch.

Optimizer

Key Flag Default Meaning optimizer --optimizer adam adam, lbfgs, or adam_lbfgs (Adam first, then L-BFGS) adam_lbfgs_switch_ratio none 0.7 Fraction of the epochs spent in the Adam phase optimizer_config.learning_rate --lr 0.005 Learning rate optimizer_config.weight_decay --weight-decay 0.0005 L2 penalty on the network weights (Adam only) gradient_clipping --gradient-clipping 1.0 Largest gradient norm of the network weights; 0 disables it. Not in the file: it is the default of TrainingConfig lbfgs none history_size 50, max_iter 20, line_search_fn strong_wolfe, tolerance_grad 1e-7, tolerance_change 1e-9 Passed to torch.optim.LBFGS
  • L-BFGS runs without gradient clipping, weight decay or adaptive weights.
  • Parameters of the equation that are being identified never receive weight decay.
  • L-BFGS safeguard: a step whose loss is not finite, or more than 10 times the loss before it, is rolled back and the L-BFGS rate is halved. After 3 such steps in a row the trainer returns to Adam.

Learning-rate schedule

Key Flag Default Meaning scheduler_type --lr-scheduler cosine cosine, reduce_lr or constant (constant only through the config) warmup_epochs none 0 Epochs of linear ramp before the schedule starts reduce_lr_params none factor 0.5, patience 50, min_lr 1e-6 The plateau schedule, and the floor of the cosine one
  • cosine runs from learning_rate to min_lr over num_epochs - warmup_epochs.
  • reduce_lr watches the epoch training loss.
  • While L-BFGS runs, any schedule other than constant is replaced by reduce_lr.

Sampler

collocation_distribution Default How points are drawn uniform yes Uniformly at random in the domain stratified no Each axis cut into equal bins with one random sample per bin (Latin-hypercube style) residual_based no RAD, residual-based adaptive distribution (Wu et al., 2023): from a uniform pool of 4 times the batch, with probability \(p \propto \lvert r\rvert^k / \overline{\lvert r\rvert^k} + c\) in the residual \(r\), with \(k = 1\), \(c = 0\) adaptive (--rl) no Experimental bandit on a 16 × 8 grid of \((x, t)\) cells, 1-D equations only; half the points from the policy, half uniform
  • residual_based falls back to uniform when the residual cannot be computed or the weights are not finite.

Loss

Key Flag Default Meaning loss_weights none residual 15, boundary 20, initial 10, data 10 The static weights \(w_r, w_b, w_i, w_d\) adaptive_weights --adaptive-weights off (strategy rbw, alpha 0.7, eps 1e-6, initial_weights [0.3, 0.4, 0.3]) lrw or rbw; replaces \(w_r, w_b, w_i\), never \(w_d\) loss_function --loss-function mse The reduction \(\ell\): mse, mae or huber huber_delta --huber-delta 1.0 Threshold of the Huber function
  • lrw: each physics weight is proportional to the inverse of the running mean of that term's gradient norm, \(w_k \propto 1 / (\bar g_k + \varepsilon)\). A term with zero gradient gets weight 0.
  • rbw: each physics weight is proportional to the running mean of that term's loss.
  • alpha: how much of the running mean is kept at each update. A lower value adapts faster.
  • Adaptive weights sum to 1. The first step uses initial_weights.

Stopping and validation

Key Flag Default Meaning early_stopping --early-stopping enabled true, patience 100, min_delta 1e-7 Stop when the validation loss has not improved by min_delta for patience epochs validation_frequency none 10 Validate, log, check early stopping and checkpoint every N epochs

Engine and normalisation

Option Flag Default Meaning derivatives --derivatives auto auto takes the residual's derivatives from the compiled engine (the C++ kernel pinnrl.native, see The native engine) where it applies and from autograd elsewhere; autograd switches the engine off normalize --normalize off Network inputs mapped from the domain to \([-1, 1]\), outputs scaled by the scales of the equation's spec, loss terms in those units

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
PDETrainer is the only training loop. The CLI, the dashboard, the notebooks and the benchmarks all use it.

from pinnrl.training import PDETrainer

trainer = PDETrainer(model, pde, config=config, device=device)

# Epoch-based, with validation, early stopping, the LR schedule and run files:
history = trainer.train(num_epochs=2000, experiment_dir="runs/my_run")

# Step-based, for studies: fixed steps or a time budget, no I/O
out = trainer.train_steps(num_steps=5000, resample_every=100)
print(out["steps"], out["train_time_s"], out["loss"][-1])

The two loops apply exactly the same update:

train train_steps Unit epochs steps, or a time budget (time_budget_s) Validation, early stopping, schedule, warm-up yes no Run files yes, with experiment_dir no Sampler the configured one the configured one, or sample_fn(model, progress) -> (x, t) Evaluation along the way every validation_frequency epochs checkpoints and on_checkpoint
  • Each train() call plans its own schedule: the learning rate restarts from training.learning_rate, and the cosine period and the adam_lbfgs switch epoch follow that call's num_epochs.
  • trainer.history holds per-epoch entries, including loss_weights when adaptive weighting is on.

docs.title: Time-marching
docs.text:
A network trained on the whole time span at once can settle on a wrong solution with a small residual: a trivial solution close to the initial condition, or a smoothed-out sharp transition. train_windows trains on a growing time window \([t_0, c_k]\) instead, where the last cutoff \(c_k\) is the end of the time domain.

cutoffs = [2.5, 5.0, 10.0]                         # the last one is the end of the time domain
out = trainer.train_windows(cutoffs, steps_per_window=4000, resample_every=50, lbfgs_steps=500)
  1. For each cutoff, it sets pde.time_cutoff, which restricts the collocation samplers, the observations and the sensor records to the window.
  2. It trains steps_per_window steps. The network and the identified unknowns carry over to the next window.
  3. After the last window it resets pde.time_cutoff.
  4. With lbfgs_steps > 0 it finishes with that many L-BFGS steps on the whole span.

Experiment H04 measures what it buys on the systems where one-shot training fails.

docs.title: Restarts
docs.text:
A network that identifies an unknown function from sensor records can fail in ways the loss curve does not show. pinnrl.training.train_with_restarts retrains from a new seed until the fit passes a test it can run without knowing the truth:

\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{k} \left(\frac{H_k[u_\theta] - y_k}{\sigma_k}\right)^2 \le \chi^2_{\text{level}}(n) \]
  • \(y_k\), \(\sigma_k\): a sensor record and its noise standard deviation.
  • \(H_k[u_\theta]\): what the sensor would read on the trained network.
  • \(\chi^2_{\text{level}}(n)\): the level quantile of the chi-square distribution for \(n\) records.

Steps:

  1. Seed, build a trainer with make_trainer(seed), and run train(trainer).
  2. Compute the sensor misfit with pde.sensor_misfit(trainer.model, level).
  3. If it passes, stop. Otherwise start again from seed + 1.
  4. After attempts runs, return the run with the lowest \(\chi^2\); result.accepted says whether it passed.
Argument Default Meaning attempts 3 The most runs to train level 0.999 The chi-square quantile a run must stay under seed 0 The first seed; attempt \(k\) uses seed + k

In J06, 22 of 36 runs collapsed to a constant fouling or stuck at a bound. In J07b, one closure in three left the basin its start had put it in. The misfit test caught every one of those failures. See Process twins.

docs.title: Reloading a run
docs.text:
To reload a finished CLI or dashboard run:

from pinnrl.training.train import load_run

pde, model, config = load_run("runs/20261023_120000_Burgers Equation_fourier_no_rl")
print(pde.validate(model)["l2_error"])

docs.title: Choosing settings
docs.text:
1. Start with feedforward or fourier, Adam at 1e-3, and uniform sampling.
  2. Change one thing at a time.
  3. Watch each loss term, not only the total. Badly scaled terms are the most common silent failure: the boundary or initial loss stalls while the residual drops.
  4. If that happens, try --adaptive-weights lrw, or raise loss_weights.boundary and loss_weights.initial.
  5. On smooth problems, try adam_lbfgs. It usually improves the last digit. It rarely rescues a run that Adam got wrong.
  6. On problems with sharp features, compare residual_based against uniform at the same budget (see Benchmarks). Do not assume it helps.
  7. For an inverse run, set weight_decay=0 and gradient_clipping=0 first (see Inverse problems).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Failure modes the package and its experiments have met. Each has a symptom, a cause and a fix. Experiment codes (F01, J06, ...) name the source of each number; see Benchmarks.

docs.title: The compiled engine is not used
docs.text:
from pinnrl import native
print(native.available(), native.unavailable_reason())

Training still works on autograd, two to eight times slower per step (I17).

Reason printed Fix no C++ compiler found macOS: xcode-select --install. Linux: install g++ compiling jets.cpp failed on Linux apt install libopenblas-dev, or point PINNRL_NATIVE_CXXFLAGS and PINNRL_NATIVE_LDFLAGS at OpenBLAS the native kernels build on macOS (Accelerate) and Linux (OpenBLAS) only None on other platforms; autograd runs
  • available() is true but pde.native_active(model) is false: the network or the problem is outside what the engine covers. See where it does not apply.

docs.title: A pause of a second or two early in a run
docs.text:
• Cause: the step for your equations is compiled once per machine, and takes over at evaluation 32.
  • Fix: none needed; later runs load it from the cache. PINNRL_NATIVE_SPECIALIZE=off skips the build.

docs.title: A stale cache
docs.text:
• Where: ~/.cache/pinnrl/native.
  • Fix: delete the directory. It is always safe; libraries are rebuilt on demand.

docs.title: TheWellNotInstalledError
docs.text: • Fix: pip install 'pinnrl[well]'. The registry works without it; loading a slice does not.

docs.title: The loss falls and the solution is wrong
docs.text:
The residual is not the error. They are linked by a stability constant \(C\):

\[ \lVert u - u_{\text{exact}} \rVert \le C\, \lVert r \rVert . \]
  • Evidence: for heat in \(d = 1 \ldots 5\) the residual stays at 2–7 % while the error grows from 2 % to 44 % (K08).
  • Fix: check against a reference: pde.validate, pinnrl.benchmarks, or pinnrl-benchmark fdm.

docs.title: A system of ODEs collapses to a constant
docs.text:
• Cause: a trivial solution satisfies the residual almost everywhere (K09).
  • Fix: time-marching windows rescue SIR (error 1.0 to 0.1 %, H04). Nothing rescues Lorenz; use the reference solver.

docs.title: adam_lbfgs diverges
docs.text:
• Evidence: an early switch diverged in 3 of 6 runs on Burgers (D01).
  • Fix: leave more of the budget to Adam (adam_lbfgs_switch_ratio, default 0.7), or run L-BFGS as a second train() call.

docs.title: Results vary more between seeds than between methods
docs.text:
• Evidence: on Burgers the error varies six-fold from seed to seed (B01).
  • Fix: compare with paired seeds and equal budgets, as pinnrl-benchmark sampling does.

docs.title: A network with torch.nn.LayerNorm trains on a wrong gradient
docs.text:
• Cause: torch.nn.LayerNorm (PyTorch 2.10) returns a wrong weight gradient for a loss with second derivatives of the network. It is 2–3 % off in norm on heat (I12).
  • Fix: use pinnrl.neural_networks.ExactLayerNorm. Same function, same parameters, same checkpoint keys.

docs.title: Timings are twice those of the benchmarks page
docs.text:
• Cause: a laptop on battery in low power mode runs at about half speed.
  • Fix: run on mains power with nothing else using the processor.

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text:
• Inverse problem: estimating a parameter \(\theta\) of the equation from data.
  • Cramér–Rao bound: the smallest standard deviation any unbiased estimate can have, \(\sigma_\theta \ge \sqrt{(F^{-1})_{\theta\theta}}\).
  • Fisher information \(F = J^\top \Sigma^{-1} J\): how much the data say about \(\theta\), from the sensitivities \(J = \partial u / \partial \theta\) and the noise covariance \(\Sigma\).

docs.title: An identified parameter stalls 1–2 % from the truth
docs.text:
• Cause: weight decay and gradient clipping act as priors on the network, and the parameter absorbs them.
  • Evidence: the heat diffusivity stalled at 1.5–2 % with them; the floor is 0.1–0.2 % without (F01, D01).
  • Fix: weight_decay=0, gradient_clipping=0 (--weight-decay 0 --gradient-clipping 0).

docs.title: The estimate is confidently wrong
docs.text:
• Cause: a PINN returns a number whether or not the data determine it. Field error does not predict parameter error.
  • Evidence: KdV's coefficients come back 18 % and 25 % low where the bound says 0.6 % and 1.4 % (F02). The Burgers viscosity is 2.5–5 times too large (F03).
  • Fix: compare with the bound: pinnrl.analysis.fisher_information. See Inverse problems.

docs.title: Two parameters cannot be told apart
docs.text:
• Cause: some combinations are one unknown for any method.
  • Evidence: on the evaporator, 0.5 K of steam bias reproduces the records of a 30 % fouling error (J04).
  • Fix: read the correlations of \(F\) before training. Fix one of the pair, or add the measurement that separates them (pinnrl.analysis.greedy_design).

docs.title: An unknown function collapses to a constant
docs.text:
• Evidence: the droplet's drying-rate closure does so from a cold start on every seed (J07).
  • Fix:
    1. Constrain it: positive, monotone, an anchor where its value is known.
    2. Start it from a pointwise estimate of the record.
    3. Judge it by the misfit through the reference solver (Process twins).

docs.title: An interval that does not cover
docs.text:
• Coverage: the fraction of repeated data sets whose interval contains the truth. A 90 % interval should cover 90 %.
  • Evidence: ensembles over initializations covered 13 %; a Laplace interval 77 % with a 2 % bias; the swarm's region 90 % (F06).
  • Fix: measure it with pinnrl.uq.coverage before reporting an interval.

docs.title: The twin fails its misfit test
docs.text:
The test runs the fitted model through a reference solver and returns

\[ \chi^2_{\text{red}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\sigma_i^2}, \]

which is near 1 for a fit.

  • Evidence: the PINN twin failed on 22 of 36 runs on the evaporator (J06) and on every run on the counter-current dryer (J13).
  • Fix:
    1. Retry from new seeds: train_with_restarts keeps the run with the best misfit.
    2. If no run passes and the model has a reference solver, use the classical estimator: ExtendedKalmanFilter, MovingHorizonEstimator, or least squares through reference().

docs.title: A filter's interval is too narrow
docs.text:
• Evidence: a model biased by 2.7 % (11 cells where 51 are needed) cut the coverage to 0.33–0.69. A steam record trusted beyond its 0.3 K accuracy cut it to 0.21–0.52 (J06).
  • Fix: refine the grid until the estimate stops moving. Estimate an instrument's offset under its prior.

docs.title: When to use a PINN, and when not to
docs.text: The package's own experiments give a narrower answer than much of the literature. Every figure here is from the benchmarks page or the experiment named next to it.

docs.title: What a PINN is
docs.text:
A network \(u_w(x, t)\) trained to satisfy an equation \(\mathcal{N}[u] = 0\), its conditions and any data:

\[ L(w) = \underbrace{\lVert \mathcal{N}[u_w] \rVert^2}_{\text{residual}} + \lambda_b \underbrace{\lVert u_w - g \rVert^2_{\partial\Omega}}_{\text{boundary}} + \lambda_0 \underbrace{\lVert u_w(\cdot, 0) - u_0 \rVert^2}_{\text{initial}} + \lambda_d \underbrace{\lVert u_w - y \rVert^2_{\text{data}}}_{\text{observations}}. \]
  • PINN: physics-informed neural network; the network is the solution, and the loss \(L\) is the equation.
  • Forward problem: the equation is known, find \(u\).
  • Inverse problem: part of the equation (a parameter \(\theta\), a function) is unknown; find it from data \(y\).
  • Classical solver: finite differences, finite elements, or the method of lines; it solves the forward problem on a grid.
  • Twin: a model of one piece of equipment, fitted to its sensors, that estimates what is not measured.
  • Misfit test: the fitted model run through a reference solver and compared with the records; a reduced \(\chi^2\) near 1 is a fit.

docs.title: Do not use a PINN when
docs.text:
1. The forward problem is well posed and a classical solver exists.

Method on 1-D heat Relative \(L^2\) error Time Explicit finite differences, 101 points (pinnrl-benchmark fdm --pde heat) about \(7 \times 10^{-4}\) about 30 ms PINN, Adam (D01) \(10^{-3}\) 120 s PINN, L-BFGS (D01) \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) 120 s

The classical solver gets a comparable error several thousand times sooner.

2. The model has a cheap, trusted forward solve and you want its states or parameters.

Unit Classical estimator PINN twin Evaporator fouling (J03, J05, J06) an 11-cell extended Kalman filter tracks the drift to 3.5 % in 0.2 s 9–16 % in five minutes; fails to train on 22 of 36 repeated runs Drying-rate closure of a droplet (J07) a monotone closure by shooting through the reference solver: 1.5–1.6 % on every seed in 8–10 s 1.7–2.1 % in six to eight minutes from a good start, one seed in three destroyed; collapses to a constant from a cold start Counter-current dryer (J13) bounded least squares recovers three parameters in 10 s every run rejected by the misfit test (reduced \(\chi^2\) 5–9)

3. You need an interval you can trust and have not checked it. A PINN returns a number for a parameter whether or not the data determine it.

  • On the evaporator the twin's own interval covers the truth 25 % of the time at the 90 % level (J06).
  • On the KdV soliton the data determine the two coefficients to 0.6 % and 1.4 %; the PINN returns them 18 % and 25 % low on every seed (F02, K01).
  • Field error does not predict parameter error.

docs.title: Consider a PINN when
docs.text:
• There is no trusted forward solver for the model, or it is too expensive to iterate. This is the open test on the roadmap: a unit with no method-of-lines form (a droplet size distribution, wall deposition).
  • An unknown function sits inside the equation (a coefficient that drifts, a closure) and you can constrain it to stay physical. A linear drift \(\alpha(t)\) of the heat equation is recovered to 4 % where a scalar model is 32 % off (F09).
  • One network should replace many solves. A parametric surrogate covers a parameter range to 0.2–2 % at a quarter to a half of the cost of five dedicated networks, and then answers in milliseconds (K45).
  • Physics has to be combined with sparse data, or the problem is mesh-free or high-dimensional. Check the error, not the residual: for heat in \(d = 1 \ldots 5\) at a fixed budget the residual stays at 2–7 % while the error grows from 2 % to 44 % (K08).

In every case, run the baseline. The package ships it so that you can:

Question The control in the package Is my forward solution right? pinnrl-benchmark fdm, the reference solutions of pinnrl.benchmarks, checked exact solutions Is my sampler helping? pinnrl-benchmark sampling: paired seeds at equal steps and equal evaluations against uniform Do the data determine this parameter? pinnrl.analysis.fisher_information, sensor_jacobian, greedy_design Is my interval calibrated? pinnrl.uq.coverage over repeated data sets; the swarm's region of equivalence Did my twin fit the records? pde.sensor_misfit, DryingDroplet.record_misfit: the fitted model through a reference solver Would a filter do better? pinnrl.process.ExtendedKalmanFilter, MovingHorizonEstimator, least squares through reference()

docs.title: Who the package is for
docs.text:
• Researchers studying PINN training, sampling or identifiability, who need a fast trainer, reference solutions and multi-seed protocols.
  • Process and control engineers who want to know what their records can determine before buying a sensor or running a campaign.
  • Teachers and students: every exact solution in the package is checked by the test suite against its equation, initial condition and boundary conditions.

docs.title: How pinnrl compares with the alternatives
docs.text:
Best at Choose it over pinnrl when DeepXDE The widest coverage: several backends, complex geometries, operator learning, many worked examples You need a geometry that is not a box, a backend other than PyTorch, or DeepONets NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo (formerly Modulus) Industrial scale on GPUs: 3-D parameterised geometries, neural operators, multi-GPU training The problem is large, three-dimensional and you have accelerators JAX-based PINN code A whole step compiled by XLA, forward and Taylor mode, GPUs, any architecture you can write You need a custom architecture or a GPU and are willing to write the training loop NeuralPDE.jl Symbolic problem definitions inside Julia's SciML ecosystem, with its stiff solvers You work in Julia pinnrl The fastest step on a CPU for small tanh networks; identifiability, calibration and misfit tools for inverse problems; process units with classical estimators You want to know whether a PINN is the right tool for your inverse problem, and how far to trust its answer

pinnrl is narrower than the first two: box domains, small networks, PyTorch on a CPU. It runs on Apple and CUDA GPUs through autograd, without the compiled step.

On speed. The same training step is timed in every framework in experiment I17. It is one step on a CPU with a small network. It says nothing about large networks on a GPU, and it measures a step, not error at equal time.

What the others do that pinnrl does not:

  • geometries that are not boxes;
  • neural operators (DeepONet, FNO at scale);
  • multi-GPU training;
  • backends other than PyTorch.

If your problem needs one of these, use the tool that has it.

What pinnrl adds:

  1. A training step generated and compiled per equation (the engine).
  2. For an inverse problem: the bound the data allow, the floor the network adds, a measured interval and a misfit test (inverse problems, theory).
  3. Process units that ship with the estimators a PINN has to beat (process twins).

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text: Conditioning and identifiability diagnostics for identified parameters (pinnrl.analysis). Two questions are kept apart: how well the data determine the parameters (sensitivities, Fisher information, the Cramér–Rao bound; exact from a closed form or from the trained surrogate by the implicit-function theorem) and how well-conditioned training is (loss-Hessian and tangent-kernel spectra).

docs.title: exact_sensitivities
docs.text:
exact_sensitivities(
    pde, parameters, x, t=None, values=None
)

du/dtheta of a closed-form solution at (x, t), shape (N, k, p).

The compiled expression is evaluated with a per-point copy of each parameter that requires grad, so the derivative comes from autograd and works for every function the expression language accepts (abs, heaviside, sigmoid, ...). It is computed in double precision.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pde Any

A CustomPDE with an expression-valued exact_solution.

required parameters Sequence[str]

Names of the parameters to differentiate with respect to.

required x Tensor

Spatial coordinates, (N, d).

required t Tensor | None

Time, (N, 1); None for a steady problem.

None values dict[str, float] | None

Parameter values to evaluate at; defaults to the PDE's true values (pde.parameters), not the current trainable guesses.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the PDE has no expression-valued exact solution, or a name is not one of its parameters.

Source code in pinnrl/analysis/sensitivity.py 
def exact_sensitivities(
    pde: Any,
    parameters: Sequence[str],
    x: torch.Tensor,
    t: torch.Tensor | None = None,
    values: dict[str, float] | None = None,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """``du/dtheta`` of a closed-form solution at ``(x, t)``, shape ``(N, k, p)``.

    The compiled expression is evaluated with a per-point copy of each
    parameter that requires grad, so the derivative comes from autograd and
    works for every function the expression language accepts (``abs``,
    ``heaviside``, ``sigmoid``, ...). It is computed in double precision.

    Args:
        pde: A ``CustomPDE`` with an expression-valued ``exact_solution``.
        parameters: Names of the parameters to differentiate with respect to.
        x: Spatial coordinates, ``(N, d)``.
        t: Time, ``(N, 1)``; ``None`` for a steady problem.
        values: Parameter values to evaluate at; defaults to the PDE's true
            values (``pde.parameters``), not the current trainable guesses.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the PDE has no expression-valued exact solution, or a
            name is not one of its parameters.
    """
    compiled = getattr(pde, "_exact", None)
    if not compiled:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{pde.config.name}: exact_sensitivities needs an expression-valued exact_solution"
        )
    unknown = [p for p in parameters if p not in pde.parameters]
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{unknown} are not parameters of {pde.config.name}: {list(pde.parameters)}"
        )
    params = dict(pde.parameters)
    params.update(values or {})
    n = x.shape[0]
    like = torch.ones(n, 1, dtype=torch.float64)
    inputs: dict[str, Any] = {}
    for i, c in enumerate(pde.spatial_coordinates):
        inputs[c] = x[:, i : i + 1].detach().double()
    if t is not None:
        inputs["t"] = t.detach().double()
    # Per-point copies of the parameters to differentiate; the others are constants.
    thetas = {
        name: torch.full((n, 1), float(params[name]), dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
        for name in parameters
    }
    constants = {name: float(v) for name, v in params.items() if name not in thetas}
    columns = []
    for field in pde.fields:
        expr = compiled.get(field)
        if expr is None:
            columns.append(torch.zeros(n, len(parameters), dtype=torch.float64))
            continue
        u = expr({**constants, **thetas, **inputs}, like)
        per_param = []
        for name in parameters:
            if name not in expr.parameters:
                per_param.append(torch.zeros(n, dtype=torch.float64))
                continue
            (g,) = torch.autograd.grad(u.sum(), thetas[name], retain_graph=True, allow_unused=True)
            per_param.append(
                g.reshape(-1) if g is not None else torch.zeros(n, dtype=torch.float64)
            )
        columns.append(torch.stack(per_param, dim=-1))  # (N, p)
    return torch.stack(columns, dim=1).to(x.dtype)  # (N, k, p)

docs.title: fisher_information
docs.text:
fisher_information(
    jacobian, sigma, parameters, rank_tol=None
)

Fisher information J^T Sigma^{-1} J for Gaussian noise and its Cramér–Rao bound.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default jacobian Tensor

Sensitivities, (N, p) or (N, k, p) (flattened over k).

required sigma float | Tensor

Noise standard deviation: a scalar, one value per observation point (N,), one per field (k,) or one per entry (N, k).

required parameters Sequence[str]

Names for the p axis.

required rank_tol float | None

Eigenvalues of F at or below rank_tol * lambda_max count as zero (default: p times the double-precision epsilon).

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If sigma has none of the accepted shapes.

Source code in pinnrl/analysis/sensitivity.py 
def fisher_information(
    jacobian: torch.Tensor,
    sigma: float | torch.Tensor,
    parameters: Sequence[str],
    rank_tol: float | None = None,
) -> FisherSummary:
    """Fisher information ``J^T Sigma^{-1} J`` for Gaussian noise and its Cramér–Rao bound.

    Args:
        jacobian: Sensitivities, ``(N, p)`` or ``(N, k, p)`` (flattened over ``k``).
        sigma: Noise standard deviation: a scalar, one value per observation
            point ``(N,)``, one per field ``(k,)`` or one per entry ``(N, k)``.
        parameters: Names for the ``p`` axis.
        rank_tol: Eigenvalues of ``F`` at or below ``rank_tol * lambda_max``
            count as zero (default: ``p`` times the double-precision epsilon).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``sigma`` has none of the accepted shapes.
    """
    if jacobian.dim() == 2:
        jacobian = jacobian[:, None, :]
    n, k, p = jacobian.shape
    J = jacobian.reshape(n * k, p).double()
    if isinstance(sigma, torch.Tensor):
        s = sigma.double()
        if s.numel() == 1:
            s = s.reshape(1).expand(n * k)
        elif tuple(s.shape) == (n, k):
            s = s.reshape(-1)
        elif tuple(s.shape) == (n,):
            s = s.repeat_interleave(k)
        elif tuple(s.shape) == (k,):
            s = s.repeat(n)
        else:
            raise ValueError(
                f"sigma must be a scalar or have shape ({n},), ({k},) or ({n}, {k}); "
                f"got {tuple(s.shape)}"
            )
        Jw = J / s[:, None]
    else:
        Jw = J / float(sigma)
    F = Jw.T @ Jw
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = torch.linalg.eigh(F)
    order = torch.argsort(eigenvalues, descending=True)
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigenvalues[order], eigenvectors[:, order]
    lam_max = float(eigenvalues[0]) if p else 0.0
    rel_tol = rank_tol if rank_tol is not None else p * torch.finfo(torch.float64).eps
    tol = rel_tol * lam_max
    keep = eigenvalues > tol
    inv = torch.where(keep, 1.0 / eigenvalues.clamp_min(1e-300), torch.zeros_like(eigenvalues))
    cov = eigenvectors @ torch.diag(inv) @ eigenvectors.T
    null = eigenvectors[:, ~keep]
    if null.shape[1]:
        identifiable = (null**2).sum(dim=1) <= 1e-12
    else:
        identifiable = torch.ones(p, dtype=torch.bool)
    std = cov.diagonal().clamp_min(0).sqrt()
    std = torch.where(identifiable, std, torch.full_like(std, math.inf))
    cov = cov.clone()
    cov.diagonal()[~identifiable] = math.inf
    denom = std[:, None] * std[None, :]
    corr = cov / denom
    corr[~torch.isfinite(denom)] = math.nan
    corr.diagonal()[identifiable] = 1.0
    smallest = float(eigenvalues[-1]) if p else 0.0
    cond = lam_max / smallest if smallest > tol and smallest > 0 else math.inf
    return FisherSummary(
        parameters=tuple(parameters),
        information=F,
        covariance=cov,
        std=std,
        correlation=corr,
        identifiable=identifiable,
        eigenvalues=eigenvalues,
        eigenvectors=eigenvectors,
        condition_number=cond,
    )

docs.title: closed_form_bound
docs.text:
closed_form_bound(pde, parameters, x, t, sigma)

The Cramér–Rao bound for parameters from observations at (x, t) with noise sigma.

A convenience around :func:exact_sensitivities and :func:fisher_information.

Source code in pinnrl/analysis/sensitivity.py 
def closed_form_bound(
    pde: Any,
    parameters: Sequence[str],
    x: torch.Tensor,
    t: torch.Tensor | None,
    sigma: float | torch.Tensor,
) -> FisherSummary:
    """The Cramér–Rao bound for ``parameters`` from observations at ``(x, t)`` with noise ``sigma``.

    A convenience around :func:`exact_sensitivities` and :func:`fisher_information`.
    """
    J = exact_sensitivities(pde, parameters, x, t)
    return fisher_information(J, sigma, parameters)

docs.title: FisherSummary dataclass
docs.text:
FisherSummary(
    parameters,
    information,
    covariance,
    std,
    correlation,
    identifiable,
    eigenvalues,
    eigenvectors,
    condition_number,
)

Fisher information for a parameter set and what it implies.

Attributes:

Name Type Description parameters tuple[str, ...]

Parameter names, in the order of every matrix axis.

information Tensor

The Fisher matrix F, shape (p, p).

covariance Tensor

The Cramér–Rao bound F^{-1} on the identifiable subspace; inf on the diagonal of a parameter with a component in the null space of F.

std Tensor

Lower bound on the standard deviation of each parameter (inf when the parameter is not identifiable from these observations).

correlation Tensor

Correlation matrix of the bound (nan where undefined).

identifiable Tensor

Per parameter, whether it lies outside the null space of F.

eigenvalues Tensor

Eigenvalues of F, descending.

eigenvectors Tensor

Columns are the corresponding parameter directions.

condition_number float

Ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue (inf when F is singular).

std / |true value| per parameter (inf when not identifiable).

Source code in pinnrl/analysis/sensitivity.py 
def relative_std(self, true_values: dict[str, float]) -> dict[str, float]:
    """``std / |true value|`` per parameter (``inf`` when not identifiable)."""
    return {
        name: float(self.std[i]) / abs(float(true_values[name]))
        for i, name in enumerate(self.parameters)
    }

docs.title: surrogate_sensitivities
docs.text:
surrogate_sensitivities(
    pde,
    model,
    parameters,
    x,
    t,
    *,
    n_collocation=2048,
    damping=0.001,
    cg_iterations=300,
    cg_tol=1e-05,
    seed=0,
)

du/dtheta at (x, t) from the trained surrogate, by the implicit-function theorem.

Pass the same pde the model was trained with: the Hessian is taken of that object's physics loss (its loss weights, boundary and initial point counts, loss function and device), at the current values of its parameters. Parameters that are not registered as trainable are made trainable for the duration of the call, so a forward-trained problem works as it is.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pde Any

The problem the model was trained on.

required model Module

The trained network, a minimum of the physics loss for the parameters' current values.

required parameters Sequence[str]

Names of the PDE parameters to differentiate with respect to.

required x Tensor

Spatial coordinates of the observation points, (N, d).

required t Tensor | None

Time, (N, 1); None for a steady problem (the network then receives t = 0, as the trainer does).

required n_collocation int

Collocation points on which the Hessian is evaluated.

2048 damping float

Tikhonov damping lambda added to H_ww (the Hessian of a trained network is singular along flat directions). When the damped Hessian still shows negative curvature, which happens when the network is not at an exact minimum, the solve restarts with ten times the damping, up to six times.

0.001 cg_iterations int

Maximum conjugate-gradient iterations per parameter.

300 cg_tol float

Relative residual at which the solve stops.

1e-05 seed int

Seed of the collocation sample (drawn in a forked RNG, so the caller's random state is untouched).

0

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a name is not a parameter of pde, or a solve diverges.

Source code in pinnrl/analysis/surrogate.py 
def surrogate_sensitivities(
    pde: Any,
    model: torch.nn.Module,
    parameters: Sequence[str],
    x: torch.Tensor,
    t: torch.Tensor | None,
    *,
    n_collocation: int = 2048,
    damping: float = 1e-3,
    cg_iterations: int = 300,
    cg_tol: float = 1e-5,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> SurrogateSensitivity:
    """``du/dtheta`` at ``(x, t)`` from the trained surrogate, by the implicit-function theorem.

    Pass the same ``pde`` the model was trained with: the Hessian is taken of
    that object's physics loss (its loss weights, boundary and initial point
    counts, loss function and device), at the current values of its
    parameters. Parameters that are not registered as trainable are made
    trainable for the duration of the call, so a forward-trained problem works
    as it is.

    Args:
        pde: The problem the model was trained on.
        model: The trained network, a minimum of the physics loss for the
            parameters' current values.
        parameters: Names of the PDE parameters to differentiate with respect to.
        x: Spatial coordinates of the observation points, ``(N, d)``.
        t: Time, ``(N, 1)``; ``None`` for a steady problem (the network then
            receives ``t = 0``, as the trainer does).
        n_collocation: Collocation points on which the Hessian is evaluated.
        damping: Tikhonov damping ``lambda`` added to ``H_ww`` (the Hessian of
            a trained network is singular along flat directions). When the
            damped Hessian still shows negative curvature, which happens when
            the network is not at an exact minimum, the solve restarts with
            ten times the damping, up to six times.
        cg_iterations: Maximum conjugate-gradient iterations per parameter.
        cg_tol: Relative residual at which the solve stops.
        seed: Seed of the collocation sample (drawn in a forked RNG, so the
            caller's random state is untouched).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a name is not a parameter of ``pde``, or a solve diverges.
    """
    unknown = [p for p in parameters if p not in getattr(pde, "parameters", {})]
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"{unknown} are not parameters of {pde.config.name}")
    device = next(model.parameters()).device
    was_training = model.training
    model.eval()
    try:
        with _temporarily_trainable(pde, parameters) as thetas:
            result = _sensitivities(
                pde,
                model,
                parameters,
                thetas,
                x,
                t,
                device,
                n_collocation,
                damping,
                cg_iterations,
                cg_tol,
                seed,
            )
    finally:
        if was_training:
            model.train()
    return result

loss_hessian_spectrum(
    loss_fn, parameters, iterations=50, seed=0
)

Extreme eigenvalues of d^2 loss / d parameters^2 by Lanczos with full reorthogonalization.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default loss_fn Callable[[], Tensor]

Returns the scalar loss as a function of parameters (it is called once; the graph is kept for Hessian-vector products).

required parameters list[Parameter]

The tensors to differentiate with respect to.

required iterations int

Lanczos steps, hence the number of Ritz values. With 50 steps the few largest and smallest eigenvalues are converged to several digits for typical PINN Hessians.

50 seed int

0 Source code in pinnrl/analysis/spectrum.py 
def loss_hessian_spectrum(
    loss_fn: Callable[[], torch.Tensor],
    parameters: list[torch.nn.Parameter],
    iterations: int = 50,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> HessianSpectrum:
    """Extreme eigenvalues of ``d^2 loss / d parameters^2`` by Lanczos with full reorthogonalization.

    Args:
        loss_fn: Returns the scalar loss as a function of ``parameters`` (it is
            called once; the graph is kept for Hessian-vector products).
        parameters: The tensors to differentiate with respect to.
        iterations: Lanczos steps, hence the number of Ritz values. With 50
            steps the few largest and smallest eigenvalues are converged to
            several digits for typical PINN Hessians.
        seed: Seed of the starting vector (a forked RNG, so the caller's state
            is untouched).
    """
    loss = loss_fn()
    grads = torch.autograd.grad(loss, parameters, create_graph=True, allow_unused=True)
    flat_g = torch.cat(
        [
            (g if g is not None else torch.zeros_like(p)).reshape(-1)
            for g, p in zip(grads, parameters, strict=True)
        ]
    )

    def hvp(v: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        hv = torch.autograd.grad(flat_g @ v, parameters, retain_graph=True, allow_unused=True)
        return torch.cat(
            [
                (h if h is not None else torch.zeros_like(p)).reshape(-1)
                for h, p in zip(hv, parameters, strict=True)
            ]
        )

    n = flat_g.numel()
    m = min(iterations, n)
    with torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[]):
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        q = torch.randn(n, device=flat_g.device, dtype=flat_g.dtype)
    q = q / q.norm()
    Q = [q]
    alphas: list[float] = []
    betas: list[float] = []
    for k in range(m):
        z = hvp(Q[k]).detach()
        alpha = float(Q[k] @ z)
        z = z - alpha * Q[k] - (betas[-1] * Q[k - 1] if k else 0.0)
        # Full reorthogonalization keeps the Ritz values honest at this size.
        for qq in Q:
            z = z - (qq @ z) * qq
        beta = float(z.norm())
        alphas.append(alpha)
        if beta < 1e-10 or k == m - 1:
            break
        betas.append(beta)
        Q.append(z / beta)
    T = torch.diag(torch.tensor(alphas, dtype=torch.float64))
    if betas:
        off = torch.tensor(betas[: len(alphas) - 1], dtype=torch.float64)
        T += torch.diag(off, 1) + torch.diag(off, -1)
    ritz = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(T).flip(0)
    return HessianSpectrum(eigenvalues=ritz, iterations=len(alphas), loss=float(loss.detach()))
